item.title: Tools Need Not Speak in Text: Latent Context Compression for Agents
item.description:
Paper

Long tool observations make agents slow and blur their judgment

The longer tool observations get, the more the context costs to compute and the more judgment wavers. This paper proposes compressing tool results not into text but into continuous vectors, keeping only the information the agent needs to decide its next action. The code is released at https://github.com/THU-Agent/Coca-cola .

1. Terms to read first

Term Meaning Why it matters
context All tokens the model has received as input so far, concatenated The agent chooses its next action from the context alone. The longer it is, the more compute it costs, and irrelevant content creeps in and blurs judgment.
tool observation The result a tool call returns (e.g., web search results) The length of the raw observation determines the context cost.
latent token A single continuous vector in embedding space, not text A candidate for packing more information into the same number of input slots.
compression rate (Comp_rate) The reduction ratio of total tokens (input+output) before and after compression It gives a single number for comparing “how much was cut.”
EM / F1 Exact match rate / token-level partial match rate They show together whether the answer was exactly right or only partially right.
KL divergence / cross entropy Difference between two action distributions / probability loss on the correct action token The loss that trains the compressor so the latent representation produces “the same action as seeing the raw text.”
LoRA A method that trains only a few added weights while keeping a large model frozen Needed to train only the compressor without touching the agent backbone.

In this paper, Coca-Cola (Context Compression via Continuous Latent Tokens) is a compressor that turns tool observations into latent tokens, and it does not touch the agent backbone.

2. Problem: context gets eaten by observations

The agent operates in a ReAct fashion. Given a question, it reasons, calls a tool, appends the returned observation to the context, and reasons again. Each step adds reasoning text, tool calls, and observations to the context, so the context length after the t-th call is roughly

$$K_t \approx |q| + \sum_{i=1}^{t}\bigl(|r_i| + |a_i| + |o_i|\bigr)$$

Here $|q|$ is the question length, $|r_i|$ the reasoning, $|a_i|$ the tool call, and $|o_i|$ the number of observation tokens. Because search returns several document chunks whole, it is the accumulated observations that grow long.

The result is Fig. 1 (left). In a web search agent that ran up to 4 steps, tool results accounted for 96.7% of all tokens. A single observation is long as well (median 1,352 tokens, p90 1,776, p95 1,861).

The cost splits two ways: computation, and a drop in accuracy. The question in Fig. 1 (right) is “the birth year of the winner of the 2016 Marrakesh ePrix.” A single line in the search results confirming that the winner is Sébastien Buemi is enough to fix the next search (“Sébastien Buemi birth date”). Yet the same results are stuffed with details such as track length, lap count, pole position, and fastest lap, and the model has to read this irrelevant content too.

3. A small example: what is kept and what is discarded

The observation lengths and latent token counts in the table below come from the paper; the remaining items are organized here for understanding.

Step Input Retained state What changes or drops Output
① Search call question q = “What year was the winner of the 2016 Marrakesh ePrix born?” q — query “winner of the 2016 Marrakesh ePrix”
② Observation arrives observation o_t = long search results (median 1,352 tokens) q, reasoning trace r_t = “winner confirmed as Buemi” Vanilla appends the entire raw o_t to the context (racing details included) Vanilla: reads o_t and picks out only the winner’s name
③ Vanilla continues [q ; r_t ; o_t] q, r_t, o_t none next search “Sébastien Buemi birth date” — the evidence is buried in 1,352 tokens
④ Coca-Cola continues [q ; r_t ; o_t] (same) q, r_t, and z_t = 128 latent tokens the raw o_t does not enter the context the agent reads only z_t and chooses the next search or the final answer

The key is the difference in the last line of ③ and ④. The raw text is not reconstructed. Latent tokens do not need to be readable by humans, so a single token is not constrained to “picking one symbol from a vocabulary list.”

4. Where existing approaches get stuck

There are two families of methods for shrinking observations. Token pruning selects and deletes less useful tokens (LLMLingua, LLMLingua-2, LongLLMLingua). Text summarization uses an auxiliary LLM to turn observations or dialogue history into a short summary (RECOMP, Search-o1, ACON).

The shared ceiling of both is that the output is still a “human-readable sequence of discrete tokens.” Because it has to form sentences, there is a structural limit on how much can be cut. What sets Coca-Cola apart is that it removes this constraint entirely.

The paper quantifies this difference in terms of capacity. Capacity is defined as the log of the number of distinguishable codewords. With vocabulary size $|\mathcal V|$, n text tokens give at most $|\mathcal V|^n$ possibilities, so

$$\mathcal{C}_{\text{text}}(n) = n\log_2|\mathcal V|$$

By contrast, for m latent tokens of dimension d, assuming each token has $d_{\text{eff}} \le d$ effective coordinates and each coordinate carries a value distinguishable at finite precision B,

$$\mathcal{C}_{\text{latent}}(m) = m\,d_{\text{eff}}\log_2 B$$

bits. That is, if $d_{\text{eff}}\log_2 B > \log_2|\mathcal V|$, the latent representation has larger capacity at the same number of input slots. The paper, however, adds its own caveat. This is a maximum capacity calculation under the assumption that “all coordinate combinations are realizable and distinguishable at finite precision,” and the authors state that the amount of information actually usable depends on the encoding ability of the compressor and the utilization ability of the agent.

5. Method: turning an observation into a few vectors

At the end of every tool call, Coca-Cola takes three inputs and turns them into a fixed number of latent tokens: the question q, the reasoning trace of the current step r_t, and the tool observation o_t. The architecture solves two difficulties in order.

First, make the compression result something the agent can actually read. The agent accepts tokens by turning them into input embeddings, and the vectors the compressor produces do not belong to that space. So the architecture splits into two parts.

  • Context-aware encoder $C_\theta$: a small language model that reads q, r_t, and o_t together and produces a hidden state. $H_t = C_\theta(q, r_t, o_t)$. The reason for not looking at the observation alone is that which part of the observation is needed depends on the question and the current reasoning state.
  • Latent adapter $A_\phi$: converts the hidden state into $m$ vectors matched to the agent’s embedding dimension. $z_t = A_\phi(H_t) \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times d}$.

These vectors are wrapped in special boundary tokens and inserted into the agent’s input embedding sequence.

$$X_t = \bigl[E_\psi(q, h_t);\ E_\psi(\langle \text{latent\_obs}\rangle);\ z_t;\ E_\psi(\langle /\text{latent\_obs}\rangle)\bigr]$$

Second, keep only the information needed for decision-making within a limited number of slots. Here the authors exploit in training the fact that the goal is not “reconstructing the raw text.” With the agent frozen, they extract the next-action distribution for the same question twice: once with the raw text and once with the latent tokens.

$$p_{\text{full}} = p_\psi(\cdot \mid q, h_t, o_t), \qquad p_{\text{latent}} = p_\psi(\cdot \mid q, h_t, z_t)$$

Matching the two distributions is Action-Preserving Training, and the loss is the sum of two terms.

$$\mathcal{L} = \lambda_{\mathrm{KL}}\,D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{\text{full}} \Vert p_{\text{latent}}) + \lambda_{\mathrm{CE}}\,\mathrm{CE}(y_{t+1},\,p_{\text{latent}})$$

The KL term reduces the difference between “the action chosen when seeing the raw text” and “the action chosen when seeing only the latent tokens,” and the cross-entropy term is an auxiliary loss that fits the actually recorded next-action token. Because the latent tokens are continuous vectors and thus differentiable, gradients flow back through the frozen agent into the compressor. $\nabla_{\theta,\phi}\mathcal{L} = \left(\partial z_t/\partial(\theta,\phi)\right)^{\top}\nabla_{z_t}\mathcal{L}$. Only the encoder’s LoRA parameters and the adapter are updated.

The training setup in Appendix A is as follows. From 4,188 tasks they built 4,363 (observation, action) pairs, held out 10% for validation, and trained on 3,927 pairs. LoRA rank 16, scaling factor 32, dropout 0.05, 8-bit AdamW (paged), learning rate linearly decayed from 1.5×10⁻⁴ to 5×10⁻⁵, $\lambda_{\mathrm{KL}}=0.3$, $\lambda_{\mathrm{CE}}=1.0$, with the KL weight warmed up over the first 20% of training steps.

At inference time, the raw observation is replaced by latent tokens at every tool call, and the agent sees only those vectors. Each observation is compressed into 128 continuous vectors, and web search was limited to at most 5 results per call and at most 5 calls per task.

The full flow, showing what goes where, is as follows.

 flowchart TD
 A["Context: question q + reasoning trace h_t + raw observation o_t"] --> B["C_θ context-aware encoder<br/>reads q, r_t, o_t together<br/>trains LoRA only"]
 B --> C["H_t : hidden state conditioned on the question and reasoning state"]
 C --> D["A_φ latent adapter<br/>maps H_t to m=128 vectors"]
 D --> E["z_t : 128 x d continuous vectors<br/>d = agent input embedding dimension"]
 E --> F["Context: q + h_t + special boundary tokens + z_t"]
 F --> G["Frozen agent generates the next action"]
 A -.->|"raw o_t is not passed along this path"| H["Discarded tokens: raw observation"]

In the figure, each value means the following. h_t is the trace prefix made of the reasoning, calls, and observations so far, m=128 is the number of latent vectors, and d is the input embedding dimension of the target agent. What the arrows carry is the state compressed from q, r_t, o_t into H_t, then compressed again into z_t. The diagonal dotted line is the discarded path: the raw observation does not cross over to the agent. In other words, the compute that shrinks is the “observation tokens” the agent must read at every step, while the compressor itself is newly added compute.

6. Experimental setup

The evaluation was conducted on a web search agent. The two model pairs are Qwen3.5-35B-A3B + Qwen3.5-4B and GLM-4.7-Flash + GLM-Z1-9B, and the benchmarks are two single-hop (NQ, TriviaQA) and two multi-hop (2Wiki, HotpotQA).

There are four baselines. Vanilla (uses the raw text as is), LongLLMLingua (token pruning), LLMSummary (text summarization), and ICAE (the same architecture with only the training objective changed to raw-text reconstruction). Because the authors did not build search-specific designs into Coca-Cola, they argue it can be applied to other tools without architectural changes.

The metrics are accuracy (EM, F1) and system efficiency (average input tokens, output tokens, compression rate, end-to-end runtime), with the compression rate defined as

$$\text{Comp\_rate} = 1 - \frac{I_{\text{latent}} + O_{\text{latent}}}{I_{\text{raw}} + O_{\text{raw}}}$$

Because it sums input and output, the compression rate comes out slightly smaller than the reduction rate seen for input tokens alone. This is why NQ+Qwen cuts input tokens by 87.7% but has a compression rate of 85.78%.

7. Results

7.1 Tokens and runtime

Qwen pair (Table 1):

Dataset Vanilla input/output tokens Coca-Cola input/output tokens Compression rate Vanilla time (s) Coca-Cola time (s) Time reduction
NQ 14,362 / 993 1,767 / 418 85.78% 96.19 64.64 32.8%
TriviaQA 10,023 / 779 1,413 / 349 83.68% 73.30 55.38 24.4%
2Wiki 37,427 / 1,510 10,745 / 933 70.01% 164.99 119.91 27.3%
HotpotQA 42,724 / 1,560 9,429 / 831 76.83% 161.39 120.88 25.1%

GLM pair (Table 2):

Dataset Vanilla input/output tokens Coca-Cola input/output tokens Compression rate Vanilla time (s) Coca-Cola time (s) Time reduction
NQ 17,389 / 888 4,265 / 536 73.73% 89.29 42.17 52.8%
TriviaQA 11,177 / 739 2,595 / 413 74.75% 91.36 41.97 54.1%
2Wiki 31,693 / 976 3,003 / 511 89.24% 106.37 46.83 56.0%
HotpotQA 28,782 / 834 4,041 / 610 84.30% 84.55 49.37 41.6%

Two levels must be distinguished here. Token savings (70.01%–89.24%) and runtime savings (24.45%–55.97%) differ in magnitude. The paper does not directly explain why time does not fall as much as the compression rate (not reported in the original). Our inference is that running the compressor (encoder and adapter) at every step accounts for part of it. There is also no separately reported runtime for the compressor alone, nor a reason for the larger savings in the GLM pair (not reported in the original).

Still, runtime was shorter than Vanilla in every setting, by 24.45%–32.80% for the Qwen pair and 41.61%–55.97% for the GLM pair.

7.2 Accuracy does not drop

Reducing Table 3 to Vanilla and Coca-Cola only:

Model pair Dataset Vanilla EM / F1 Coca-Cola EM / F1
Qwen NQ 23.67 / 33.17 24.78 / 37.33
Qwen TriviaQA 56.10 / 62.87 59.20 / 67.07
Qwen 2Wiki 17.30 / 26.94 24.00 / 32.34
Qwen HotpotQA 11.00 / 16.41 25.70 / 33.75
GLM NQ 21.50 / 26.08 23.50 / 31.45
GLM TriviaQA 41.50 / 44.57 51.50 / 59.41
GLM 2Wiki 26.50 / 31.29 28.00 / 36.20
GLM HotpotQA 20.50 / 25.89 23.50 / 30.76

Coca-Cola has higher EM and F1 than Vanilla in all eight settings. It produced the best score in 13 of 16 dataset-metric pairs, and took both EM and F1 in six of the eight model-dataset combinations, including all four GLM combinations. Even with compression of up to 89.24%, answers improved. The authors interpret this as “filtering out irrelevant content in long observations can mitigate the attention dilution problem.” The largest gain is Qwen HotpotQA, where EM jumps from 11.00 to 25.70 and F1 from 16.41 to 33.75.

Against the baselines, two patterns appear.

  • ICAE (same architecture, with only the training objective changed to reconstruction) loses to Coca-Cola on compression rate. Coca-Cola is higher in all eight settings (2Wiki+GLM: 89.24% vs 74.12%). ICAE also trailed in all four GLM settings on accuracy. The exception is Qwen+TriviaQA, where ICAE scored EM 61.80 / F1 69.27, higher than Coca-Cola (59.20 / 67.07). ICAE’s compression rate, however, is 66.92%, far below Coca-Cola’s 83.68%.
  • LLMSummary had slightly higher compression rates in three settings: 2Wiki+Qwen (71.30% vs 70.01%), HotpotQA+Qwen (78.90% vs 76.83%), and NQ+GLM (74.62% vs 73.73%). But in all three, EM and F1 were lower than Coca-Cola’s (NQ+GLM: EM 16.00% vs 23.50%). Also, on Qwen+2Wiki, LongLLMLingua’s F1 of 34.25 edged out Coca-Cola (32.34), while its compression rate was 41.96% vs 70.01%.

The point of this comparison is that the criterion for “what to keep,” rather than “how much to cut,” is what preserves accuracy.

7.3 What drives performance

Number of latent tokens m (Fig. 3, NQ+GLM). As m increases from 8 to 128, F1 keeps rising: 26.34 → 27.79 → 28.81 → 29.96 → 31.45. The compression rate fluctuates between 78.83% and 82.56% for m ≤ 64 (81.27 / 82.56 / 78.83 / 80.99) and then falls to 73.73% at m = 128. The authors set the default to 128 because preliminary experiments showed it to be the best efficiency-performance trade-off. Within the tested range F1 is still rising, so whether another trade-off point is possible has not been tested further (not reported in the original).

Conditioning inputs (Table 4, NQ+GLM, m = 128).

Condition EM (%) Compression rate (%)
Full: q, r_t, o_t 23.50 73.73
w/o Reasoning State: q, o_t 21.45 80.43
w/o Task Goal: r_t, o_t 20.02 78.38
Observation-only: o_t 18.34 79.94

Removing the reasoning state drops EM by 2.05 points, removing the question (task goal) drops it by 3.48 points, and removing both drops it by 5.16 points. This means “the observation alone cannot determine the information needed for decision-making.” The reason the drop is smaller when the reasoning state is removed, the authors explain, is that in single-hop NQ the current subgoal almost overlaps with the original question. The ablated versions actually have higher compression rates, 78.38%–80.43%, but they lose EM in exchange. The interesting part is the bottom row: the observation-only version, with all conditioning inputs removed, still beats the compression baselines’ best on NQ+GLM with EM 18.34% (best 17.00%) and compression rate 79.94% (best 74.62%), ICAE included. The paper’s interpretation is that even without conditioning, action-preserving training is what beat the baselines.

7.4 Case study: where latent tokens change the judgment

The question in HotpotQA #377 is “Jens Risom introduced what type of design, characterized by minimalism and functionality?” Both approaches issued the same first search and received 5 URLs, sharing 3 of them.

  • Vanilla: Rank 1 is ABT Modern ("… played a pivotal role in shaping Mid-Century Modern furniture design") and Rank 3 is Chairish (“one of the first designers to introduce Scandinavian design to the United States”). Unable to tell the two apart, it took Mid-Century Modern as the answer, and a confirming search did not change it.
  • Coca-Cola: Chairish is at Rank 1 and ABT Modern at Rank 2. By keeping the evidence directly tied to the question (Scandinavian design) in the front, it reached the correct answer (Scandinavian design) with fewer searches.

In other words, compression does not carry “more” information; it keeps “what will be used for the next decision.”

8. Limitations and when to apply it

First, the constraints the authors state directly or that emerge from the experimental design.

  • The validation scope is limited to web search QA. The authors argue that “there are no search-specific designs, so it can be applied to other tools without architectural changes,” but the actual experiments cover only four QA benchmarks on a web search agent. Whether the same gains appear with other tools such as code execution or API calls was not measured (not reported in the original).
  • The information capacity analysis is only an upper bound. The authors themselves add the caveat that “the information actually usable depends on the encoding ability of the compressor and the utilization ability of the agent.”
  • Training and use require the agent to be frozen. During training the agent is frozen and only the LoRA and the adapter are updated, and the adapter is trained to match the input embedding dimension d of a specific agent. Changing the agent model would presumably require redesigning and retraining the compressor (not reported in the original).
  • m = 128 is a trade-off, not the F1 optimum. Within the tested range (8–128) F1 kept rising, while the compression rate fell at m = 128. The authors state it is the trade-off point from preliminary experiments.
  • The compressor training data is 4,363 pairs. Whether this scale is sufficient when extending to tools and domains with long observations and very different characteristics has not been validated (not reported in the original).

Next, constraints that follow from the design even though the authors do not list them as “limitations.”

  • When observations are short, the gain may shrink or reverse. If observations are short, the cost of one more pass through the compressor may exceed the savings. The paper shows gains under the premise of long, highly redundant web search observations, and did not measure the cost-benefit for scenarios with only short observations (not reported in the original).
  • Generalization to other model scales and agent architectures is open. The experiments are limited to two model pairs. Whether accuracy holds for agents using function-calling APIs or for much larger models has not been confirmed.
  • Long horizons were examined only to a limited extent. Search was limited to at most 5 results per call and at most 5 calls per task. Whether compression error accumulates in much longer multi-step interactions needs separate validation.

9. Takeaways

The core of this technique is not “how much to compress” but “what to keep.” The evidence is the comparison: ICAE, aiming at raw-text reconstruction, had a lower compression rate in the same architecture, while Coca-Cola, aiming at action preservation, gained both compression rate and accuracy.

When to apply it: it suits multi-step agents whose tool observations are long and highly redundant, in environments where a compressor can be additionally trained and operated while the agent backbone stays frozen. At inference the agent always ran on a single GPU, and in settings that used additional GPUs, only the compression model was placed on that GPU (4×A100-80GB; during training the agent was placed on 3 GPUs and the encoder and adapter on 1). Conversely, when observations are short, when the agent model changes often, or when non-search tools dominate, it has not yet been validated, so a trial application is needed.

The paper’s more fundamental message is this: the interaction between tools and agents does not need to rely on explicit text tokens. Tools only need to pass, as a compressed latent representation, the information sufficient for subsequent decisions.

Tables from the paper

Tables converted mechanically from the arXiv e-print LaTeX source. The numbers are the paper’s own and did not pass through a model.

Table 1. Efficiency comparison across four web-search QA datasets using Qwen3.5-35B-A3B and Qwen3.5-4B. Best results are in bold. Blue annotations under \name\ indicate reductions (%) relative to Vanilla in token usage and runtime.

item.title: AutoCompress: Automated Hardware-Guided Model Compression
item.description:
Paper

AutoCompress: Model Compression That Puts Serving Constraints Directly into the Search Objective

Introduction

When engineers deploy a large language model to a real service, the first question they hit is not “how much should we shrink it?” but “which axis should we shrink, and by how much, to survive on this device and this workload?” AutoCompress (NVIDIA, arXiv:2611.08290) turns that question into a cost model measured directly in the serving engine, and finds the answer by putting latency, throughput, and memory limits into the architecture search objective. This post starts from the problem that “parameter count alone cannot predict serving cost,” then covers examples of what remains and what disappears when one axis is narrowed, each step of the method, and results from three deployment scenarios and the 120B single-GPU case, in that order.

1. Problem: Parameter Count Alone Cannot Predict Serving Cost

1.1 Terms We Need First

Reading a compression paper requires distinguishing the components that make up serving cost.

Term Meaning Why it matters
latency time for a single request to finish key metric for services where a human waits each turn, such as game NPCs
throughput tokens processed per unit time on servers with bursty requests, total volume determines serving cost
GPU memory device memory where weights and per-request state reside exceeding the limit means the model itself will not fit
MoE (Mixture of Experts) layer that uses only some of several small FFN experts many parameters but little compute → compression axes appear in expert count and width
Mamba / SSM layer that keeps past information in a recurrent state uses a state cache instead of a KV cache → this state size also enters the memory calculation
FFN width intermediate hidden size inside an expert shrinking it reduces parameters and compute together
top-k routing activates only the top k experts reducing the expert count changes this selection rule itself
knowledge distillation method that uses a large model’s output probabilities as the training target for a smaller model standard means of recovering quality lost to compression
supernet / router a bundle of candidates sharing weights, plus a decision network choosing which size to use allows searching combinations on the order of $10^{42}$–$10^{52}$ without training each one

1.2 Same Parameter Count, Different Latency

The paper’s first figure shows where the problem starts. On an RTX 5070, running two architectures with the same total parameter count of 3.61B (1.26B active), the wider and shallower one recorded 674 ms and the narrower and deeper one 911 ms. The narrower, deeper one is 35% slower (Figure 1a). Conversely, on an H100, two architectures producing the same throughput (~7,355 and ~7,375 tok/s) had 8.8B and 19.3B parameters, one 2.2x the other (Figure 1b).

In other words, parameter count alone cannot predict serving cost. The cost of processing one request depends jointly on the architecture’s shape (width, depth, expert count), the workload (batch size, context length), the hardware, and which kernels the serving engine chooses.

1.3 Three Services Require Different Limits

Game NPC Local coding agent Data center inference
Hardware 1× RTX 5070 (12 GB) 1× RTX 5080 (16 GB) 8× H100 (TP1 × DP8)
Parent model Nemotron Nano 3 Elastic 12B (12.4B / 2.1B active) Nemotron 3.5 Lightning (31.6B / 3.6B active) Nemotron 3.5 Lightning (31.6B / 3.6B active)
Workload batch 1, input 2,048 + output 256 tokens batch 1, cache 262,144 + input 16,384 + output 1,024 tokens batch 128 per GPU, input 8,192 + output 65,536 tokens
Limit latency ≤ 750 ms, memory ≤ 4.0 GiB latency ≤ 11.5 s, memory ≤ 13.96 GiB ≥ 7,330 tok/s per GPU (+50% vs. parent)
Parent measured 1,147 ms, 8.76 GiB 12.44 s, 23.67 GiB 4,922 tok/s per GPU

The rationale for each limit is as follows. The 4 GiB in the game scenario leaves 8 GiB for rendering, the 750 ms follows voice-agent standards, and the workload length comes from the upper bound on sample length in the NPC Dialogue V2 dataset (§4.1). The 11.5 s in the local coding scenario is the average time for one LLM step in a real production coding-agent trace (TraceLab), and 13.96 GiB is the limit vLLM sets with its default memory utilization on an RTX 5080. The TP1×DP8, batch-128 combination for the data center was chosen by sweeping parallel layouts and batch sizes to the point where whole-node throughput is maximized.

The parent model fails to meet the target in every scenario. In other words, the fact that “we must compress” is already settled, and the remaining question was “what shape should the reduction take?”

1.4 Memory Prediction Is Also Wrong When Approximate

Apart from parameter count, the memory estimation method itself also misses serving cost by a wide margin. The paper’s appendix reports that the conventional approach—weights (at deployment precision) + per-request KV cache + recurrent state + MoE activation buffers—underestimates vLLM memory by 31%–43% on six real RTX serving models (Appendix B.1).

Two examples in Figure 12 show the gap. For the 3.6B model (39 layers) on an RTX 5070, the conventional formula gave 2.58 GiB, the paper’s cost model 3.99 GiB, and the measurement 3.93 GiB (limit 4.0 GiB). For the 13.6B model (52 layers) on an RTX 5080, the values were 9.36, 13.95, and 13.61 GiB, respectively (limit 13.96 GiB). Breaking down the composition of measured memory, in the RTX 5070 example the parameter formula accounted for 66%, “workspace sized by the widest layer” for 15%, and the remaining 19% for page-cache rounding plus CUDA context, graph pools, and non-PyTorch memory. In the RTX 5080 example the shares were 69%, 24%, and 7%.

Breaking the calculation into explicit terms cut the error by about an order of magnitude. This error shows that the convention of adding weights, KV cache, recurrent state, and MoE activation buffers misses serving memory, which means that without a cost model it is hard to set a compression target.

2. A Small Example: What Remains and What Disappears When One Axis Is Narrowed

2.1 The Mask Determines the “Surviving Channels”

Consider an axis with only two candidates, width 64 and width 128. If channels are sorted by importance, which candidate you pick determines which channels survive. The paper states the rule as follows (§2.3).

  • Channels 1–64: both candidates keep them, so the mask value is always 1
  • Channels 65–128: they survive only when the width-128 candidate is chosen, so the mask value is $y_{128}$

The mask value is “the sum of probabilities of the candidates that keep that component.” This one line is AutoCompress’s unit of search.

Applying the same rule to the routing FFN width candidate set in Table 2 (1856, 1536, 1280, 1024), suppose the router gives probabilities $y_{1024}=0.05$, $y_{1280}=0.10$, $y_{1536}=0.15$, $y_{1856}=0.70$, as in an illustrative example (not experimental numbers from the paper).

Channel interval Survival condition Mask value Remaining state
1–1024 all candidates include it 1.00 always remains in the computation
1025–1280 width 1280 or larger chosen 0.95 5% diluted
1281–1536 width 1536 or larger chosen 0.85 15% diluted
1537–1856 width 1856 chosen 0.70 30% diluted

Early in the search these values move continuously between 0 and 1, and gradients reach the router logits through the mask. As the search proceeds, the logit scale $\kappa_t$ increases linearly from 1 to 10 and the temperature $\tau_t$ drops geometrically from 1.0 to 0.05 (§4.4), so the probabilities converge to one candidate. Once converged, the mask hardens into a deterministic choice that keeps only the top widths by importance (Figure 3b).

2.2 The Limit Forces This Choice

The structure determined by the mask goes straight into the cost model. In the profiling table of Figure 4, narrowing the FFN width of the same MoE layer (128 experts) from 1856 to 1536 lowers that layer’s prefill time from 25.9 ms to 20.3 ms and its decode step from 52.3 µs to 49.6 µs. In the same table, reducing Mamba heads from 64 to 48 takes prefill from 6.1 ms to 4.5 ms and decode from 42.8 µs to 31.9 µs.

Summing the per-layer times obtained this way produces the predicted latency T, and the decision uses the ratio $\rho$ of T to the limit. If $\rho > 1$, the budget is exceeded and incurs a penalty; if $\rho < 0.98$, the search is seen as “leaving capacity unused by saving too much of the limit” and a penalty pushes it toward larger capacity. Only in the 98%–100% band is the penalty zero (§2.3). Allowing a width-0 candidate expresses layer removal within this framework. If the routing width is 0 and the shared width is positive, the layer becomes a dense MLP; if both widths are 0, the layer itself disappears (§2.2). The layer time of a removed layer is treated as 0.

 flowchart TD
 A["Input: routing FFN width candidates 1024 / 1280 / 1536 / 1856<br/>channels are already sorted by importance"] --> B["Router assigns a probability y to each candidate<br/>example: 0.05 / 0.10 / 0.15 / 0.70"]
 B --> C["Mask = sum of probabilities of candidates that keep the interval<br/>1–1024: 1.00 / 1025–1280: 0.95 / 1281–1536: 0.85 / 1537–1856: 0.70"]
 C --> D["Early search: through continuous masks<br/>gradients reach the router logits"]
 D --> E["Late search: logit scale 1→10, temperature 1.0→0.05<br/>probabilities converge to one candidate"]
 E --> F["Per-candidate structure: choosing 1856 keeps 1,856 channels<br/>choosing 1536 deletes the 1,537–1,856 interval<br/>choosing width 0: dense MLP if shared width is positive, layer deleted if both are 0"]
 F --> G["Cost model: sum layer times t_ℓ to get predicted latency<br/>MoE 128 experts: FFN 1856 → prefill 25.9 ms / decode 52.3 µs<br/>FFN 1536 → prefill 20.3 ms / decode 49.6 µs"]
 G --> H{"ρ = predicted latency ÷ latency limit"}
 H -->|"ρ > 1: over"| I["Budget penalty → update logits → re-search other widths"]
 H -->|"ρ < 0.98: slack"| K["Unused-budget penalty<br/>push toward larger capacity"]
 H -->|"0.98 ≤ ρ ≤ 1.00: band"| J["Zero penalty<br/>search continues, extract discrete structure after gate convergence"]
 I --> B
 K --> B

The $\rho$ branch in the diagram has three paths: over ($\rho>1$), slack ($\rho<0.98$), and the 98%–100% band. Both over and slack update the router logits through penalties, and in the band the penalty is zero. The mask values 0.95, 0.85, and 0.70 are probability sums, so during the search they are continuous values between 0 and 1; when the probabilities converge to one candidate, they harden to 1 or 0.

3. Method

3.1 Deployment Target and Four-Step Procedure

AutoCompress takes a “deployment target $\mathcal{D}$” as input. $\mathcal{D}$ specifies the hardware, serving configuration, precision, and workload, including batch size, cached prefix length, and input/output lengths. On top of that sit a memory limit, a latency limit, or a throughput requirement (or a combination) (§2.1).

The overall procedure has four steps.

  1. Build a cost model tailored to the target deployment environment (§3).
  2. Sort the parent model’s components by importance and reorder the weights to initialize a supernet in which candidates share weights (§2.2).
  3. Train the architecture router and the supernet together, using a distillation loss from the frozen parent plus resource penalties (§2.3).
  4. Detach the selected architecture from the parent weights and recover quality through distillation (§2.4).

3.2 Search Space and Shared Weights

The search axes split into global and per-layer axes. Hidden size is global; the Mamba head count is treated as a global candidate set (64, 56, 48, 40, 32) for Lightning 3.5 and per layer as “keep 64 or remove” for Nano 3 12B. The per-layer axes are the routing expert count $E_\ell$, routing FFN width $F_\ell$, and shared FFN width $S_\ell$, each with its own logits per layer. Candidate values are determined by the parent model and the deployment target.

Axis Nemotron 3.5 Lightning (RTX 5080 / H100) Nemotron Nano 3 12B (RTX 5070)
Hidden size 2688, 2432, 2176, 1920, 1664, 1408 1920, 1792, 1664, 1536, 1408, 1280
Mamba head count 64, 56, 48, 40, 32 (global) 64 or removed (per layer)
Routing expert count 128, 112, 96, 80, 64 128, 96, 64, 32
Routing FFN width 1856, 1536, 1280, 1024 960, 704, 448, 192, 0
Shared FFN width 3712, 2816, 1920 3712, 2688, 1856, 1024, 0
Depth fixed (Mamba and MoE layers removable) same

Before deployment constraints are applied, the number of candidate combinations is about $2.37\times10^{42}$ for Lightning 3.5 and about $1.20\times10^{52}$ for Nano 3 12B (§4.2). These combinations cannot be profiled one by one or distilled one by one. So the method uses two devices.

First, weight sharing. For candidates of different widths to use the same weights, there must be an order of “which channel to keep first.” AutoCompress ranks the parent’s components (residual channels, Mamba heads within a head group, experts, routing and shared FFN channels) by activation-based importance, then reorders the weights so that higher-ranked ones come first (§2.2, a procedure taken from Minitron’s importance-based pruning). A width-1856 candidate uses the first 1,856 of this order, and a width-1536 candidate uses only the first 1,536. Thus every candidate shares the prefix of the same supernet weights.

3.3 The Router Draws a Probability per Candidate to Build a Soft Mask

For each axis, the router learns a logit $z_c$ for each candidate value. The choice is sampled with Gumbel-softmax (Equation 1).

$$y_c=\frac{\exp((\kappa_t z_c+g_c)/\tau_t)}{\sum_j \exp((\kappa_t z_j+g_j)/\tau_t)}$$

$z_c$ is the logit of choice $c$, $g_c$ is independent standard Gumbel noise, and the sum in the denominator runs over all choices on that axis. $\kappa_t$ (logit scale) sets how strongly the learned preference is reflected relative to the noise, and $\tau_t$ (temperature) sets how close the relaxed choice gets to one-hot. The process seen earlier, where “the mask hardens from continuous values to a decision,” is driven by tuning these two scales.

The sampled probabilities turn directly into the soft masks from §2.1. Thanks to these masks, gradients reach the architecture choices, continuously tuning the relaxed choice instead of scoring candidates discretely. One batch of 2,048 sequences (8,192 tokens each) is split evenly into 32 independently sampled configurations (§4.4).

3.4 Cost Model: Latency and Throughput

Instead of profiling the whole architecture directly, measure per-layer times and add them up (§3.1).

$$\hat{T}^{(a|\mathcal{D})}=T_0(d|\mathcal{D})+\sum_{\ell=1}^{L} t_\ell(a_\ell; d|\mathcal{D})$$

$d$ is the global hidden size, $L$ is the parent’s layer count, $a_\ell$ is the configuration of layer $\ell$, $t_\ell$ is the measured GPU time of that layer (0 for removed layers), and $T_0$ is a fixed term combining embedding, LM head, sampling, and serving-engine overhead.

The measurement procedure is summarized in Figure 4. About 10 different layer configurations are placed into one short model filled with dummy weights and run in the actual serving engine, and an Nsight Systems trace is cut at layer boundaries to read prefill and decode separately. A single run fills in measurements for multiple layers. Example rows from Figure 4 are as follows (profiling model, hidden size 1408).

Hidden size Layer configuration Prefill (ms) Decode (µs)
1408 Mamba, 64 heads 6.1 42.8
1408 Mamba, 48 heads 4.5 31.9
1408 MoE, 128 experts, FFN width 1856 25.9 52.3
1408 MoE, 128 experts, FFN width 1536 20.3 49.6
1408 MoE, 96 experts, FFN width 1856 25.6 51.8
1408 Attention, 32 heads 857.1 213.5
1408 non-layer (embedding, head, overhead) 685.0 262.0

What this table shows is that the cost of an individual layer varies greatly by structure. Reducing MoE FFN width from 1856 to 1536 (5.6 ms) has a larger effect than reducing Mamba heads from 64 to 48 (1.6 ms), and attention layers and non-layer overhead account for a large share of prefill time in this profile. The savings vary widely by layer, showing that which axis to shrink is an important question in the search.

Note that a throughput requirement is expressed as an “upper bound on serving time” under a fixed workload (§2.3, Appendix C).

3.5 Cost Model: Memory

Memory is computed in five terms (§3.2).

$$\hat{M}^{(a|\mathcal{D})}=W+C+P+R+\epsilon_{\mathcal{D}}$$
  • $W$: weights, computed from tensor shapes and deployment precision.
  • $C$: request cache, the sum of the attention KV cache and the Mamba convolution/SSM cache, sized by the target sequence length and batch size.
  • $P$: prefill workspace, governed by the query-head configuration and prefill chunk size.
  • $R$: runtime buffers, including the MoE matmul workspace and the Mamba projection workspace, sized by the widest of the relevant layers.
  • $\epsilon_{\mathcal{D}}$: the rest that cannot be modeled, such as CUDA context and graph allocations. It is set to the maximum difference between measured memory and $W+C+P+R$ across several server startups.

The slack term $\epsilon_{\mathcal{D}}$ is collected during latency profiling without extra runs (Figure 4). Deployment precision is summarized in Appendix C. Experts, shared experts, and the LM head are stored in NVFP4, Mamba projections in FP8, attention in BF16, the KV cache in FP8, and the Mamba state in FP32. In other words, “what is stored in which number format” is the backbone of the memory-limit calculation.

3.6 The Objective Mixes Quality and Budget into One Equation

The router and supernet are trained together, and the objective is the sum of the distillation loss and resource penalties (§2.3, Equation 2).

$$\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KD}}+\alpha\sum_r\left[\max(0,\rho_r-1)+\max(0,\,1-\delta-\rho_r)\right]$$

$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KD}}$ is the forward KL from the frozen parent’s token distribution to the sampled supernet’s distribution. $\rho_r$ is the predicted cost under the soft architecture divided by that resource’s budget. If the latency cap is $T_{\max}$, then $\rho_T=T/T_{\max}$. $\alpha$ balances resource constraints against distillation, and $\delta$ is the allowed unused budget. The paper uses $\delta=0.02$, so the penalty is zero only in the 98%–100% band of each cap. $\alpha$ was chosen as 0.3 from an H100 sweep and reused on the RTX 5080, while 1 was used on the tighter RTX 5070 (§4.4).

3.7 Extraction and Recovery

When the search converges (each gate gives the leading candidate a probability of at least 0.95), the candidate with the largest logit at each router gate is chosen to fix a discrete architecture, and that structure is re-evaluated with the cost model. Then the corresponding slice is cut from the importance-sorted parent weights for initialization, and quality is recovered through logit distillation (§2.4). Recovery starts from the parent’s sorted weights, not from the trained supernet weights. The student receives only the parent’s output logits as a supervision signal, and both methods are trained on the same data in the same order with the same batch size and learning-rate schedule (batch 2,048 sequences × 8,192 tokens, max learning rate $4\times10^{-5}$, min $5\times10^{-6}$) (§4.5).

3.8 Baseline: Minitron++

Existing pruning techniques do not directly support AutoCompress’s combined search space and deployment constraints. So the paper adapts Minitron’s pruning and screening procedure to its own cost model to build a baseline called Minitron++ (§4.3). The conditions are as follows.

  • It uses the same cost model, the same importance-sorted parent, and the same deployment budget.
  • However, per-layer widths must be uniform and all layers are kept.
  • Candidates are drawn from the combinations in Table 2, but only for the RTX 5070 are Mamba head counts allowed from 64 down to 8 in steps of 8, and width-0 candidates are excluded.
  • Only candidates that reach at least 95% of each resource cap and cannot increase any axis further without shrinking another axis or violating a constraint are kept → 6, 11, and 95 candidates on the RTX 5070/5080/H100, respectively. The reason for using a wider band than AutoCompress’s 2% band is that with a 2% band only one candidate survives at most on the RTX 5080.
  • Each candidate receives 100 distillation iterations (about 1.7B tokens), and the candidate with the lowest average loss over iterations 76–100 is chosen. On the H100, the 95 candidates are first sorted by loss and only the top 5 are trained.
  • The final selected architecture receives the same recovery training as the AutoCompress student.

In short, the key difference in the comparison is whether per-layer widths are uniform and all layers are kept, or whether width and expert count are searched differently per layer.

4. Results

4.1 Accuracy Under the Same Budget

These are the results in Table 3. Avg8 is the unweighted average of scores on eight benchmarks: AIME25, LiveCodeBench v5, MMLU-Pro, MATH-500, GSM8K, IFEval, IFBench, and GPQA-Diamond. IFEval and IFBench use prompt-level strict accuracy, and the rest use pass@1 (§4.6). Search tokens are the amount used for structure selection, KD tokens are the amount used for recovery training, and KD loss is the average over the last 25 iterations.

Scenario Method Search tokens KD tokens KD loss AIME25 LCB v5 MMLU-Pro MATH-500 GSM8K IFEval IFBench GPQA Avg8
RTX 5070 AutoCompress 4.18B 30B 0.1909 0.42 1.11 26.46 36.40 47.54 55.13 24.49 21.78 26.67
RTX 5070 Minitron++ 8.49B 30B 0.2366 0.00 0.48 19.76 29.90 34.29 43.76 17.43 15.21 20.10
RTX 5080 AutoCompress 2.85B 10B 0.1637 52.71 49.44 67.45 93.60 92.87 83.64 55.61 55.87 68.90
RTX 5080 Minitron++ 8.57B 10B 0.1710 48.75 43.81 67.89 92.70 92.93 79.57 49.83 56.94 66.55
8×H100 AutoCompress 3.00B 10B 0.1809 55.42 48.02 64.80 92.80 92.49 82.53 53.74 53.09 67.86
8×H100 Minitron++ 9.98B 10B 0.1820 53.54 47.78 64.43 92.85 92.72 81.38 52.04 53.60 67.29

Across the three scenarios, the Avg8 differences are 6.57, 2.35, and 0.57 percentage points, and the final distillation losses are 19.3%, 4.3%, and 0.6% lower (§5.1). Of the three results, the gain is largest on the RTX 5070 and smallest on the H100.

Search cost also dropped. The architecture-selection tokens used by Minitron++ are about 2.0x, 3.0x, and 3.3x those of AutoCompress (§5.2), in the order RTX 5070, RTX 5080, H100. Recovery training tokens are identical for both methods, so this saving belongs to the structure-selection stage. Search tokens can be seen as the amount consumed up to the point where the structure is fixed out of 250 steps (batch 2,048×8,192 tokens). The fixing points are step 170 on the RTX 5080, step 249 on the RTX 5070, and step 179 on the H100, which correspond to 2.85B, 4.18B, and 3.00B, respectively (§4.4).

4.2 Budget Compliance Confirmed by Measurement

Figure 5 shows how full each resource is relative to the latency and memory limits or the H100 throughput target. The denominator of each ratio is the corresponding limit or target.

Resource utilization (vs. limit/target) Parent AutoCompress Minitron++
RTX 5070 · latency 152.9% 98.6% 95.4%
RTX 5070 · memory 218.9% 98.3% 99.2%
RTX 5080 · latency 108.2% 96.6% 94.9%
RTX 5080 · memory 169.5% 97.5% 98.7%
8×H100 · throughput per GPU 67.2% 101.0% 102.1%

In both RTX scenarios, the AutoCompress student measured 739.7 ms and 3.93 GiB (RTX 5070), and 11.1 s and 13.61 GiB (RTX 5080), meeting both latency and memory limits, and on the H100 it exceeded the throughput target (Figure 2, §5.1). The exact absolute latency and memory values of the Minitron++ student are not reported in the paper; only the ratios in Figure 5 are given.

4.3 Scaling: 120B on a Single B200

The estimated BF16 serving memory of Nemotron 3.5 Super (120B) is about 280 GB, which exceeds the 180 GB capacity of a B200. This case was not a matter of slightly exceeding the budget; without compression, the goal of single-B200 BF16 serving could not be met at all. The model selected by AutoCompress supports a maximum batch of 16 at a 131,072-token context and uses a measured 178 GB (Figure 6a). Parameters dropped from 120B to about 74B, a 38.3% reduction.

The selected structure has per-layer MoE routing expert counts of 240–496 and MoE intermediate sizes of 1536–2560 (the parent has 512 and 2688, respectively), and keeps 88 backbone layers, a hidden size of 4096, and a shared-expert intermediate size of 5376 (Appendix D). The search converged within 4B tokens, and recovery used 68B tokens at 8,192 context and 48B tokens at 131,072 context, for 120B tokens in total. Search and recovery used 32 GB200 nodes (128 GPUs) for about 64 hours.

Quality is 54.74 as the unweighted average of nine metrics (GDPval-AA v2 as an index, the other eight as percentages), 2.85 points below the parent’s 57.58. It is also 9.30 points above the 45.44 average of the 120B reference model Nemotron 3 Super (Figure 6b, Figure 14). In this case the Minitron++ baseline was not run because of training cost, so the improvement over the existing method is not reported in the paper.

4.4 Why the Search Chose That Structure

In the diagnostic record of the RTX 5080 search (Figure 9, §6.3), the shared-expert intermediate size settled first and stayed at its maximum size. Mamba heads and hidden size settled next (the main text §6.3 says iterations 41 and 50; the Figure 9 labels say 42 and 52), and routing width (iteration 129) and expert count (iteration 155) settled last. The distillation gradient norm was large for shared and global choices, while the budget gradient norm was large for the remaining MoE choices.

The choice to keep the shared experts is consistent with relatively low serving cost. At hidden size 2688, cutting the shared-expert intermediate size nearly in half saves only 7.5 ms and 5 MiB per layer, whereas cutting the MoE intermediate size similarly saves 33.7 ms and 307 MiB per layer. Even for the same width reduction, axes with large and small savings are clearly distinct, and keeping the shared experts reads as a choice that preserved the low-cost axis.

On the H100, AutoCompress and Minitron++ chose the same hidden size and Mamba head count. The difference came on the MoE side. Minitron++ keeps the routing expert count and intermediate size the same across layers, while AutoCompress chose both differently per layer. Under the same throughput target, AutoCompress’s distillation loss was 0.6% lower and its Avg8 was 0.57 percentage points higher (§6.3).

4.5 Effect of Two Design Choices

The configuration that initializes the router output layer to zero and removes router warmup produced a distillation loss 10.9% lower than the random-initialization + warmup configuration (Figure 7, §6.1). Random initialization creates a selection bias, and learning-rate warmup limits the early updates that would correct that bias before the distribution sharpens.

The MoE expert masking method is also compared. Top-k score masking reduces traffic to experts that survive only in larger architecture candidates, nearly eliminating the gradient those experts give the router. In contrast, output masking, which applies the mask after selection, keeps access to those experts during the search. Output masking distributes experts evenly, keeps distillation gradients stable, and lowered distillation loss by 23% (Figure 8, §6.2). In the KD gradient graph of Figure 8, the difference between the two methods is shown as ≈430x.

5. Limitations and When to Apply It

I start with the limitations visible in the paper.

The additive assumption of the cost model. Because it predicts total latency by summing per-layer measured times, predictions can miss when kernel selection, cache behavior, or overhead changes as the architecture changes (§3.1). The paper validates predictions on held-out architectures not used to build the timing table. The median absolute error was 0.6% for RTX 5070 latency, 1.7% for RTX 5080 latency, and 1.6% for H100 throughput (Figure 11). However, validation was done within the target serving engine and hardware. Also, variance across repeated runs and error bars are not reported in the paper, so the benchmark scores in Table 3 should be read as point estimates from the final checkpoint.

Tied to a single serving engine. All serving was done in vLLM 0.27.1, and the cost model is built by profiling directly on the target hardware, workload, and precision (§4.1, Appendix C). If the engine or hardware changes, profiling must be redone. This cost is not negligible (Table 4).

Deployment target Number of runs Timing table entries GPU hours
Local coding (RTX 5080) 60 468 3.5
Data center throughput (H100) 180 408 24.8
On-device NPC (RTX 5070) 96 660 4.5

Building a cost model for just one H100 data-center target took 180 runs and 24.8 GPU hours. This value is separate from search tokens and is a fixed cost of preparing a cost model for each deployment target.

A comparison gap in the scaling case. The 120B→74B case did not run Minitron++, so this paper alone cannot show the improvement over the existing method.

Narrow evaluation scope. Avg8 is the unweighted average of eight benchmark scores; IFEval and IFBench use prompt-level strict accuracy, and the rest use pass@1. Results were obtained on Nemotron-family parent models with hybrid Mamba, attention, and MoE structures. Generalization to models with other structures was not validated, and because this paper deals with compression of a pretrained parent, it does not evaluate pretraining convergence itself.

From a reviewer’s perspective, the fact that the cost model is measurement-based is both an accuracy advantage and an operational burden. The profiling pipeline must be maintained whenever the deployment environment changes. In addition, because the cost model is calibrated to the fixed workloads in Table 1, cost accuracy when real traffic departs from the assumed batch and length distribution is not validated in the paper. The comparison is also limited to a deployment-adapted Minitron++, so there is no comparison with other per-layer search tools in the paper.

In summary, AutoCompress fits best teams that have fixed deployment hardware and workload, have the resources to profile a cost model in that environment, and can perform distillation recovery after compression. Its value is especially high in cases like on-device game NPCs or compressing a 120B model to 74B to fit on a single B200, where it removes the manual work of translating deployment requirements into a parameter budget. Conversely, if the serving engine or hardware changes often, profiling cost grows, and generalization to other structures or other baselines is not confirmed in the paper.

Tables from the paper

Tables converted mechanically from the arXiv e-print LaTeX source. The numbers are the paper’s own and did not pass through a model.

item.title: LoopVQ: Sub 1-bit KV Cache Quantization for Looped Transformers
item.description:
Paper

Introduction

A looped transformer is a model that reuses the same group of layers several times. It saves parameters, but each iteration step has to keep its own key/value cache, so the serving bottleneck shifts from the weights to the cache. This post summarizes the observations, design, and measured results of LoopVQ, a method that compresses that cache to under 1 bit per element.

Terms to know first

Looped transformer. An architecture that reuses the same $L_b$ decoder layers $T$ times. The $t$-th loop step takes the previous step’s output $h^{(t-1)}_{1:N}$ as input and computes $h^{(t)}_{1:N} = F_\theta(h^{(t-1)}_{1:N})$, and the final output distribution $p_j$ is read from the hidden state $h^{(T)}_j$ of the last step. Only one thing matters here. Each loop step leaves its own keys and values in the cache, so the cache is $T$ times larger than in a non-looped model that uses the same weights. The evaluated models Ouro-1.4B and 2.6B use $T=4$, and Huginn-3.5B runs 32 iterations.

KV cache. Memory that stores the keys and values of past tokens during autoregressive generation and uses them to compute attention for the next token. The paper defines that token $j$ produces a key $k^{(t,\ell)}_{j,h}\in\mathbb{R}^D$ and a value $v^{(t,\ell)}_{j,h}\in\mathbb{R}^D$ for each loop step $t$, layer $\ell$, and KV head $h$. The longer the context, the more heads and layers, and, as noted above, the more loop steps, the larger this memory grows.

Quantization. Compression that stores values at lower precision to reduce memory. The paper emphasizes that quantization does not discard tokens; it only shrinks the cache.

Vector quantization. A method that splits a $D$-channel vector into $D/G$ chunks of $G$ consecutive channels and stores each chunk as the index of the nearest entry in a codebook $\mathcal{B}=\{e_1,\dots,e_K\}\subset\mathbb{R}^G$. Following equation (2) of the paper exactly, the index is chosen by $a(z)=\arg\min_{r\le K}\|z-e_r\|_2^2$ and reconstruction is $\hat z = e_{a(z)}$. If the codebook size is $K=2^b$, each chunk costs $b$ bits, that is, $b/G$ bits per element. In the sub-1-bit regime this post targets, existing vector quantization loses a great deal of accuracy.

Bits per element. The number of bits used to store one channel in the cache. At 0.5 bits, that is 0.5 bits per element, a 32x compression relative to 16 bits (bf16).

Codebook and calibration. The codebook is initially built from offline calibration data. The paper summarizes that prior work uses $k$-means weighted by each chunk’s importance $\omega_n=\|\partial L/\partial z_n\|_2^2$ (equation 3). $\omega_n$ is the squared gradient norm with respect to the next-token loss $L$ and equals the diagonal trace of the empirical Fisher information. What matters here is that this weight alone cannot capture the problems that arise in a looped architecture.

RoPE (rotary position embedding). A technique that applies a position-dependent rotation to key vectors to represent relative positions. The paper quantizes keys before applying RoPE, reconstructs them in attention, and then applies RoPE. The reason is in Appendix C. RoPE rotates keys in the same channel group differently at each position, so a single code group tied together before rotation scatters across many entries in the codebook.

SGLang. A serving framework that executes structured LLM programs efficiently. This paper attaches a LoopVQ-specific attention kernel to it and measures efficiency.

1. Problem: the cache is the bottleneck, and redundancy remains along the loop axis

1.1 Saving parameters makes the cache larger

Figure 1a of the paper plots each model as a point. The horizontal axis is KV cache size per token (8KB–2MB), and the vertical axis is bf16 weight memory (2GB–32GB). Ouro-1.4B has 6x the KV cache per token of the non-looped Llama-3.1-8B, and at moderate context lengths its cache memory already exceeds its weights. In other words, when serving a looped model, the real bottleneck is the cache, not the weights.

Figure 1b of the paper plots GSM8K accuracy against bits per element (0.25–4), showing that existing vector quantization (CQ, TaSQ) collapses sharply once it goes below 1 bit (bf16 baseline 86.1, Ouro-2.6B).

1.2 The iteration axis still holds untapped redundancy

The $T$ caches of one layer are computed by applying the same projection weights to the hidden states of the same token. So the keys and values across steps resemble each other.

  • Fig. 2a: Pre-RoPE keys of one attention head in Ouro-1.4B are plotted across four steps, and the four steps show nearly identical channel patterns. Across all of Ouro-1.4B, the correlation between adjacent steps rises from 0.69 between the first two steps to 0.94 between the last two.
  • Fig. 2b: Color shows the mean $|r|$ over all (loop step, channel) coordinate pairs within a 16-channel group. The parts connecting the same channel across adjacent steps form bright lines, while different channels in the same group are dark. Numerically, the mean $|r|$ between adjacent steps of the same channel is 0.85, while between different channels in the same 16-channel group it is 0.16, and the gap is even wider for values.
  • Fig. 2c: With bit width and codebook size fixed, it compares the reconstruction error (NMSE) of $k$-means under two grouping schemes: “$G$ channels of one step” and “$G/4$ channels across four steps.” Grouping along the loop axis reduces the error to roughly half at 0.5 bits on Ouro-1.4B, and reduces it substantially at every bit width on both Ouro and Huginn (§3, Fig. 2 of the paper).

The axis existing vector quantization uses is the “channel axis.” A looped model’s cache has one more redundancy axis next to it: the “iteration axis.”

1.3 But the perceived quantization error differs by step

When one grouped vector represents several steps together, it matters which step inside it incurred the error. An error introduced early propagates through all later steps, while an error in the last step stays confined to that step.

Table 1 of the paper quantizes only one step while keeping the others at full precision, then measures the KL divergence between the full-precision output and the quantized output (loop-axis grouping + Fisher-weighted $k$-means codebook, measured on sequences not used for calibration).

Quantized step 0.5-bit KL 0.25-bit KL
1 0.069 0.123
2 0.018 0.029
3 0.013 0.026
4 0.030 0.065

Quantizing the first step is the most harmful, and the third step the least. The gap between the two steps is about 5x.

2. A small example: one index stands in for four steps

Below is an illustrative example built from Ouro-1.4B’s actual settings ($D=128$ channels, $T=4$ steps, 8-bit code $K=256$, $G=16$ at 0.5 bits). It is a construction for explaining the mechanism, not measured values from the paper.

Stage Existing vector quantization (CQ) LoopVQ
Input The key of one token, one layer, one head. A 128-channel key is computed separately across four loop steps, leaving four copies in the cache Same
Retained state Each step’s 128 channels are split into eight 16-channel chunks, and an 8-bit index is stored per chunk. Eight per step, 32 indices total. The codebook is built separately per step, so there are four copies The same 128 channels are split into 32 chunks of 4 channels, but one chunk ties together 4 channels from each of steps 1–4 (16 channels total). The index count is the same at 32, and the codebook is a single copy shared by the four steps
Change / omission / rejection Ignores inter-step correlation (adjacent-step $ r
Output Reconstructs four copies of keys for the four steps. Reconstruction error is large Reconstructs the same four copies of keys. Grouping along the loop axis reduces the 0.5-bit reconstruction error to roughly half (Fig. 2c of the paper, general $k$-means)

In other words, LoopVQ does not use more memory. It keeps the same number of storage slots and puts similar values together in those slots to reduce reconstruction error.

3. Method

3.1 Loop-axis vector quantization

The authors split the $T$ steps into consecutive blocks of $T_c$ steps (Ouro has $T=T_c=4$, so one block; Huginn has 32 steps in 8 blocks). One code covers $c=G/T_c$ channels in each of the $T_c$ steps within the block. Equation (4) of the paper defines this combined vector, and equation (5) is the rule by which each step slices out its own share (coordinate $iT_c+m$ of the combined vector) from that index for reconstruction.

  • Because one code represents $T_c$ steps at once, bits per element stay at $b/G$. Memory does not grow.
  • Keys are quantized before RoPE, reconstructed in attention, and then RoPE is applied (§2, Appendix C).
  • The codebook is initialized with Fisher-weighted $k$-means. Here $\omega_n$ sums the squared gradients over all $T_c$ steps covered by the combined vector (§4.1).

3.2 Loop-aware codebook fine-tuning

Fisher-weighted $k$-means misses something. Because this objective penalizes each code vector’s error independently, it cannot express the cross terms that arise when an earlier step’s error propagates to later steps. Appendix A.1 shows that for small errors the objective can be approximated as $J(B)\approx\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_s[\delta^\top F\delta]$, and that weighted $k$-means only matches the diagonal blocks $F_{nn}$ and always discards cross terms of the form $F_{nn'}$. No reweighting removes this limitation. Moreover, it allocates precision equally to every step inside the combined vector.

So the authors fix the model weights and fit the output directly. For a calibration sequence $s$, they take the full-precision cache $C$ and its output distribution $p_j$, compute the output $q_j(\mathcal{B})$ when all $T_c$ steps attend to $\hat C(\mathcal{B})$, the cache reconstructed from the codebook $\mathcal{B}$, and minimize $J(\mathcal{B})=\mathbb{E}_s[\frac{1}{N}\sum_j \mathrm{KL}(p_j\|q_j(\mathcal{B}))]$ from equation (6). The sum runs over the $N$ positions after the bf16 sink tokens. This objective captures both error propagation across steps and per-step sensitivity differences.

  • Codebook entries are updated directly by backprop through this objective. The arg min selection does not need to be differentiated, so codebook entries receive exact gradients and no straight-through estimator is needed (Appendix A.2).
  • Assignments are recomputed with the current codebook at every iteration, so the encoder at training time and the encoder at inference time do not diverge.
  • As a result, KL divergence relative to the full-precision output drops to roughly half on Ouro-1.4B (Fig. 4 of the paper: starting from a $k$-means codebook and repeating fine-tuning).
  • Training setup: fine-tune on 12 of the 16 calibration sequences (Adam, learning rate $10^{-3}$, one sequence per iteration, 4 epochs), then pick the epoch with the lowest KL on the remaining 4 (§5.1).

3.3 Combining with TaSQ

TaSQ handles the channel axis. Equation (10) in Appendix B is a transform that multiplies the key’s channels by weights $w$, divides by a per-token scale $\sigma$, and rearranges them with a permutation $P$. The goal is to make channels that share a code more correlated. LoopVQ handles the loop axis, so the two are orthogonal. TaSQ+LoopVQ applies the TaSQ transform first and then groups along the loop axis, so one code covers (the $c$ channels chosen on the channel axis) × (the $T_c$ steps on the loop axis).

The permutation $P$ is obtained from the $T_cD\times T_cD$ covariance matrix formed by stacking the $T_c$ step keys of a block, tying each step’s RoPE pair $\{i,i+D/2\}$ together so that a group has $G=cT_c$ coordinates. The only cost is storing the per-token key scale $\sigma$ in fp16, which is 16/(HD) bits per key element, about 0.008 bits for Ouro and 0.003 bits for Huginn. That is why Table 2 shows key bit widths of 0.508/0.5 (Ouro) and 0.503/0.5 (Huginn).

Huginn has segments without a loop axis. The two-layer prelude and coda are encoded separately per layer, like CQ. For reference, Huginn-3.5B runs 32 iterations of a four-layer core block and adds the prelude and coda, producing 132 KV caches per token.

3.4 SGLang implementation: when indices are created and how they are read

The flow in Fig. 3 of the paper is as follows. Each loop step writes its own cache, but in the encoding stage $c=G/T_c$ channels are grouped across $T_c$ steps to produce one index. That index is shared by the $T_c$ steps, and at inference each step $t$ reads the same index as its own key and value through its own codebook slice $\mathcal{B}_t$.

The storage and lookup structure in Fig. 5 of the paper reads in three stages.

  1. Storage layout. The first $n_s$ tokens (sink) and the most recent $n_r$ tokens stay in bf16 across all steps, and only the tokens in between are stored as codebook indices. The cache is paged in units of 8 tokens, and $n_s$ and $n_r$ are multiples of 8, so a page is entirely bf16 or entirely quantized. Because one index is shared by $T_c$ steps, a quantized page has only one index row per step block, giving the same memory per token as encoding separately per step at the same $G$. The experiments use 8/64 for general benchmarks and 64/256 for reasoning and long-context benchmarks.
  2. When indices are created. A combined vector can be encoded only after all $T_c$ steps of the block have been computed. So in prefill, each step’s keys and values are held until the last step of that block, then distances to all codebook entries are computed with tensor-core matrix multiplication and encoded in one go. In decode, the new token’s keys and values are written to the bf16 recent region (once the forward pass finishes, all steps for that token are present), and every 8 generated tokens the oldest page is converted to indices across all layers and steps, keeping the recent region at $n_r$–$n_r$+7 tokens.
  3. How attention reads. At loop step $t$, the dedicated kernel loads the codebook slice $\mathcal{B}_t$ into shared memory once and looks up keys and values from registers using each token’s index. bf16 pages are read by SGLang’s Triton decoding kernel, and the two results are merged in Flash-Decoding style by combining the logsumexp of the splits. Quantized keys are reconstructed, after which the kernel applies RoPE using precomputed per-position sine and cosine tables. The number of indices read per head per token is $D/c$.

The implementation is available at https://github.com/mscheong01/LoopVQ .

4.1 General benchmarks

The evaluated models are Ouro-1.4B, Ouro-2.6B, and Huginn-3.5B, and the metric is average accuracy (%) on GSM8K, MATH500, HumanEval, and MBPP. All use greedy decoding (Table 2 of the paper). CQ is the baseline vector quantization that uses a separate codebook per loop step and layer.

On Huginn-3.5B as well, LoopVQ and TaSQ+LoopVQ are higher than both baselines according to Table 2.

4.3 Long-context retrieval

Fig. 6 of the paper is split into four panels (Ouro-1.4B and Ouro-2.6B × 0.5 bits and 0.25 bits). The horizontal axis is context length (4K–64K), the vertical axis is accuracy (%) averaged over RULER’s 8 NIAH tasks with 3 seeds, and the curves are BF16, CQ, TaSQ, LoopVQ, and TaSQ+LoopVQ. CQ and TaSQ stay well below BF16 at all lengths, while LoopVQ finds a considerable number of needles at 0.5 bits, and TaSQ+LoopVQ is highest at every length and bit width.

LongBench (16 English tasks) in Appendix D.5 follows the same order. In average accuracy, CQ and TaSQ are 7–13 points below BF16, LoopVQ is higher than both baselines in every setting, and TaSQ+LoopVQ comes within 1.5 points of BF16 at 0.5 bits.

4.4 When quantization lengthens reasoning, the per-token latency gain also fades

Fig. 10 of the paper shows the distribution of tokens generated by Ouro-1.4B-Thinking at 0.5 bits on GPQA-Diamond. The horizontal axis is the number of generated tokens (0–32K), the vertical axis is the fraction of problems (%), and the bars show the shares of 32K cap hits, early failures, and non-terminations. CQ and TaSQ exhaust the 32K budget on most problems, generating about 2x as many tokens as BF16. LoopVQ and TaSQ+LoopVQ, by contrast, follow BF16’s length distribution at 0.5 bits, and at 0.25 bits only TaSQ+LoopVQ still does (Appendix D.4).

Appendix D.4 measures the opposite direction as well: early termination. On BF16, the fraction of generations finishing within 2K tokens is 16% and 22% for Ouro-1.4B-Thinking and Ouro-2.6B-Thinking, while at 0.25 bits it rises to 33% and 59% for CQ and 30% and 47% for TaSQ. LoopVQ and TaSQ+LoopVQ stay at or below 30% in every setting. In other words, the per-token throughput gain carries through to actual time to complete an answer.

4.5 System efficiency

The measurement environment is a single RTX 6000 Ada 48GB, the target is Ouro-1.4B-Thinking, and sink and recent were kept in bf16 at 8 and 64 tokens (§5.3).

Kernel and latency. The decode kernel reads only $D/c$ indices per head per token, so it reads 8x (0.5 bits) to 16x (0.25 bits) fewer bytes than bf16 keys and values. Long-context decode is bound by cache reads, so this saving grows with context length (Fig. 8b of the paper, batch 1).

Context length 1K 8K 32K
0.5-bit decode latency +3% −17% −47%
0.25-bit decode latency +3% −18% −49%

Prefill, by contrast, gets slightly slower because block-wise encoding cost is added. On Ouro-1.4B at context lengths 4K, 16K, and 32K, it is +9%, +7%, and +5% at 0.5 bits and +8%, +6%, and +4% at 0.25 bits, with the overhead shrinking as context grows (Fig. 8a). On Ouro-2.6B it is 5–9% slower. The time breakdown in Appendix D.3 reports that with batch 16 and 2K input prompts, attention time per generated token falls from 1.87ms for bf16 to 0.63ms (0.5 bits) and 0.54ms (0.25 bits) for LoopVQ, and that encoding accounts for under 1% of decode time and 5–7% of prefill time. At batch 1, attention dominates decode time at 32K for bf16, but for LoopVQ attention stays smaller than the linear layers.

Throughput. For long generations, the KV cache limits batch size.

In Fig. 7 of the paper, the horizontal axis is batch size (up to 128), the vertical axis is throughput (tok/s), and the three panels are for output lengths 4K, 8K, and 16K (all with 2K inputs). The gaps between the vertical line at bf16’s maximum batch and the LoopVQ curve are shown as 3.2x, 3.7x, and 4.3x. On Ouro-2.6B-Thinking, whose cache is heavier, they are 5.0x, 5.2x, and 6.1x, and on an A100 (40GB) they are 2.8x–3.7x (Appendix D.1, D.2). On the A100, 32K decode latency drops to −51% at 0.5 bits and −56% at 0.25 bits relative to bf16.

4.6 Effect of each design element and calibration data

Looking at the two elements separately (Table 4 of the paper, Ouro-1.4B), loop-axis grouping produces most of the gain. Adding fine-tuning (FT) on top has little effect on GSM8K, raises accuracy on HumanEval, and is most pronounced when added to TaSQ. Using both together gives the best or tied-best result in every setting. At 0.25 bits, grouping gives a larger gain over CQ when applied to TaSQ.

Calibration data also influences the results. Fig. 9 of the paper recalibrates while swapping the calibration corpus among WikiText-2, C4, and SlimPajama. CQ varies by up to 11 points on GSM8K, whereas TaSQ+LoopVQ varies by up to 4 points (GSM8K) and 1 point (HumanEval) and stays best on every corpus. Increasing the number of calibration sequences consistently raises accuracy (Table 5 of the paper, at 0.25 bits LoopVQ GSM8K 57.5→60.8, HumanEval 22.6→28.0, from 8 to 32 sequences).

Calibration cost is modest. On a single RTX 6000 Ada, Ouro-1.4B takes 6.1 min for $k$-means plus 2.3 min for fine-tuning, and Ouro-2.6B takes 14.3 min plus 5.9 min (on an A100, 5.5+2.0 min and 11.2+4.6 min), and even with more sequences the cost stays in the minutes range.

5. Limitations and when to apply it

Limitations stated by the authors. First, the efficiency comparison is only against BF16 serving. The serving efficiency of each method depends on kernels optimized for its own cache format, and since it is hard to match all methods to an equal level of optimization, they state that they avoided a comparison that would favor the most heavily optimized method. Second, they did not compare accuracy against FlashLoop and ResidualQuant, KV cache quantization methods designed for looped transformers. Both use scalar quantization at a minimum of 1 bit per element and target 2–4 bits, and they do not present settings below that, so they cannot be matched at the same bit width in the sub-1-bit regime LoopVQ targets.

Conditions for application. This technique assumes a loop axis, so it cannot be used as-is on ordinary LLMs without an iterative structure. Even with an iterative structure like Huginn, segments that are not looped, such as the prelude and coda, must be encoded separately in the existing way. The gain is pronounced for long contexts and long generations, and for short contexts or prefill-heavy workloads it can actually be slower because of encoding cost. The codebook must be calibrated per model and separately for the Thinking variants (depending on the calibration corpus, CQ varies by up to 11 points on GSM8K), and although calibration cost is in minutes, it must be redone each time.

Assessment. For serving looped models that have few parameters but are cache-bound, over long contexts and long generations, LoopVQ is a better option than existing vector quantization in the sub-1-bit regime. However, the efficiency comparison was against BF16 serving, and comparisons under kernel optimization equal to other quantization methods, as well as accuracy comparisons with FlashLoop and ResidualQuant, remain open.
