item.title: SpecPilot: Autonomous Algorithm Discovery and Systems Optimization for Speculative Decoding
item.description:
Paper

Introduction

Speculative decoding is a technique that commits multiple tokens together when a large model is invoked once, accelerating language model decoding where memory bandwidth is the bottleneck. This paper points out that public implementations of this technique fail to capture much of the permissible speedup, and has a coding agent re-measure the bottleneck for each deployment environment and discover optimizations on its own. The result is a large increase in speedup for both single requests and batching, without training or loss of output quality.

1. Background: what you need before reading

1.1 What speculative decoding does

When a drafter (a small model that proposes) proposes multiple tokens after a prefix, the target (the large model that verifies) verifies those tokens in a single forward pass. Each token uses one row. In greedy decoding, it accepts the longest prefix matching the target’s argmax and appends that argmax as a bonus. This paper calls the number of tokens accepted in one pass $\tau$, where $\tau \in [1, m+1]$.

Here, the “published baseline implementation” is called stock; stock supports both the drafter drawing tokens one at a time sequentially (EAGLE-3) and drawing an entire block of 8–16 positions in a single pass (DFlash2, DSpark). The parallel drafter outputs the top 16 candidates and their scores at each position. DSpark adds a Markov head on top, conditioning the score on the previous token.

$$\ell_s(y) = \mathrm{bases}(y) + \left[W_1[x_{s-1}],\, W_2[y]\right]$$

In other words, DSpark takes the “immediately preceding token” as input when scoring candidates (Equation 1 in the original).

1.2 ‘Lossless’ and ’exact pass’

In this paper, an exact pass means a pass that verifies once with the target’s exact weights. Lossless is defined as “every accepted token lies on a path verified by an exact pass and equals that pass’s argmax.” However, even an exact pass can differ slightly from its own earlier AR result due to floating-point operation order such as GEMM tiling order, and this happens only for tokens whose logits are nearly tied. In practice, when stock first diverges from AR, the log-probability difference between the two tokens was at most 0.232 nat. A low-precision verification pass, by contrast, can change even tokens far from a tie. So checking losslessness would require outputs to be exactly identical, which would then reject even lossless systems.

1.3 Terminology

Term Meaning Why it was needed in this article
Speculative decoding A technique where a small model proposes tokens and a large model verifies them at once, committing multiple tokens together The paper’s starting point
Drafter / target The small proposing model / the large verifying model To separate “proposal” from “verification”
stock The baseline implementation published by each project The baseline the paper compares against
$\tau$ The number of tokens accepted per step To decompose speed into “token count × step cost”
Exact pass A pass that verifies with exact target weights The reference for defining losslessness
Lossless A state where every accepted token is on an exact-pass path and equals its argmax What guarantees “output unchanged”
exact replay A method that re-executes recorded draft lattices and target outputs offline, recomputing only tree selection and verification To reproduce metrics like $\tau$ without timing noise
paired run A measurement method that runs the same request on two GPUs and compares the times of the two systems To distinguish a few-percent gain from noise

2. Problem: why public implementations are slow

2.1 For a single request, step time is “reading weights”

When there is one request, adding more candidate rows to verify barely increases time. Before the first round, GEMM time was 17.88 ms verifying one row and 18.58 ms for 64 rows. Increasing rows 64× added only 0.7 ms.

The reason is that most of the step time goes to reading target weights from memory. Of the 23.61 ms single step measured after the first round, 80% went to reading target weights (linear layers and LM head). At H100’s peak bandwidth of 3.35 TB/s, reading these weights takes 92% of the time needed to read all bytes in the step.

So for a single request, “the cost of reading weights” is effectively fixed, and adding verification rows on top is nearly free. Yet stock does not use that free region. Among candidates the drafter sorted by score at each position, it picks only the single highest-scoring one and verifies it as one chain. The other candidates are discarded, and those discarded candidates often contain the next token the target actually wants.

2.2 In batching, each request adds row cost

Once batching kicks in, the order flips. Each request takes its share of attention, recurrent state updates, and prefill computation, and prefilling a new prompt re-reads the weight stream. So weight reading no longer dominates the step. stock’s speedup over AR is 3.40× at 1 request and drops to 1.89× at 24 requests on FP8 Qwen3.8-27B, and from 3.73× to 1.49× at 32 requests on Qwen3.5-4B (BF16).

The “verify more” optimization that was a gain for a single request turns into a straight loss under batching, because each verification row now costs real time.

2.3 The same technique cuts both ways across deployments

The optimal choice depends on serving shape (single request/batching), drafter, target, and GPU. The original gives three cases.

  • Checking first with a low-precision target copy: Fast for a single request, but in BF16 Qwen3.8-27B batching the extra check approaches the cost of a whole step, making it 13% slower.
  • Draft tree ignoring parent conditioning: Because DSpark scores conditioned on the previous token, a tree that ignores this conditioning accepts only half the tokens a conditioned tree accepts.
  • Hybrid target and a different GPU: In Qwen3.8-27B, 48 of 64 layers are Gated DeltaNet (GDN), so the recurrent state must be updated separately for each tree node. Meanwhile, RTX PRO 6000 lacks Hopper’s wgmma instruction, so kernels must be rewritten.

There is no universal optimization. The more per-deployment manual tuning people do, the harder it becomes to sustain.

2.4 A small example: candidates discarded in one step

The table below is an illustrative example built to explain the structure and is not from the original paper. The paper’s $\tau$ measurements are presented separately later.

Input — After the prefix “The cat sat on the”, DFlash2 proposed 4 positions in one pass. The candidates and scores at each position, and the token stock picked for its chain, are as follows.

Position Drafter candidates and scores Token stock put in the chain
1 mat(.40) > rug(.25) > floor(.20) mat
2 is(.55) > was(.30) is
3 soft(.30) > warm(.28) > a(.25) soft
4 bed(.35) > place(.30) bed

Change, omission, rejection — stock hands this chain to the target at once and verifies it in positional order.

Verification order Prefix verified Target argmax at that prefix Chain token Verdict What remains
1 The cat sat on the mat mat match → accept 3 candidates at position 2
2 … mat is is match → accept 3 candidates at position 3
3 … mat is a soft mismatch → verification stops target argmax a added as bonus
4 — — bed omitted (unverified) 2 candidates at position 4 unverified

Output — stock commits three tokens mat is a in one step.

What remains — At the point where verification broke off, the drafter already had the token the target wanted among its candidates. That is a at position 3 and place at position 4 that follows. stock discards this branch, but in tree verification that keeps candidates as branches, mat → is → a → place survives and can accept up to four tokens in one step.

The original quantifies the size of this structure with exact replay. stock’s 8-position chain accepts only $\tau = 4.25$ tokens, whereas the oracle that keeps accepting as long as the target’s greedy token is within the drafter’s top 16 gives 6.42 at 8 positions and 8.20 at 16 positions. That is, reviving discarded candidates nearly doubles tokens accepted per step.

3. Method: SpecPilot’s search loop

SpecPilot has a coding agent iterate in rounds to find “it depends on the deployment” without manual tuning. Each round starts from the previous round’s final system, and a new deployment starts from stock plus the verified entries in memory.

3.1 The flow of one round

Phase Reads Does State left behind
Phase 0 cost model Last round’s draft lattice, kernel profile, measured step time Recomputes $\tau$ and $c$ and picks the largest gap among the ceiling’s three factors to set direction One gap for the next round to attack
Phase 1 exploration The chosen gap Gives one direction to one GPU and a sub-agent implements it as a patch. The sub-agent first measures headroom with the cheapest evidence (exact replay, microbenchmark, 1-GPU timing), and builds a new algorithm only when headroom after subtracting runtime overhead is at least 3% Patch candidates per direction and estimated gains
Phase 2 integration Per-direction patches An integration sub-agent stacks patches on the current best system and times them under the same approval rule A new system if approved
Phase 3 kernel tuning Profile of the new system A kernel sub-agent starts with the kernel farthest from its byte floor Tuned kernels
Phase 4 seal check Unseen requests, up to 4096-token outputs Compares time against stock (paired run) and reruns token forcing to decide A sealed final system if it passes
Memory distill Passed mechanisms Stores code delta, variant registry, correctness contract, and a summary of evidence, limits, and unverified areas as one entry A memory entry that new deployments and the next round draw on again

3.2 The cost model computes “remaining speed”

The cost model decomposes speedup over AR into two terms.

$$S(N) = \frac{\tau(N)}{c(N)}, \qquad c(N) = \frac{T_{\text{step}}(N)}{T_{\text{AR}}}$$

$\tau(N)$ is the number of tokens a step accepts when verifying $N$ rows, $T_{\text{step}}(N)$ is step time including drafting, $T_{\text{AR}}$ is AR step time in the same engine, and $c(N)$ is the relative cost. Because it separates whether the speed is lacking due to small $\tau$ or large $c$, each round can choose which of the two to attack.

It also computes a ceiling to compare how far it can go. The “byte floor” for each kernel type is the larger of the time to process FLOPs at 60% of peak dense throughput and the time to read bytes at 90% of peak bandwidth. The ceiling decomposes into the product of three factors.

$$\frac{\tau_{\text{best}}}{\tau} \cdot \frac{T_{\text{prof}}}{T_{\text{floor}}} \cdot \frac{T_{\text{step}}}{T_{\text{prof}}}$$

The first is “if the tree is built better” ($\tau$ that any tree could accept), the second is “if kernels are made faster” (the gap between profiled step time and the byte floor), and the third is “if time outside the profile is reduced” (the gap between the profile and actual step time). Each round attacks the largest factor.

3.3 Agents propose, the controller approves

The key is separating the agent that modifies the system from the controller that measures performance. A master agent plans directions, each direction occupies one GPU and a sub-agent implements it as a patch. The controller is a script that agents can only call and cannot modify. It runs two systems on two GPUs with the same requests to make a paired run, running twice and swapping the GPUs.

The approval criteria are strict. The 95% confidence lower bound of the gain must exceed “1% + twice stock’s own noise” (stock noise is below 0.1% for a single request on H100), and a patch that also changes the output must exceed about 3%, because patches that change output carry the possibility of loss.

3.4 Token forcing: checking output against stock too

There are two risks here. A few-percent gain can be buried in timing noise, and more dangerously, an agent rewarded only for speed can take a shortcut that slightly changes the output. The authors built a defective system with a bias planted in the logits and measured accuracy. The defective system’s accuracy change fell in an interval containing zero (lossless −0.3 points [−1.6, +0.7], defective −1.6 points [−3.6, +0.3]), so accuracy could not catch the defect.

So they inspect output directly with token forcing. They pass the system’s output tokens one by one through a scorer (the target of a stock engine using an FP32 LM head) via teacher forcing, and count it as a mismatch when a system token differs from the scorer’s argmax. The margin of a mismatch is the log-probability difference to that argmax. stock itself shows mismatches on 0.72% of tokens due to kernel rounding, almost all of them ties.

There are two decision rules. Reject if the mismatch rate is 0.5%p higher than stock, or if large mismatches (events) with margin at least $2\delta$ are more frequent than stock. Here $\delta$ is the near-tie threshold that Phase 0 sets by rounding “the maximum margin when stock first diverges from AR” up to a multiple of 1/8.

The results were clear. The lossless systems’ mismatch rates were 0.73% and 0.52%, keeping to stock’s 0.72% and 0.53%, while the defective system was filtered out at 2.0% and 2.4%. Of the defective system’s 200 large-mismatch events, 192 and 191 were unexplained.

3.5 Verified optimizations accumulate in memory

A passed mechanism is stored as one memory entry. An entry contains a code delta relative to the other entries it requires, a variant registry, correctness contracts and options, and a summary of evidence, limits, and unverified areas. An entry survives only “when applying it to stock together with its required entries exactly reproduces the original system’s code.” Reused entries are retuned and remeasured in a new deployment and are not counted as new discoveries. Memory currently has 140 entries, each with up to 12 requirements. These 140 entries cover every evaluated configuration, and 15 of them are specific to sm 120 (RTX PRO 6000).

3.6 What actually changed across three rounds

Three rounds on single-request Qwen3.8-27B (DFlash2, H100) are a good example. Throughput went from stock’s 184 tokens/s to 416 tokens/s in three rounds. Each round the cost model recomputed the ceiling and changed the target.

Round Gap indicated by the ceiling What the agent built Throughput Evidence
1 $\tau$ (token count) best-first tree verification 184 → 270 tokens/s Extra rows are nearly free, so the tree’s effect dominates. Exact replay showed there were few better trees for this lattice, moving the next gap to step cost
2 Step cost (weight bytes) W12 12-bit weights 270 → 370 tokens/s Weight reading is 80% of the step. Byte arithmetic identified 25% of the 15.30 ms weight read as headroom, and a denser 11-bit variant was rejected because a microbenchmark showed 3× slower decoding
3 Unit of the step TLV (two drafts per exact pass) 370 → 416 tokens/s The W12 single-pass step is about 25% above the byte floor and the tree had hit the lattice limit, so the remaining gain lay in the ceiling’s assumption itself, “one exact pass per draft”

Approvals came in pieces per round. In round 2, the first patch was approved at 1.076× in a paired run and the revised kernel at 1.063×, and W12 was sustained through three approvals across two rounds. Round 3’s approvals were tail-step skip 1.010×, INT4 drafter 1.022×, W12 layout/boundary correction 1.045×, TLV 1.037×, prefill graph/Q-pass gate 1.015×, and draft-exact-pass fusion 1.010×.

There is an experiment comparing the effect of the cost model. In the same environment, a single-agent loop with only the cost model removed reached just 1.34× over stock after three rounds. SpecPilot reached 2.13×. The difference lay in the kind of bottleneck. The loop without the cost model dug only into the visible metric “tokens per step,” adding a 24-node tree, longer drafter blocks, and cheaper drafter weights. It did not touch target weight reading, which was 80% of the step.

4. Four techniques the agent found

All discovered mechanisms are lossless. As defined earlier, every accepted token is on an exact pass and matches that pass’s argmax. Approaches that do not keep snapshots or that rewind the recurrent state only change the exact pass’s own rounding, so losslessness is preserved.

4.1 W12: a 12-bit lossless weight format

If the bottleneck for a single request is weight reading, the direct approach is to reduce the number of bytes read. A binade is an interval divided by powers of two ($2^e$ or more and less than $2^{e+1}$). For each output channel, W12 picks a 16-binade window $[E_n-15, E_n]$ covering most of that channel’s weights and stores the weights inside the window in 12 bits.

Plane Bits Value stored In the 8-bit view
A 1 + 3 Sign + top 3 mantissa bits Included
E 4 Exponent offset $e-(E_n-15)$ Included
B 4 Bottom 4 mantissa bits Excluded

That is, A+E is the “8-bit view,” and that is what the Q pass reads. Weights outside the window, or that are zero or denormal, go into a per-channel sparse escape list and are restored exactly. The escape rate is only $7.33\times10^{-5}$ on Qwen3.8-27B, and across 8 models it compresses to 12.013–12.020 bits/weight. Converted-layer weights shrank from 44.67 GB to 33.58 GB, and total weight memory from 51.1 GB to 39.8 GB (Tables A2, A6). At load time the server checks the restored tensors bit-for-bit against the checkpoint.

More important than the format is the kernel. W12 GEMM restores 12 KB records (a 128×64 weight tile, the first 8 KB the 8-bit view and the last 4 KB the low mantissa bits) in registers and passes them as wgmma register operands. The restore arithmetic hides behind memory reads and effectively disappears. Because the stream-K kernel splits the reduction loop across thread blocks in a fixed order, GEMM is deterministic.

Performance must be viewed at two levels. At the kernel level, W12 GEMM beat cuBLAS on every projection layer of Qwen3.8-27B: 1.19–1.47× at 1 row and 1.17–1.35× at 32 rows. However, the first W12 kernel only reached 0.80–0.89× of cuBLAS time at 32 rows, i.e. it was slower. On RTX PRO 6000, with no wgmma, it was ported to mma.sync and achieved 1.18–1.68× across all 13 tile shapes. The 128-byte swizzled activation layout enables 48-row tiles, so W12 GEMM time stays flat as rows grow, while cuBLAS slows from 8 rows onward.

The LM head is handled separately. On H100, W12 leaves the LM head in BF16 but uses an INT8 copy that discards “tokens proven unable to be the argmax” via a per-row Cauchy–Schwarz error bound, then exactly rescores only the surviving tokens. The argmax never changes. LM head latency dropped from 878 µs to 482 µs. On RTX PRO 6000 this certified head was slower than BF16 (2598 µs vs. 1750 µs), so there it was converted to W12.

4.2 Best-first tree verification for hybrid targets

From the candidate lattice produced by the parallel drafter, stock verifies only one high-scoring chain. SpecPilot’s tree scores each edge with the log-softmax score “given the parent,” producing a best-first tree that keeps the $N$ nodes with the highest path score $\sum \log p(\text{child} \mid \text{parent})$. Unlike DDTree’s marginal scores, it includes parent conditioning, so the same builder runs unchanged on DSpark lattices.

The drafter draws 16 positions, twice the training block size, and the tree verifies 32 nodes to depth 15 (verifying more nodes than draft positions).

The problem is recurrent layers. A GDN head updates a fixed-size state $h$ at each token.

$$h_t = \alpha_t\left(I - \beta_t k_t k_t^\top\right) h_{t-1} + \beta_t k_t v_t^\top, \qquad o_t = h_t^\top q_t$$

stock verification snapshots $h$ at each verification position, so using a tree requires one snapshot per node. At $N=24$, per-node snapshots need about 18 GB. SpecPilot drops snapshots and recomputes the state along each root path. A path-verification kernel walks each path from the committed state, and a commit kernel replays accepted paths through all 48 GDN layers, matching stock kernels and chains bit-for-bit.

A faster kernel is the WY verification kernel. Following TreeWY, it turns the chain of rank-one updates into matrix products and solves all paths at once on tensor cores. It splits an FP32 state into three BF16 pieces that together represent the full 24-bit mantissa exactly, and tensor-core products accumulate in FP32, staying within one BF16 ulp of the path-kernel output. Across 48 GDN layers on H100, verification dropped from 1485 µs with the path kernel to 542 µs with the WY kernel, and commit from 208 µs to 119 µs.

The tree effect itself is reproduced with exact replay. On an 8-position lattice, $\tau$ rose from stock’s chain 4.25 to 5.38 for a 32-node best-first tree, and drafting 16 positions reaches 5.85 at 32 nodes and 6.25 at 63 nodes. At 16 nodes, the best-first tree matches an EAGLE-2-style top-4 tree (5.03 vs. 5.02) and beats the Sequoia tree (4.71). Wider trees are a loss. In the W12 system, one node above 32 costs about 0.17 ms per step, not 0.063 ms.

4.3 TLV: two-stage verification that rations exact passes

TLV breaks the ceiling’s assumption, “one exact pass per draft.” One cycle consists of two drafts and two passes.

 flowchart LR

 D1["Draft ① (1.05 ms)<br/>builds a candidate tree"] --> Q["Q pass (11.5 ms)<br/>inspects the tree reading only the 8-bit view<br/>does not touch the target's KV cache or recurrent state"]
 Q --> C["Commit chain C<br/>Q-pass argmax path + bonus token<br/>does not accept tokens yet"]
 C --> D2["Draft ② (1.05 ms)<br/>builds a fresh subtree from the end of C"]
 D2 --> E["Exact pass (14.9 ms)<br/>verifies C + 32-node subtree with W12 weights<br/>updates the KV cache and recurrent state here"]
 E --> G["Append time 1.6 ms"]
 G --> O["Output: longest matching path confirmed by the exact pass + bonus<br/>11.67 tokens per exact pass"]

The colors mean three things. Purple is the stage where the drafter builds candidates, independent of target state. Blue is a pass that only inspects without changing the target’s KV cache and recurrent state. Orange is the only pass that actually updates target state. This color boundary is exactly the boundary of losslessness, because only the orange pass accepts tokens.

The Q pass truncates the subtree redrawn from the end of C to $N-|C|$ nodes and attaches it under C, and one exact pass verifies the combined 32-node tree and accepts the longest matching path. In TLV, $\tau$ means tokens accepted per exact pass, and $T_{\text{step}}$ is the time of the two-pass cycle including both drafts.

The key is that the Q pass does not use a separate low-precision target model. It reads the 8-bit view already nested in the W12 record (the first 2/3 of the record) as-is. With discarded mantissa bits set to the midpoint, the Q pass matches the exact pass’s top-1 token at 98.7% of positions. So the Q pass only “pre-selects the path the exact pass will accept.”

The result is that tokens accepted per exact pass rose from 6.16 to 11.67 (Figure A3). The final H100 system’s cycle is about 30 ms, the sum of 2×1.05 ms drafting, 11.5 ms Q pass, 14.9 ms exact pass, and 1.6 ms appending.

4.4 Three choices for batching

In batching, every row is a cost. So these three mechanisms only choose “which rows to draft and verify.” Because they only choose, they are lossless.

Shared node budget. Instead of dividing a budget among requests, the whole step shares one node budget and fills nodes starting from the highest path log-probability. A best-first tree is prefix-closed, so each request’s share is also a valid tree. At 24 requests on an FP8 target, a 192-node budget sits in the flat region of target GEMM cost, so cost does not grow until the next tile. On DSpark, this approach accepted 6–14% more tokens than giving each request an equally sized tree.

Per-request drafter block. Each request chooses its number of draft positions from 16, 12, and 8 based on recent acceptance rate and draft confidence on the GPU, with tree depth limited accordingly. This keeps the FP8 target’s drafter within 256 rows, which is the end of the drafter GEMM’s flat region and holds 17–24 requests. The measured gain is 1.040×.

Prompt admission. Prompt rows for a new prompt are merged into the verification step, so one weight stream handles the prompt and generation together. This pays off only when computation is hidden behind weight reads, so the scheduler admits only prompts it would have made wait anyway. On FP8 targets, prompts up to 384 tokens enter as chains of prompt rows, and both FP8 final systems use this approach. In BF16 Qwen3.8-27B batching, prompts enter in a 128-row region that shares the verification step’s projection and MLP GEMMs. Admitting only waiting prompts gave a 3.5% gain at 24 requests (a non-paired measurement), and admitting all short prompts was a loss.

5. Results

5.1 Measurement conditions

Four targets (Qwen3.8-27B, Qwen3.5-4B, Gemma-4-12B, Muse-Glimmer-30B), three drafters (DFlash2, DSpark, EAGLE-3), two GPUs (H100 SXM5, RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition, sm 120, measured bandwidth 1.51 TB/s), and five benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH500, HumanEval, MBPP, MT-Bench). The server uses a fixed SGLang v0.5.20 build. All single-request runs are BF16, and batching ran only on H100 with FP8 (Qwen3.8-27B) and BF16 (Qwen3.5-4B, Gemma-4-12B). Decoding is fixed to greedy with thinking enabled. The agent is Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code.

The gain is defined as the geometric mean of the output-speed ratio across benchmarks and batch sizes. All gains over stock come from sealed final systems obtained through two paired runs, and every final system passed token forcing. Speedup over AR is measured by interleaving AR, stock, and SpecPilot.

The stock baselines were also tuned per GPU and serving shape. On H100, DFlash2 runs with its training block size and deployment settings as-is. RTX PRO 6000’s best stock is block 12 + Triton attention, 9.9% faster than the H100 setting. No EAGLE-3 configuration beat the default by more than 2.4%. On H100 single request, stock DFlash2 using a DDTree tree was 4.82× over AR as a stronger baseline.

For single requests, most of the gain comes from $\tau$. stock verifies only one chain and $\tau$ stays around 4–5, whereas SpecPilot raises tokens accepted per exact pass from 6.16 to 11.67 with TLV (Figure A3) and $\tau$ in Table 1 rises to 12.64–13.08. The weaker stock is, the larger the gain. Gemma-4-12B has stock slower than AR (0.68×) and uses the sequential drafter EAGLE-3, and its most improved batch was 3.11×.

Absolute speedup in batching is lower than for single requests. Because row costs are real in batching, doubling $\tau$ does not translate into as much gain as for a single request. On FP8 Qwen3.8-27B it is 4.16× vs. AR at 16 requests (stock 2.20×) and 3.72× at 24 requests (stock 1.89×). BF16 Qwen3.8-27B is 5.94× at 6 requests and 5.39× at 10 requests. $\tau$ itself also rose in batching: 5.2–5.6 on FP8 targets (stock 4.5–4.6) and 5.7–6.0 on BF16 (stock about 4.6).

The sealed final systems beat stock on every benchmark and every batch size. Single-request gains ranged from 2.08× on MT-Bench (H100, DFlash2) to 2.55× on MATH500 (PRO 6000, DFlash2). Gemma-4-12B’s gain grew with batch size, from 2.80× at 16 requests to 3.43× at 48 requests.

5.4 When memory moves to a new deployment

Memory did real work when moving to different drafters and models on the same GPU.

To DSpark. Applying the tree, W12, and TLV entries to the new DSpark lattice in a single approval produced a sealed 2.110×, and an INT6 copy for the Q pass was added.

To EAGLE-3. In a new deployment attaching the sequential drafter EAGLE-3 to Gemma-4-12B, the agent reimplemented two designs from memory (W12 on the MLP, prompt admission). The first round’s seal check gave 2.67×, and afterward acceptance-probability-calibrated node selection, prompt admission, an n-gram chain attached to the EAGLE tree, and a single-KV-head attention kernel brought it to a final 3.11×.

To a new GPU platform. RTX PRO 6000 has 99 KB of shared memory per thread block and no wgmma. Porting H100’s tree and W12 entries (W12 to mma.sync, tree verification to a Triton attention backend) gave a sealed 1.92× by itself. Adding split-KV verify attention (splitting a request’s KV sequence across thread blocks) and INT6/INT8 Q-pass copies brought it to 2.44×. This exceeds that deployment’s ceiling of 2.12×, which TLV could do because the ceiling assumes “one draft per pass.”

To a new model family. Muse-Glimmer-30B, a dense model without recurrent layers, reused memory except for the GDN entries. The first approval applied the tree, W12, TLV, and INT6/INT8 copies at once, and added exact sliding-window attention to a 32-node tree. Kernel fusion including L2 prefetching brought it to a final 2.21×.

Beyond speculative decoding. W12 is a format independent of speculative decoding. Running only AR decoding in SGLang is 1.19–1.28× faster for a single request (Muse-Glimmer-30B, Qwen3.8-27B, Gemma-4-12B, Llama-3.1-8B) and 1.13–1.20× faster at 32 requests. With 14–22% less weight, the KV cache pool grows 2.03× on Qwen3.8-27B and 2.54× on Muse-Glimmer-30B. It is not tied to the engine either. In Hugging Face Transformers with static cache and CUDA graphs, Llama-3.1-8B decodes 1.12× faster for a single request.

6. Limitations

Scope stated by the authors. A mechanism’s gain depends on serving shape. Wide tree, W12, and TLV were all gains in three single-request Qwen3.8-27B deployments, but in batching a 24-node tree was a 14.9% loss on FP8 targets, a 24-position block was a 9.9% loss on BF16, and TLV was a 13% loss. TLV’s Q pass reduces only attention and recurrent-layer bytes, so when the Q pass accounts for 0.80–0.88 of the step, one cycle must accept nearly twice the tokens of a single-pass step just to break even. Conversely, the “choose rows” family (shared node budget, per-request block, prompt admission) is a gain in batching.

The ceiling’s assumptions are also not exact. The byte floor is set by the 60%/90% rule, and the ceiling assumes “one exact pass per draft.” After TLV broke that assumption, it actually exceeded the ceiling (2.12×).

The loop is expensive. One round takes 7–20 hours and 20–86 GPU-hours. The 13 completed rounds total 164 hours and 530 GPU-hours, and only 54 of the 486 code changes the agent made led to approval. The agent API cost itself is not quantitatively reported in the original (not reported in the original).

The definition of losslessness also includes stock’s own floating-point rounding. For tokens whose logits are nearly tied, it can differ from AR.

A judgment the reader adds. The evaluation is limited to greedy decoding (thinking mode), and whether the same gains hold under sampling or beam search has not been verified (not reported in the original). GPUs are also only the two platforms H100 and RTX PRO 6000, so transfer to other generations and vendors is unknown. The evaluated mechanisms were measured on a fixed SGLang v0.5.20 build, and only W12 has engine-independent results. The verification that agent-written code receives still needs a human to read it.

7. Summary

The substance of this paper is not a particular kernel but a procedure. SpecPilot first measures “where speed is leaking” with a cost model, hands the gap to agents, has a controller approve with paired runs and seal checks, and keeps passed mechanisms in memory to carry to the next deployment. This procedure led to weight compression (W12), tree verification, and exact-pass rationing (TLV) for single requests, and to row-selection rules for batching.

In practice, two things must come together. One is an artifact usable on its own, like W12, and the other is the procedure “re-measure that environment’s bottleneck before applying.” W12 gives 1.19–1.28× beyond speculative decoding and grows the KV cache pool up to 2×. Trees and TLV, by contrast, are mechanisms that become losses when the serving shape changes, so it is better to rerun the cost model from scratch than to copy them as-is.

item.title: Kronecker Delta Rule for Long Context Linear Attention
item.description:
Paper

Introduction

As context grows longer, softmax attention’s compute grows quadratically with context length, and the key-value cache grows proportionally to context length. Linear attention, which avoids this, compresses context into a fixed-size matrix memory, but the problem remained that editing that memory disturbs other memories already stored. This paper proposes the Kronecker delta rule, which narrows the scope touched by a single update, and KronLSTM, which implements it as gates.

Background: How Is a Fixed-Size Memory Rewritten?

For each token, a transformer keeps all key-value pairs of preceding tokens and, when a query arrives, compares against all of them. The number of comparisons becomes the square of context length, and the number of pairs to store grows proportionally to context length. Linear attention folds this part. It folds information from tokens seen so far into a single matrix $S$, and when a query arrives it multiplies that matrix by a vector to retrieve the answer. The cost disappears, but all information is trapped inside the matrix, so how to later revise information already written becomes the problem.

The paper organizes this problem into two branches. First, if memory grows without bound, the retrieved values grow with it and training becomes unstable. LSTMs suppress accumulation with a forgetting gate, but to remember long contexts that gate must stay pinned at 1, so information from the beginning of the context is eventually diluted. xLSTM adds normalizer and stabilizer states to curb memory scale, but normalizing by a ratio of large numbers itself creates numerical and optimization instability in large models. Second, DeltaNet-style models using the delta rule keep memory bounded by converging to a stationary distribution, but when stored values are corrected, other stored values are also disturbed. Obtaining both properties at once is the starting point of this paper.

Let’s first look at what linear attention stores and how it reads. When token $t$ arrives, it computes key $k_t$ and value $v_t$ and adds their outer product $v_t k_t^\top$ to memory. When query $q_t$ arrives, it multiplies memory by the query to retrieve $h_t = S_t q_t$. This single multiplication reads out a weighted sum of the stored values (§2.1, Eq. 1).

The problem arises when this write is an addition. Continuously adding by the Hebb rule makes memory scale grow proportionally to context length, and later writes bury earlier values. There is no means to correct an association once stored. The delta rule solves this by first subtracting the value stored at the current $k_t$ position and then writing the new value $v_t$ (§2.1, Eq. 2). This takes one step toward making $S_t k_t$ closer to $v_t$, mathematically one gradient descent step on $\tfrac12 \|S_t k_t - v_t\|^2$. However, this correction direction is determined by the current memory content $(S_t k_t - v_t)$. So other values sharing a key with $k_t$ are also disturbed, and the interference accumulates as context grows longer.

A Small Example: The Trace a Single Update Leaves

The numbers below are not reported values from the paper but made up to illustrate the concept (not reported in the original). Take a 2×2 memory $S$ and set a new key/value, a target association, and a step size. The memory is laid out with values as rows and keys as columns.

Setting Value
Memory $S$ (rows=values, columns=keys) [[0.5, 0.7], [2.0, 0.9]]
New key to write $k$ [1, 0]
New value to write $v$ [0, 1]
Currently stored association $v^\top S k$ 2.0
Target association $c$ 1.0
Step size $\beta$ 0.5
Other pairs already stored $(k', v') = ([1,0], [1,0])$, $(k'', v'') = ([0,1], [0,1])$

After updating once with each of the two rules and placing the memory and the read results of the three pairs side by side, the difference becomes clear.

Rule Memory after update $S'$ Target pair read $v^\top S' k$ Key-only overlapping pair $v'^\top S' k'$ Pair orthogonal in both key and value $v''^\top S' k''$
Delta rule (Eq. 2) [[0.25, 0.7], [1.5, 0.9]] 2.0 → 1.5 0.5 → 0.25 (broken) 0.9 → 0.9
Kronecker delta rule (Eq. 3) [[0.5, 0.7], [1.5, 0.9]] 2.0 → 1.5 0.5 → 0.5 (preserved) 0.9 → 0.9

The delta rule makes the correction in the direction of the vector $S_t k_t - v_t$ and spreads it across the entire column in the $k$ direction. Thus the target association drops to 1.5, but other memories using the same key (0.5 → 0.25) are also disturbed. The Kronecker delta rule looks only at the single scalar $v^\top S k$ and reverses the error, and the reversal direction $v k^\top$ is, in this example, 1 only in the bottom-left cell of the 2×2 matrix with the rest 0. So only the target association drops to 1.5 and the remaining cells stay as they are. The value $[1,0]$ orthogonal to the new value $[0,1]$ is protected even when keys overlap.

Figure 1 of the original shows this difference across three models at once. The legend distinguishes ’newly stored cells’, ’erased cells’, and ‘cells changed by the update’, and a one-line summary sentence draws the conclusion. mLSTM’s update affects all stored values, Gated DeltaNet affects stored values with overlapping keys, and KronLSTM affects only stored values where both keys and values overlap. This single sentence is the paper’s entire claim.

Method: The Kronecker Delta Rule

Generalizing the idea from the previous example: read how strongly memory currently associates key $k_t$ with value $v_t$ as a single scalar, and move that scalar toward the target $c_t$. The correction direction is determined solely by the input pair $(k_t, v_t)$, not by the contents stored in memory (§2.1, Eq. 3).

$$ S_{t+1} = S_t - \beta_t \big(v_t^\top S_t k_t - c_t\big), v_t k_t^\top = \underbrace{S_t - \beta_t (v_t^\top S_t k_t) v_t k_t^\top}_{\text{erase}}

  • \underbrace{\beta_t c_t v_t k_t^\top}_{\text{write}} $$

The amount erased is determined by $\beta_t$ and the amount written by $c_t$. Reparameterizing the target as $\tilde c_t = c_t/\beta_t$ removes the step size from the write term, fully separating the two roles. If $c_t \equiv 1$, the association is stored with unit strength; if $c_t = 0$, only that association is erased.

Two things differ from the delta rule. First, the dimension of the correction target differs. The delta rule corrects a $d_v$-dimensional vector residual $S_t k_t - v_t$ and distributes it across the entire column in the key direction. The Kronecker delta rule corrects a single scalar residual and sends that amount in only one direction, $v_t k_t^\top$. Second, what the interference depends on differs. The change in the association of another stored pair $(k_i, v_i)$ is (§2.1, Eq. 5, Appendix Property A9)

$$ \Delta\big(v_i^\top S k_i\big) = -\beta_t \big(v_t^\top S_t k_t - c_t\big)\,\big(v_i^\top v_t\big)\,\big(k_t^\top k_i\big) $$

That is, it is proportional to the product of value overlap and key overlap. The delta rule’s interference is determined by key overlap alone, and Hebbian writes keep accumulating regardless of key or value. So a stored value orthogonal to the new value is protected even if keys overlap. The example above was exactly that case.

The amount of information that can be held also differs. The three elements $(k_t, v_t, c_t)$ impose one linear constraint on the $d_k d_v$ entries of memory. So exactly $d_k d_v$ scalar associations can be stored (Appendix Property A11), compared with the delta rule holding $d_k$ in units of value vectors. A single key can hold multiple mutually orthogonal values, and reading returns their sum.

This minimality is supported by proof, not observation (Appendix A3.4). Choosing the Newton step $\beta = 1/(\|k_t\|^2\|v_t\|^2)$, the correction amount is the smallest among possible corrections, and simultaneously minimal in all unitarily invariant norms such as Frobenius, spectral, and nuclear (Theorem A1, A2). More strongly, the only correction that does not leave the target key direction and target value direction is the one from this step (Theorem A3). And this definition is also the answer to why it disturbs other memories least. When probe pairs are isotropic, the expected interference is $\sigma_k^2\sigma_v^2\|E\|_F^2$, so the correction minimizing $\|E\|_F$ is exactly the one minimizing expected interference (Theorem A4).

Vectorized, this rule takes the same form as Widrow–Hoff online least squares. Using the Kronecker feature $a_t = k_t \otimes v_t$ and the vectorized memory $s = \mathrm{vec}(S)$, we get $v_t^\top S k_t = a_t^\top s$ (Appendix Property A7)

$$ s_{t+1} = \big(I - \beta_t a_t a_t^\top\big) s_t + \beta_t c_t a_t $$

which reduces to the above. Since the transition factor is a generalized Householder matrix that does not include $c_t$, it can be used as-is in DeltaNet’s chunkwise-parallel training scheme by replacing $k_t$ with $a_t$. The target value enters only the driving term. Moreover, when $\beta_t\|a_t\|^2 \in (1,2)$, negative eigenvalues appear in the transition factor, yielding the same state-tracking ability as the delta rule family.

Stability is summarized by two theorems (§2.1, Theorem 1, 2).

  • Expectation and stationary distribution. Since the update is linear, the expected iteration exactly satisfies $\mathbb{E}[s_{t+1}] = (I - \beta \bar A)\mathbb{E}[s_t] + \beta \bar b$. The unique fixed point of this recurrence is the least-squares memory $s_{LS} = \bar A^{-1}\bar b$, and the expectation converges linearly to it without bias at any order. The iteration sequence forms a time-homogeneous Markov chain on $\mathbb{R}^{d_k d_v}$, has a unique stationary distribution $\pi_\beta$, converges geometrically from any initialization, and the mean of the stationary distribution is exactly $S_{LS}$.
  • Memory norm bound. The Frobenius norm of the least-squares memory is sandwiched on both sides by the explained target energy. $\frac{\mathbb{E}[c^2]-\mathbb{E}[\rho^2]}{\lambda_{\max}(\bar A)} \le \|S_{LS}\|_F^2 \le \frac{\mathbb{E}[c^2]-\mathbb{E}[\rho^2]}{\lambda_{\min}(\bar A)}$. And in the non-expansive region $\beta\|a_t\|^2 \le 1$, the stationary state and every iteration starting from $S_0=0$ are bounded within $\mathbb{E}[\|S_t\|_F^2] \le 4\,\mathbb{E}[c^2]/\lambda_{\min}(\bar A)$. The 4 in front decays exponentially to 1 after the first step.

There is one point to be honest about here. The property of a stationary-state bound independent of length is itself a common feature of the delta rule family. DeltaNet has a corresponding bound (Appendix A4). What sets KronLSTM apart is the form of interference and capacity, not the existence of a bound. Also, this bound is the basis for replacing mLSTM’s normalizer and stabilizer states, but the Gated DeltaNet family does not use such states to begin with, so the advantage of ‘stable without normalization’ is a relative advantage over mLSTM·xLSTM.

The KronLSTM Block: Separating Forget, Erase, and Write

To lift the rule into an actual layer, each of the three terms in the update equation must be made a gate determined by the input (§2.2, Eq. 10).

$$ S_{t+1} = \underbrace{S_t F_t}_{\text{forget}} - \underbrace{\beta_t \big(v_t^\top S_t F_t k_t\big) v_t k_t^\top}_{\text{erase}} + \underbrace{c_t v_t k_t^\top}_{\text{write}} $$
  • Forget. $F_t = \mathrm{diag}(f_t)$ is a diagonal matrix multiplied only along the key dimension, so it keeps or decays the memory of each key direction differently depending on the input. Because the multiplication happens on the right, each column of memory decays independently.
  • Erase. $\beta_t$ is a per-head scalar gate, determined within (0,1) by feeding a linear projection of the input into a sigmoid (Eq. 11). It sets the degree of erasure.
  • Write. $c_t$ is also a per-head scalar gate determined within (0,1) (Eq. 11). It sets the degree of new writing.

The forget gate $f_t$ is made by raising a sigmoid to a per-head learned positive exponent: $f_t = (1 - \sigma((s_f)_t))^\alpha$, $\alpha = \exp(a_{\log})$ (Eq. 12). The sigmoid determines the retention rate of each key direction depending on the input, and the exponent readjusts that head’s retention time scale. Since $\alpha$ is learned in log space, the baseline retention time scale of each head spreads across different orders of magnitude.

Following the flow in Figure 3 of the original: split input $x_t$ into three linear projections (query, key, value), and pass each through a short causal depthwise convolution, SiLU, and $\ell_2$ normalization. Update memory $S_t$ with key and value, read $S_t q_t$ with the query, and pass through the output gate, per-head RMSNorm, and output projection to the next layer. The only state the block carries is the per-head memory; there are no mLSTM normalizer or stabilizer states. So it can directly replace the attention slot.

Since keys and values are $\ell_2$-normalized and $\beta_t$ is bounded in (0,1) by a sigmoid, $\beta_t \|k_t\|^2 \|v_t\|^2 = \beta_t < 1$. Every update lies in the non-expansive region, so Theorem 2 applies, and the forget gate’s entries being less than 1 makes convergence even stronger.

There is one more theoretical bonus (Appendix A5). Comparing how many steps the initial memory remains readable: in a design where keys and values are independent and values are normalized, $\bar A = \bar K \otimes \bar V$, so $\lambda_{\min}(\bar A) = \lambda_{\min}(\bar K)\lambda_{\min}(\bar V)$, and KronLSTM’s slowest-decaying mode decays $d$ times slower than DeltaNet’s. That is, at the same $\beta$, the retention time scale of initial memory is roughly $d$ times longer. The price, however, is the trade-off that ‘adaptation becomes $d$ times slower’. Losing less memory is not free.

Results

Experimental Setup

We pretrained a 1.5B parameter model on FineWeb-Edu for 100B tokens at 8k context. Baselines are Gated DeltaNet (GDN), Kimi Delta Attention (KDA), Mamba-3, and Gated DeltaNet-2 (GDN-2). All experiments were run in two settings. One is a pure linear model, and the other is a hybrid mixing sliding window attention (SWA) with window 2048 and linear attention at 5:1. SWA is used so that memory usage stays constant regardless of context length. The 1.5B model has 24 layers, hidden 2048, 16 heads, and $d_{qk} = d_v = 128$, and all comparison models share the corpus, tokenizer, optimizer, schedule, batch, and seed, changing only the sequence mixer. The numbers below are only values quoted from Tables 1–4, Tables A3·A4, and Figs. 5·6 of the original.

Language Modeling (Table 1)

Evaluated on five commonsense reasoning tasks (HellaSwag, PIQA, ARC-easy, ARC-challenge, WinoGrande) and LAMBADA. Avg-6 is the average accuracy over the six tasks.

Model Linear Avg-6 ↑ Linear LAMBADA ppl ↓ Hybrid Avg-6 ↑ Hybrid LAMBADA ppl ↓
GDN 57.73 12.58 57.99 12.95
Mamba-3 57.31 12.95 58.54 13.01
KDA 58.12 12.67 57.85 12.60
GDN-2 57.94 12.54 58.79 11.85
mLSTM 57.18 13.87 57.35 14.38
KronLSTM 59.72 11.72 59.56 11.18

KronLSTM is first on 5 of 6 tasks in the pure linear setting, and its Avg-6 is 1.6 points higher than the second-place KDA. In the hybrid setting it is also first in both Avg-6 and perplexity, but the gap to second-place GDN-2 is 0.8 points, narrower than in the linear setting. Mixing in SWA moves average accuracy by at most about 1 point. mLSTM, Mamba-3, and GDN-2 are most affected by SWA, while GDN and KDA barely change, and KronLSTM stays in the lead regardless of setting.

Recall Ability (Table 2)

We ran six real-document recall benchmarks at 2k context (SWDE, SQuAD, FDA, TriviaQA, NQ, DROP).

Model Linear Avg-6 ↑ Hybrid Avg-6 ↑
GDN 29.81 35.27
Mamba-3 28.41 36.96
KDA 29.17 36.01
GDN-2 29.39 35.85
mLSTM 28.79 36.37
KronLSTM 30.31 37.40

KronLSTM is first on average in both settings and first on 3 of 6 tasks. However, its strengths are concentrated in the early individual tasks. In the linear setting, DROP is 19.31, the lowest of the six models, and NQ is also 15.46, lower than mLSTM (15.11). The SWA hybrid raises overall by 5–9 points.

RULER Long-Context Retrieval (Table 3)

This task hides one sentence in a long context and asks the model to find it. Models pretrained at 8k are evaluated at 4k, 8k, and 16k, with 16k being extrapolation beyond the pretraining context. Tasks consist of S1–S3 (hiding a unique sentence among natural language sentences), MK, MQ, and MV.

Among linear models, KronLSTM is first or second at every length except S1, and first at every length on S3 and MQ. In the hybrid setting it is first in the length average of every task and first on all tasks at 16k. The widening gap with length is the paper’s core evidence, and it shows in the numbers for MQ and MV.

Linear model MQ 4k MQ 8k MQ 16k MV 4k MV 8k MV 16k
GDN 44.8 21.2 8.6 46.8 23.5 13.8
GDN-2 28.4 13.4 2.7 38.1 21.4 5.1
KronLSTM 47.2 24.8 12.7 43.3 24.6 17.6

On MQ, the gap to the leader widens from 2.4 points at 4k to 4.1 points at 16k. On MV, it trails GDN by 3.5 points at 4k, then leads by 1.1 points at 8k and 3.8 points at 16k. This is consistent with the interference analysis (Property A9), which says interference accumulates as context grows and the side with less interference gains the advantage.

S1 goes the opposite way. S1 is the most artificial task, repeating the same noise sentence, and pure linear KronLSTM falls far behind (66.2 at 4k, 11.6 at 16k, whereas GDN is 100.0 at 4k and 99.2 at 16k). The authors interpret this as residuals accumulating on repeated keys. In the hybrid setting, by contrast, KronLSTM is first even on S1 (16.2 at 16k, while baseline models are 12.6 or below). The hybrid’s baseline linear models fall on S1 to 51.8 at 4k, 26.6 at 8k, and 12.6 at 16k, which is roughly equal to the fraction of context covered by the window. This means the needle is recovered only when it lies inside the window, showing that they barely rely on recurrent memory.

32k Context Extension (§3.3, Table 4)

We branched the 1.5B linear KronLSTM and GDN-2 runs at 75B tokens and continued training the remaining 25B tokens at 32k context. The data is a long-document mixture drawn from ProLong-64K. This makes the token count exactly match the models pretrained at 8k. GDN-2 was chosen as the comparison baseline because it separates erase and write.

Model Avg-6 ↑ LAMBADA ppl ↓ Recall Avg-6 (2k) ↑
GDN-2 58.75 8.36 29.95
KronLSTM 60.19 7.66 31.08

Both models benefit from length extension. Recall accuracy rises and perplexity drops by about 4 points. KronLSTM leads in Avg-6 and perplexity and is better on 5 of the 6 recall tasks (only FDA is led by GDN-2: 18.15 vs 19.60).

On RULER NIAH as well (original Table A4), it leads GDN-2 from 16k on five natural-language-based tasks. At 16k, S3 is 41.8 vs 7.4, MV is 30.1 vs 8.9, and S2 is 27.6 vs 10.2; at 32k, S2 is 5.6 vs 2.6, S3 is 8.6 vs 0.8, and MV is 11.3 vs 7.2. The exception is S1 (pure linear 32k: KronLSTM 81.4, GDN-2 97.8).

Figure 4 of the original shows NIAH per-task accuracy from 4k to 32k side by side with GDN-2 in both linear and hybrid settings. Two things to read. First, at short lengths the two models are similar, but as length grows KronLSTM leads on most tasks. Second, at 32k both models’ retrieval accuracy drops substantially relative to 16k. It means the gap widens, not that high accuracy is maintained at 32k.

Effect of Separating Write Rules (Appendix A6.2)

There is a section checking what the design separating forget, erase, and write actually changes. The ablation results on the 1.5B/100B baseline are as follows.

Variant Avg-6 ↑ LAMBADA ppl ↓ Recall Avg NIAH 4k NIAH 8k NIAH 16k
Default (separated) 59.72 11.716 30.3 59.5 30.5 14.3
Apply β to both sides (coupled) 60.00 11.479 30.8 46.9 29.4 11.8
Remove value $\ell_2$ normalization 59.41 11.844 31.3 39.6 32.7 12.6
Fix target to 1 58.17 12.495 30.1 41.9 26.2 10.1

In language modeling the differences are small. The coupled variant is in fact marginally ahead within 0.3 points, and fixing the target to 1 worsens accuracy by 1.6 points and perplexity by 0.8 points. On recall benchmarks the coupled variant leads by 0.5 points and the no-normalization variant by 1.0 point. On NIAH, however, the order reverses. At 4k the default model leads the coupled variant by 12.6 points and the no-normalization variant by 19.9 points, and at 16k the default model leads all three variants. That is, the learned write gate and separated write matter most for recall within the pretraining context, and have little effect on language modeling.

State Tracking (§3.4)

Widening the range to (0,2) with $\beta_t = 2\sigma(w_\beta^\top x_t + b_\beta)$ enables the negative eigenvalue mechanism. We trained on parity, $S_3$ permutation, and modular arithmetic up to training length 128 and evaluated up to 1024. KronLSTM is comparable to GDN on parity and $S_3$ and both lead Mamba-3. On modular arithmetic, Mamba-3 wins.

Training Throughput (§3.5)

We measure end-to-end throughput of the pure linear 1.5B model on a single NVIDIA H100 (80GB). One step handles 16,384 tokens, and the shape varies from 2K×8 to 16K×1. KronLSTM runs at 36.8–44.5K tokens/s, 11–18% faster than GDN-2 across all batch shapes, and within 4–8% of KDA up to 8K×2. GDN with scalar decay still has the highest speed because its kernel is the cheapest. While a step contains two or more sequences, throughput is almost flat, and all models slow down at 16K×1. This is because the inter-chunk recurrence is parallelized only along the sequence and head directions.

Limitations and Open Questions

  • It loses on S1 (pure linear). On the most artificial task, made of repeated noise sentences, pure linear KronLSTM falls far behind GDN·GDN-2. The authors interpret this as residual accumulation on repeated keys. This condition does not apply to natural language retrieval, but the same problem could recur in data with many repeated patterns. In the hybrid setting it actually leads even on S1, so the condition dependence is large.
  • Absolute accuracy drops at 32k. It is true that KronLSTM leads GDN-2, but both models’ retrieval accuracy drops substantially at 32k relative to 16k. It is a relative advantage in ‘handling long contexts better’, not a claim that high accuracy is maintained at 32k.
  • State tracking is not always the best. It loses to Mamba-3 on modular arithmetic. It is strong for general-purpose long-term memory, but does not always win on tasks requiring precise tracking of specific state transitions.
  • The speed advantage is relative to a specific kernel implementation. It is faster than GDN-2 but slower than GDN, whose kernel is the simplest. This is a metric whose ranking could flip depending on the level of kernel optimization.
  • The validation scale is small. The main experiment is 1.5B/100B tokens, and the 400M results are in the appendix. At 400M/40B, KronLSTM is also first with an average of 48.43, raising the average by 2.1 points over mLSTM and lowering LAMBADA perplexity from 43.40 to 28.28, but both scales are small. The authors leave ‘scaling up and mixing with full softmax attention in a hybrid’ as future work (§4).
  • The stability guarantee does not hold under all conditions. The norm bound is a result in the non-expansive region $\beta\|a_t\|^2 \le 1$, and this property is common to the delta rule family that KronLSTM shares with DeltaNet (Appendix A4). The $d$ times longer retention time scale is the trade-off that ‘adaptation becomes $d$ times slower’ (Appendix A5.5). Also, this analysis rests on the assumption that inputs are i.i.d.
  • The scale at which it can be used in practice has not been reported. There is no result in the original reproducing the advantage at 1.5B/100B with larger models and longer contexts (not reported in the original).

In summary, KronLSTM is particularly suited to environments where context is long, many keys overlap, and natural-language-oriented information must be stored for a long time rather than repeated noise. Its value is that it narrows the scope touched by a single update, that this narrowness is guaranteed mathematically, and that the path from that guarantee to actual recall performance is connected end to end within the paper. Conversely, the advantage shrinks for inputs with many repeated patterns, for cases where a kernel fast enough with a simple recurrent structure is already available, and for tasks requiring precise state transitions such as modular arithmetic. The S1, modular, and 32k drops above are all results the paper reports itself, but any other judgment about applicability is the reviewer’s interpretation and not reported in the original.

item.title: TAO: Tool-Aware Joint Scheduling for LLM-Based Agentic Serving
item.description:
Paper

TAO: Tool-Aware Joint Scheduling for LLM-Based Agentic Serving

Original: Shuhuai Li et al., “TAO: Tool-Aware Joint Scheduling for LLM-Based Agentic Serving” (arXiv:2610.37230v1, preprint). The following account is based solely on the attached original text.

Introduction

Agents alternate between model inference and external tool execution. While a tool runs, that session’s GPU demand becomes suspendable; how this gap is used and which node the session is attached to when it returns determine response time. This paper proposes TAO, a framework that binds both problems into a single scheduling problem.

1. Problem: GPUs idle while tools run

1.1 Sessions and CGDC

Let us call the entire interaction of an agent a session. A session is a unit of work that alternates between model requests and tool calls. During a model request, the session occupies one GPU node; during tool execution, it waits for results outside the inference service.

The paper calls this arrangement CGDC (Clustered GPUs with Distributed CPUs). GPUs are clustered in nodes and share inference capacity, tools run on distributed CPUs outside them, and tool CPU/RAM is managed separately from the GPU admission budget. In other words, there is time that does not count against the GPU budget.

Roles are predefined as well. The scheduler records each session’s state and controls session admission, while the serving engine manages residency and eviction of physical KV cache (source: §2.1).

1.2 The expensive thing is “not being able to reuse the KV cache”

If a session’s next request can reuse the KV prefix produced by the previous turn, it skips prefill computation entirely. But whether that prefix is still alive is determined by “which node it was attached to” and “how much time has passed.” If a session returning after a tool finishes is placed on the same node, the cache is alive and it is fast; if it is sent to another node or pushed out by capacity pressure, prefill must be recomputed.

Conversely, evicting an active inference session requires immediate recomputation. When recomputation and restoration repeat, capacity is wasted on state that must be rebuilt (source: §2.1, §2.2).

1.3 interrupt and restart

At a tool boundary the scheduler can do two things.

  • interrupt: release the model admission of a session running a tool and return node resources.
  • restart: reassign a session whose tool has finished to an appropriate node and continue the existing interaction.

Both actions are just session state transitions, decoupled from the inference engine implementation. The paper’s starting point is that these two decisions ultimately reduce to the same session evaluation. Whether to interrupt is decided by ranking session values, and interrupted sessions enter the waiting pool together with newly arriving sessions. The paper handles joint evaluation in this waiting pool and the resume decision together (source: §2.2).

1.4 Two things existing schedulers miss

Existing serving systems mostly follow an “evaluate-then-decide” pattern. They evaluate node features at the session level, then decide where and when to serve.

Original Figure 1. The left panel shows the CGDC structure, and the right panel shows the two problems the paper targets.

  • Problem 1 — evaluation misses tool-return readiness. Tool timing was already used before, but only as a proxy for KV reuse or token count. For example, predicting tool duration to set KV retention time, or discounting a session’s token demand over time while a tool runs. These values get mixed into fixed scoring rules or hand-picked thresholds.
  • Problem 2 — decisions are made with per-session heuristics. The per-session scoring and routing rules of llm-d and SGLang allocate inference opportunities one session at a time. But sessions compete for the same node capacity, so admitting one session can remove the slot where a more valuable combination of other sessions would have fit. Labels in the right panel such as “Short but Low Cache,” “Urgent but Tool Running,” and “Session Still Waiting in Pool” point to this illusion (source: §1, §2.2).

2. A small example: while one session waits 12 seconds

To get the concept, follow a hypothetical coding session S. The numbers in this section are a hypothetical example for understanding and are not reported in the original.

Step What happens on the GPU State left behind
Input S sends its first request carrying 8,000 tokens of repository context. Node b1 prefills 8,000 tokens and creates a KV cache, and S occupies a GPU slot on b1.
Response The model generates 200 tokens. 200 tokens accumulate in S’s history.
Tool call S calls a test-running tool. The tool runs on CPU for 12 seconds. S returns its GPU slot (interrupt). Another session starts using b1’s slot, and b1’s KV cache remains but can be evicted under capacity pressure.
Value computation The scheduler computes the value of S and each node pair. The b1 pair gets cache credit (decayed from the observation), return readiness, and token count.
Change, skip, reject If b1 has room, DP assigns S to b1. Because the cache is alive, prefill computation is skipped. If b1 is full, S is assigned to another node b2 and prefill is recomputed. If no node has room, S is rejected and remains in the waiting pool.
Output After 12 seconds the tool result arrives and S requests the GPU again. If the assigned node’s cache is alive, it continues without prefill; otherwise it prefills again.

Two things emerge from this example. One is that “whether it returns to a node with a live cache” determines response speed, and the other is that “if you know when the tool will finish,” you can raise S as a GPU placement candidate just before that and eliminate the wait. The paper turns these two into values called ‘cache credit’ and ‘return readiness.’

3. Method

3.1 Two-stage pipeline: evaluate → decide

TAO operates in two stages. First it attaches a value to each session–node pair in the waiting pool (evaluation), and based on those values a dynamic program selects and places waiting sessions all at once (decision). Because evaluation and decision are separated, changing the value function leaves the scheduling procedure intact (source: §3.1).

 flowchart LR
 OBS["Observation: remaining KV on node b1 and<br/>remaining tool time of session S"] --> VAL["Value computation: k=decayed cache credit, r=1 (returning soon), t=token count"]
 VAL --> DP["DP: stores the best value per capacity state and<br/>assigns S to b1"]
 DP --> CHK["Re-check against live state just before apply<br/>(discard the plan if the selected session's signature or eligibility changes)"]
 CHK --> RUN["b1 reuses S's prefix<br/>skips prefill computation, generates first token"]
 DP -. "insufficient remaining capacity on b1" .-> BFD["BFD fallback: place on b2<br/>prefill must be recomputed"]
 BFD --> CHK

The concrete numbers in this diagram, like the example in Section 2, are not reported in the original. Each box is a state change. The first box is the observations (remaining cached token count and remaining tool time), the second is the result of turning them into values, the third is the process of recovering a placement from the values, and the last is what happens in actual execution. The dotted line is the case where capacity is insufficient and it takes another path. The serving engine’s role (physical KV allocation, reuse, eviction) does not disappear. The scheduler only reads on top of it “where the cache remains and when it can be reclaimed” as values. What shrinks is prefill recomputation, which disappears through cache reuse, and return waiting, which disappears through readiness.

3.2 Three values attached to each session–node pair

For each session i and node b pair, the paper attaches three values (source: §3.2, Eq. (2)).

$$v_{i,b} = (k_{i,b},\ r_i,\ t_i)$$
  • k_{i,b} — cache credit of session i remaining on node b. It shrinks as the observation ages.
  • r_i — return readiness. A 0/1 signal indicating whether session i is likely to request the GPU again soon because its tool is about to finish.
  • t_i — token count of session i. Represents the accumulated context size.

The key design is that these three are compared in lexicographic order rather than mixed in a weighted sum. Cache credit is examined first; if equal, readiness; if still equal, token count. The order itself is fixed, and only the values change over time. The paper justifies this order for three reasons (source: §3.2). First, prefix reuse eliminates prefill recomputation outright, so cache credit comes first. Second, when decay makes credits similar, readiness distinguishes sessions that are “returning soon” from those “still far away.” Third, when credit and readiness tie, larger accumulated context is preferred, but the optimizer also accounts for the capacity cost that context occupies when determining the overall assignment set.

The assignment constraints are as follows (Eq. (1)). Session i can go to only one node ($\sum_b x_{i,b} \le 1$), cannot exceed node b’s remaining capacity C_b ($\sum_i w_i x_{i,b} \le C_b$), and ineligible pairs cannot be assigned. The goal is the assignment that lexicographically maximizes the sum of values over all pairs (Eq. (3)).

3.3 Credit decays with observation age

Using the observed cached token count k⁰ as-is leaves old observations as a frozen signal. The paper computes credit by multiplying by $2^{-\tau/h}$ according to the time τ elapsed since observation (source: §3.3, Eq. (4)).

$$k_{i,b}(t) = k^0_{i,b}\,2^{-\tau/h},\quad \tau = \max(0,\, t - t^{\mathrm{obs}}_{i,b})$$

The half-life h is set to 10 seconds, and the computed credit is rounded before being used in evaluation. The basis is measurement. In a DeepSeek-V4 Flash trace on two nodes each with 4×H100, the binned median of observed cached token retention declines clearly over time (original Figure 3). The median was drawn with a technical exponential fit over populated bins, and each point carries a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. Giving large weight to old observations leads to wrong decisions, so decay is necessary.

The half-life is only a scheduler parameter and is distinct from the time constant fitted from the trace. Physical retention and eviction of the actual cache remain the serving engine’s responsibility.

3.4 Readiness tells “returning soon” as 0/1

Readiness identifies sessions that will need the GPU again soon. If the tool interface exposes progress or a completion deadline, it uses that first. Claude Code’s Monitor delivers background task events, and OpenCode reports termination after a Bash timeout (source: §3.4). Without direct timing evidence, it estimates the remaining time from historical tool duration records. The estimation order is per-tool history → global history → 5-second default. It collects the sample count, mean, sample variance, and observed range of completed calls, builds a conservative estimate with a finite-sample margin, subtracts the time already elapsed, and clips at zero (Eq. (5), Appendix A).

When the predicted remaining time enters the horizon H=1 second, r=1. The decision uses three things together (Eq. (6)). If tool completion has already been observed, r=1. If the predicted deadline has passed but completion has not yet been observed, it grants only a temporary probe opportunity instead of remaining “ready” indefinitely. Otherwise, it decides only if the predicted timestamp was updated within 30 seconds. Observed completion takes precedence over prediction.

This signal is tied to the scheduling period (1 second). A session with readiness 1 is raised as a GPU placement candidate and can emit its first token as soon as the tool finishes.

3.5 Select and place at once with dynamic programming

Once all values are assigned, the decision problem becomes “dividing items among multiple knapsacks.” Each node b is a knapsack with remaining capacity C_b, and each session i is an item with admission cost w_i and per-node value v_{i,b}.

The problem with existing approaches is that they solved this per session. Putting sessions one by one into the node that looks good in sequence blocks the slot where a more valuable combination could fit later.

The paper splits capacity into fixed units (quantum Δ), then, adding candidates one at a time, stores “the best value obtainable at each capacity state with the j candidates so far” with a DP that finds the exact optimum over a frozen, discretized snapshot (source: §3.5, Eq. (7)).

$$D_j(s) = \operatorname{lexmax}\left\{ D_{j-1}(s),\ \operatorname{lexmax}_{b\,\mathrm{eligible}}\left[ D_{j-1}(s - \bar{w}_j e_b) + u_{j,b} \right] \right\}$$

Here $\bar{w}_i = \lceil w_i/\Delta\rceil$, $\bar{C}_b = \lfloor C_b/\Delta\rfloor$, and $u_{j,b}$ is the term holding the value and count when candidate j is put on node b. Each candidate tries both “skip” and “assign to b,” so all feasible solutions are covered. However, because of rounding, a plan that was feasible before discretization may be excluded.

The computation runs in an isolated asynchronous worker, and just before applying, it re-checks against the live state (whether the selected session’s signature and eligibility are unchanged), then applies only the longest plan prefix that current capacity allows. If the signature changes, it discards the entire plan. The preparation and pool readiness cost is less than 0.12% of total runtime in the 4-replica sweep (source: §3.5, Appendix I).

Per-node cache observations are decayed with O(nm) preprocessing and folded into values, and nodes with the same cache can be grouped into g ≤ m capacity dimensions (physical KV blocks are not moved). When the state budget is exhausted, it falls back to best-fit-decreasing (BFD) placement. The admission cost w_i is the memory demand of the session’s total token count minus shared token capacity, and C_b is updated at each scheduling point as the node’s remaining capacity (Appendix B.1).

What the DP actually chooses differently

Original Figure 10. Each program is distinguished by a different hue, translucent spans are that program’s admission weight, and dark overlays are retained cache credit. The horizontal axis is admission weight (thousand tokens), and the height of each node’s horizontal bar is that node’s limit.

  • (a) short-first affinity greedy: node 1 leaves 13.6k cache with 8.4k free, node 2 has 20.1k free.
  • (b) dynamic programming: it leaves 16.8k cache (+3.2k, +23.2%), node 1’s free space shrinks to 1.4k and node 2’s free space grows to 27.1k.

While maintaining the same total safe token retention, the DP preserves more cache credit. The exact values are 16,791 tokens versus 13,624 tokens (source: Appendix H).

Original Figure 11. Each session’s width is its admission weight (including the 512-token reserve), and the number beside it is the program ID and cache credit.

  • (a) short-first affinity greedy: admits 6 programs and defers program 177, a long-context one. Cache 10,397 tokens.

That is, the heuristic fills slots with short programs and pushes out a valuable session, while the DP admits that session too (source: Appendix H).

4. Results

4.1 Metrics and comparison conditions

There are three metrics. Latency is the average end-to-end task time (including model inference + tool execution), TTFT is the average time to first token, and decode throughput is generated tokens per second (TPS). In the component analysis, it additionally measures prefix-cache hit rate, latency from tool completion to first token, and pause wait. Pause wait is the time an interrupted session waited, including tool-call latency.

There are four comparison targets: vLLM’s round-robin (RR) and cache-aware (CA) schedulers, the KV-aware scheduler Dynamo, and ThunderAgent, which uses BFD placement with token-count scheduling. Deployments are DeepSeek-V4 Flash on 2 nodes × (4 H100 per node), Qwen3-32B on 4 nodes × (2 H100 per node), and GLM-4.7 on 1 node × 8×H100 (TP8). The workload is SWE-bench Lite (SWE-Lite) using the mini-SWE-agent harness; DeepSeek additionally runs Terminal-Bench 2.0 with Claude Code, and Qwen additionally runs SWE-verified (source: §4.1).

The paper reports up to 26.8% latency reduction, up to 36.3% TTFT reduction, and up to 29.5% decode throughput increase across 12 model–workload–concurrency settings, with the comparison baseline being the best evaluated baseline per metric (source: abstract).

4.2 Main results: where it won and where it lost

In the DeepSeek-V4 Flash SWE-Lite results, each cell is the improvement over the best competing value for that metric (source: original Table 1).

Metric (improvement) 16 workers 32 workers 64 workers
Latency reduction 2.4% 5.4% 26.8%
TTFT reduction 7.4% 13.3% 36.3%

The improvement grows with concurrency. At 64 workers, TAO’s latency is 185.410 s, far better than the best competing 253.228 s, TTFT is 0.224 s versus 0.351 s, and decode throughput is 2,021.523 versus 1,561.307 tok/s. At 16 workers the gaps are narrower: 113.264 s versus 116.011 s, 0.135 s versus 0.146 s, and 934.967 versus 889.590 tok/s. That is, the more sessions compete for node capacity, the more pronounced the effect of “optimal placement at once” and “valuation reflecting cache and readiness” (source: §4.2).

4.3 Serving dynamics: don’t cram everything in at once

Original Figure 4. This is a running-request-count trace when GLM-4.7 runs 300 SWE-Lite tasks at 160 workers (TP8), with each run aligned to zero at the first client request. TAO finished the workload at 60.0 minutes, ThunderAgent at 70.9 minutes, vLLM CA at 164.3 minutes, vLLM RR at 176.8 minutes, and Dynamo at 189.4 minutes. TAO keeps the number of concurrently running requests low throughout the middle of the run while finishing earlier. That is, it stably admits additional sessions while keeping the concurrent request count low. Corresponding traces for 96 and 128 workers (TAO 53.9 and 59.2 minutes, ThunderAgent 60.1 and 66.2 minutes) are in Appendix D (source: §4.2, Appendix D).
