The largest drop is the last row. Reverting the DP to simple BFD placement drops decode from 1417.97 to 1233.72 tok/s and increases mean TTFT from 0.154 to 0.195 s. This means that good valuation alone is not enough if placement is myopic; performance falls sharply, supporting the design rationale that “evaluation” and “decision” play different roles. Removing readiness lowers decode to 1363.06 and increases tool end→first token to 0.227 s. The effect of removing cache value is relatively small (1398.35). It is also notable that the ablation effects are not monotonic. The “without cache value and readiness” row (1373.51) shows higher decode than the “without readiness only” row (1363.06). However, compared with the gap to the last DP→BFD row, this irregularity is not large.

Cache-aware evaluation. In a fixed workload replay of 218 tasks, the DP placement was held identical to the ThunderAgent control while only the valuation was changed. Cache token ordering raised prefix-cache hit rate by 0.19%p and reduced mean pause wait by 4.5%. Adding cache credit decay on top raised hit rate by 0.31%p and decode throughput by 1.68%. Figure 5 shows the reduction in physical prefill, TTFT, and pause wait together (source: §4.3, original Figure 5).

Tool readiness. In paired 32-worker SWE-Lite runs, enabling readiness raises decode throughput by 4.03%, reduces latency from tool completion to first token by 10.88%, and lowers mean pause wait from 1.067 s to 0.972 s. The left CDF in Figure 6 shows the distribution from tool completion to first output token, and the right shows the prediction error distribution. Across 10,967 completed tool predictions, mean absolute error is 0.410 s and 82.9% are within 0.5 s (the return-latency CDF has 10,481 and 10,673 observations, and the prediction panel has 10,967 predictions) (source: §4.3, original Figure 6).

Concurrent placement. Of 23 replay snapshots with multiple candidates, 6 (26.1%) improved the lexicographic objective and the other 17 matched the short-first heuristic. Across all 35 recoverable cases including single-candidate cases, 6 (17.1%) improved and 29 (82.9%) matched. That is, on this criterion the DP was never worse, and it gained on snapshots with severe contention (source: §4.3, Appendix H).

4.5 Mixed workloads and supplementary evaluations

Mixed workload (source: original Table 3). In a Terminal-Bench + SWE-Lite mix (389 tasks), latency (+12.2/+23.2/+13.8%) and decode (+12.2/+8.6/+4.4%) improved at all of 32, 64, and 128 workers, and only 32-worker TTFT trailed at −5.5%. AutomationBench (800 tasks) improved all three metrics at 32 and 64 workers. At 128 workers, however, all three trailed: latency 563.114 s versus 523.676 s (−7.0%), TTFT 19.123 s versus 3.166 s (−504.0%), and decode 1,013.157 versus 1,140.862 tok/s (−11.2%). The direction of gain and loss varies by workload.

Low-concurrency fallback (source: Appendix E.1, Table 5). DeepSeek-V4 Flash was placed on a single TP8 node and swept from 4 to 64 workers. At 4–8 workers, TAO’s mean task latency is within 2.3% of the best baseline, decode throughput stays at or above 92% of the best, and mean TTFT is 15–20 ms higher than the best. At 32 and 64 workers, ThunderAgent falls far behind (at 64 workers, latency 475.033 s versus 226.268 s, TTFT 9.332 s versus 0.423 s). This confirms that TAO does not collapse even when scheduling headroom shrinks.

InferenceX replay (source: Appendix F, Table 7, Figure 9). DeepSeek serves a fixed corpus consisting of 393 AgentX traces, a 1-million-token context limit, and an 1,800-second profiling window on 2 nodes × 4×H100. TAO ranks first in decode throughput at all of 16, 32, and 64 workers (+4.2/+1.8/+10.1%), and TTFT ranks first only at 16 workers; at 32 and 64 workers the cache-aware scheduler is lower. In Figure 9, TAO’s prefix-cache hit rate ranks first at all worker counts.

Composition with another KV management engine (source: Appendix E.2, Table 6). Layering TAO on TokenCake increases decode throughput from 785.159 to 886.772 tok/s and from 1,292.584 to 1,347.373 tok/s at 16 and 32 workers, and at 64 workers improves latency from 509.018 to 274.892 s, TTFT from 1.590 to 0.593 s, and decode from 790.491 to 1,414.547 tok/s. However, the authors also report that in this run the program’s pause, resume, and migration never occurred, and they acknowledge that attributing the effect to the mechanism requires a separate run.

Sensitivity to long tool latency (source: Appendix G, Table 8). SWE-Lite sessions instantiated with MiniSWE (6,995 model requests, 6,942 tool records) were given per-session fixed additional latencies of 1–5 s, 2–10 s, and 4–20 s. Compared with readiness off, TAO reduced makespan by 20.72/16.42/19.28% and mean session latency by 21.57/20.57/17.91%. The longer the latency, the larger the fraction of cases where readiness changes the actual placement decision: 1.65% → 3.94% → 7.93%. Compared with an Oracle that provides the known true time, history-based prediction cuts mean absolute error by 99.53–99.69% (0.025–0.030 s) and approaches Oracle in runtime performance.

5. Limitations and applicability judgment

5.1 Limitations the paper itself states or that follow structurally

  • Optimality holds only over the discretized snapshot. The DP is exact on the frozen, discretized snapshot, but rounding can exclude plans that were feasible before discretization (source: §3.5).
  • It does not guarantee global online optimality. The loss from asynchronous application is presented as a conditional bound in terms of value fluctuation ε_{s,t}, opportunities A_{s,t} arising from feasibility changes, and execution loss T_{s,t} (Eq. (12)). $$\max_{x \in X^\Delta_t} U_t(x) - U_t(y_t) \le A_{s,t} + 2\epsilon_{s,t} + T_{s,t}$$ The comparison point of this bound is not the planning moment but the fresh snapshot optimum of the same state observed at application time. It therefore does not guarantee end-to-end latency or regret against a globally optimal online policy. The 0/1 jump in readiness does not automatically fit the exponential-decay assumption, so a separate jump allowance is needed (source: Appendix B.2, Appendix C).
  • Readiness prediction is not a calibrated probability. It is only a scheduling heuristic with a finite-sample margin and does not provide calibrated coverage for individual calls. If neither per-tool nor global history exists, it relies on the 5-second default (source: Appendix A).
  • Resource boundary assumption. It assumes that CPU and RAM for external tools are managed separately outside the GPU admission budget. Situations requiring additional resource constraints or interaction-dependent values need an extension of this admission model (source: §2.1, §3.4 — the latter is the reviewer’s interpretation).
  • Overhead accounting is partial. The recorded scheduler work time covers state preparation and completed pools, so failed probes and BFD executions are not in the time account. That ratio is therefore not a measure of CPU utilization or request latency overhead (source: Appendix I).

5.2 Points a reviewer would note

  • Scalability was not validated on node count. The DP’s state space grows with the number of nodes and capacity quantization. Nodes with the same cache are grouped into g ≤ m capacity dimensions, and when the state budget is exhausted it falls back to BFD. The measured fallback rates are 5.24% for DeepSeek 64 workers and 3.06–8.98% for the Qwen sweep. However, the reported measurements cover deployments up to 4 nodes (TP2×4), and deployments with far more nodes were not validated (source: §3.5, Appendix I, Table 9).
  • Readiness depends entirely on signal quality. It works best in environments where the tool interface exposes progress and deadlines or where historical statistics are valid. For tools without such signals it relies on the 5-second default, and the accuracy guarantee there is limited (source: §3.4, Appendix A).
  • There is no starvation-avoidance mechanism in the original. The third coordinate, token count priority, applies only when both cache credit and readiness tie. That a session with a larger token count gains placement priority in that case is shown by the admission of session 177 in Figure 11, but no starvation-prevention mechanism is specified. The fact that the snapshot is re-solved at each scheduling point appears to be a mitigating factor (source: §3.2; the mitigating factor is the reviewer’s interpretation).
  • Coupling with the engine is still at the design stage. The composition with TokenCake worked, but pause, resume, and migration were not triggered, so whether that mechanism actually contributed is unconfirmed (source: Appendix E.2).

5.3 Applicability judgment

This design is particularly suited to agent serving with frequent tool calls, many sessions competing for node capacity, and predictable tool durations. SWE-bench-style coding agents, multi-agent orchestration, and Looped Agent are examples. The paper states that it is also compatible with chatbot load.

Conversely, in workloads with few tools or where prediction is difficult without tool signals, the benefit of valuation shrinks. Indeed, at AutomationBench 128 workers all three metrics trailed. In deployments with very many nodes, DP cost and benefit must be validated separately.

item.title: Look Only When Needed: Certificate-Guided Visual Routing for Efficient Diffusion VLMs
item.description:
Paper

The problem: re-reading the image at every step

Diffusion language models that answer questions from images do not complete a response in one pass. While filling in the blanks over many steps, they re-read an image that barely changes from the beginning at every step. LOWN asks “does this step really need the image?” every time, and re-reads only when necessary, cutting decoding cost substantially.

Instead of drawing one token at a time from the left like autoregressive models, diffusion language models start with the entire response masked. At each step they examine all remaining blanks and simultaneously resolve the $k$ masks with the highest confidence. This is called “unmask,” and $k$ is the response length divided by the number of steps (source: §3.1). In image-input diffusion language models (DVLM, e.g., LLaDA-V), image tokens are fixed in the input sequence rather than the response and enter along with it. An “image token” is a numeric fragment that makes the picture processable by the model.

The share of image tokens is overwhelming. Across the 10 benchmarks evaluated, image tokens account for 89–97% of the total input, and the cost of a single forward pass without the image is only about 3–10% of the original (benchmark averages 2.5–10.1%) (source: §1, Figure 1b, Table 8). Because DVLM uses bidirectional attention, it cannot reuse the key-value cache of autoregressive models as is, and passes the entire input through again at every step. As a result, most of the decoding cost goes into “re-reading an image that does not change.”

When the image is actually needed

Before designing LOWN, we numerically checked whether the image is truly needed at every step. Following the standard decoding path as is, we ran two forward passes side by side at each step. The “FULL forward” computes probabilities with an input that includes image tokens, while the “TEXT-ONLY forward” computes probabilities from the same partial response with only the image tokens removed and the position IDs kept unchanged (source: §3.2, Appendix A). Because the progress state is determined solely by the FULL forward, the decoding path itself is identical to the baseline. The TEXT-ONLY output is only recorded and not reflected in the state.

The comparison results come down to three points:

  • For 83.4% of the positions to be unmasked, the two forwards predicted the same token as top-1. For 85.0% of the final tokens, the value had already been predicted as top-1 at the same position before unmasking (source: §3.2, Table 6). Cases where the image flips the decision are rare.
  • The top-1 disagreement between the two forwards was largest in the early denoising steps for 8 of the 10 benchmarks, and shrank as the response took shape. There are exceptions such as DeCapBench (source: §3.2, Figure 2a).
  • The fraction of steps where the image changed at least one unmask decision—the image-dependent step ratio—varies widely by benchmark.
Benchmark Image-dependent step ratio
MMBench 7.9%
ScienceQA 8.2%
MME 10.6%
GQA 10.9%
MathVista 17.9%
ChartQA 24.5%
CapArena 32.7%
DeCapBench 33.4%
LLaVA-Bench 37.8%
DocVQA 43.8%

The average across the 10 is 22.8% (source: §3.2, Figure 2b, Table 6). Fixing a schedule of “read the image every n steps” cannot track this variation well. The point at which the image is needed depends on the input and the step, so it has to be judged on the fly at each step. Fortunately, the material for that judgment is already there. The TEXT-ONLY forward provides predictions at the same positions at about 3–10% of the cost of the FULL forward (source: §3.2, Table 8).

LOWN: looking only when the image is needed

LOWN starts from “let us reuse the prediction made the last time we looked at the image.” Whenever it runs a FULL forward, it separately stores the top-1 predictions and their confidence for the positions still blank. These stored values are called “anchors.” An anchor is just a token value and a few confidence numbers, so LOWN itself does not keep large state like attention keys and values.

Each step first computes predictions for the remaining positions with a TEXT-ONLY forward. If these predictions match the anchors, LOWN certifies the anchor predictions as “predictions likely to remain valid without the image and after the state has changed.” Because the two predictions differ in both whether the image was seen and which point in the state they were computed from, a match is used as an approximate signal that both conditions were satisfied together. No absolute confidence threshold is needed (source: §4.1).

Concretely, it lists the blank positions in descending order of anchor confidence and counts from the front the positions where “TEXT-ONLY prediction == anchor” to form a certified prefix. The scan stops at the first mismatch. If the prefix length is at least $k$, it skips the image and unmasks the entire prefix with the anchor values. If it is below $k$, it runs the FULL forward to refresh the anchors, then unmasks $k$ positions—the positions where the two predictions differ first, and the rest in order of FULL confidence (source: §4.2).

 flowchart TD
 A["Current response state (partially masked)<br/>run TEXT-ONLY forward without the image"] --> B["Compare each masked position's top-1 prediction and<br/>confidence against the anchor (previous FULL values)"]
 B --> C{"Number of consecutive matches<br/>in descending confidence ≥ k ?"}
 C -->|"Yes"| D["Skip the image<br/>fix all certified positions to the anchor values"]
 C -->|"No"| E["FULL forward with the image<br/>refresh the anchors with new values"]
 E --> F["Fix k positions: mismatched positions first,<br/>the rest in order of confidence"]
 D --> G{"Any masked positions left?"}
 F --> G
 G -->|"Yes"| A
 G -->|"No"| H["Response complete"]

Below is an illustrative example. The token split and numbers are constructed independently of the paper’s example, and $k=2$ is assumed.

Suppose that at some step the response is in the state “The cat ? ?”. Positions 1 and 2 are already fixed, and positions 3 and 4 are still masked. The anchors saved by the previous FULL forward (predictions and confidence for the masked positions) and the predictions of this step’s TEXT-ONLY forward are as follows.

Position Anchor value (last FULL) Anchor confidence TEXT-ONLY prediction Verdict
3 sat 0.92 sat certified ✓
4 on 0.81 mat mismatch ✗

Scanning in descending confidence (position 3 → 4), position 3 matches and position 4 diverges, so the certified prefix is {position 3} with length 1. Because this is less than $k=2$, the image cannot be skipped, so the FULL forward runs. The FULL forward predicts position 3→“sat” and position 4→“on”, refreshes the anchors, unmasks position 4 (where the two predictions differed) first, and then unmasks position 3. Output: “The cat sat on”.

Conversely, if TEXT-ONLY had matched the anchors at both positions, the prefix length 2 ≥ $k$ would hold, the FULL forward would be skipped, and the two values would be fixed as is. If the certified prefix is longer than $k$, more than $k$ positions are fixed in the same step, reducing the total number of steps as well. Both branches fix at least $k$ positions, so LOWN never uses more steps than the $T$ steps of baseline decoding (source: §4.2).

There is one caveat. Two adjacent positions predicted independently in the same step can receive the same token, and fixing them as is produces a repeated word in the response. To prevent this, the prefix is cut if the token ID equals that of an already fixed neighbor or a neighbor accepted earlier in the same scan (source: §4.1, Appendix B.1).

Cost decomposes as $R = f + \sigma\rho$. $f$ is the fraction of the baseline $T$ steps that run a FULL forward, $\sigma$ is the ratio of the number of steps LOWN runs to the baseline $T$, and $\rho$ is the relative cost of one TEXT-ONLY forward (source: §4.3). Certification lowers $f$, and accepting the whole prefix lowers $\sigma$. $\rho$ is at the 2.5–10.1% level per benchmark depending on the share taken by the image (source: Table 8). Unlike token pruning, which reduces the cost of a single FULL forward, LOWN reduces the number of times the FULL forward runs. The two methods operate on different axes (source: §4.3).

Performance: how much is saved and how much is kept

Comparison at the same compute

For competing methods, we chose the cheapest setting in each method’s own hyperparameter grid that uses FLOPs at or above LOWN’s, so if LOWN scores lower, it does so at equal or higher cost (source: Table 1, §C.3). The table below compares methods at matched compute on LLaDA-V.

Method MathVista ScienceQA ChartQA DocVQA Average (10)
LLaDA-V (original) 59.10 76.50 78.16 83.91 100.0%
RedVTP (token pruning) 51.70 70.70 74.32 83.39 93.0%
ZOO-Prune 53.70 73.87 76.44 78.73 94.2%
KLASS (schedule) 56.70 75.01 73.64 75.36 91.9%
LOWN 56.00 78.83 78.36 82.31 99.6%

The average column is the mean of normalized scores across all 10 benchmarks. Only CapArena is normalized as $100+\text{score}-\text{baseline score}$ (source: §C.1). LOWN retains 99.6% on average at 0.353× decoding FLOPs and ranks first among acceleration methods on 8 of the 10 benchmarks (source: §5.2). On 4 of the 10 benchmarks, LOWN scores higher than the original. In the table above, ScienceQA (78.83 vs 76.50) and ChartQA (78.36 vs 78.16) are such cases. Clipping the cap at 100% still gives 98.6% (source: §5.2). RedVTP drops more sharply, to 93.0%. Pruning erases visual information permanently, whereas LOWN can look at the full image again at the steps where it is needed (source: §5.3, Figure 6).

Combining with pruning and caching

Whereas pruning reduces the number of visual tokens processed per forward, LOWN decides at each step whether to process the image. Because the two axes overlap, using them together compounds the savings. Combined with RedVTP (50% retention), it retains 98.3% at 0.223× FLOPs and ranks first on all 10 benchmarks (source: §5.2, Table 1). Combined with the key-value cache (Fast-dLLM), it cuts generation time by an additional 38.1–50.1% relative to Fast-dLLM, saves an additional 44.1–58.9% of FLOPs, and decodes 5.6–7.0× faster than LLaDA-V alone (source: §5.2, Table 2). However, the scores of this combination are lower than Fast-dLLM alone on all three tasks (by 5.0 points on LLaVA-Bench) and within 2.0 points of the original (source: §5.2).

Wall-clock time and other backbones

The performance table above is based on analytical compute (FLOPs). Actual wall-clock time, measured on an H200 with batch size 1, shows LOWN alone cutting generation time by 57.4% on average and up to 73.2% (source: §5.2, §D.1). The gap from the FLOPs reduction (64.7%) is hard to compare directly because of differences in what is measured. FLOPs is a matrix-multiplication-centric analytical value excluding the vision encoder and non-matrix operations, while time includes multimodal preparation and vision encoding within the execution flow (source: §B.2, §D.1).

The same rule transfers as is to LaViDa, and extends to VidLaDA under a controlled video protocol. On LaViDa it retains 99.7% of the score at 0.174× FLOPs. On the video model VidLaDA-8B, under a controlled 128-token decoding protocol, EgoSchema scores 60.2 at 0.255× FLOPs (original 60.6) and MLVU scores 43.3 at 0.272× (original 41.8) (source: §5.2, Table 3).

Why adaptive judgment beats a fixed schedule

Compared with “read the image every n steps” or random schedules, adaptive judgment is indeed better. It achieves 4.9–13.0% higher task-normalized quality than random schedules matched on the number of FULL passes, and a period-4 schedule at similar compute is 4.0 points lower on MathVista (source: Table 4). Breaking down the cost contribution, image-access routing alone reduces FLOPs by 27–68%, and adaptive acceptance—consisting of disagreement-first ordering and accepting the whole prefix—reduces it by another 21–43% on top. Adaptive acceptance raises scores on 7 benchmarks, and on the rest the normalized

item.title: On the SPOT: Enhancing Speculative Decoding for Diffusion Language Models via Commit-Order Prediction
item.description:
Paper

Diffusion language models must decide ‘what’ and ‘where’ at the same time

Diffusion language models generate sentences by repeatedly filling masked tokens. To decode exactly, each model forward must commit only the single most certain masked position as a token, which is slow; committing multiple positions at once to increase speed degrades generation quality. This paper moves speculative decoding, a lossless acceleration technique validated on autoregressive models, to diffusion language models, but finds the solution by predicting not tokens but the order of which position to fill next.

The authors first show one observation experimentally. Looking only at the probability distribution left by the target model in the previous forward, the token that belongs at each position can mostly be predicted in advance (92% for the first block commit and over 90% thereafter), but which position will be filled next is rarely predicted. So they reuse tokens from the old distribution as-is, and a small 0.62M-parameter model (SPOT) predicts only the commit order to build a tree of candidate states. The target verifies that tree with a single batched forward. On SDAR-8B, this reduces target forwards by up to 6.8× and raises throughput up to 3.4× versus standard decoding (§1, §5.2).

Background: decoding that fills a block one slot at a time

The target of this paper is a block-causal diffusion language model. An active block has positions of length $L$ (the paper mainly uses b32, i.e. $L{=}32$), and each position is either a token or a mask. A single forward returns a full-vocabulary probability distribution for every masked position. The target then selects only the position whose top probability is highest and fills it with that position’s argmax token. This is called commit, and the paper counts the number of target forwards as NFE (number of function evaluations) (§3).

The issue is that attention within a block is bidirectional. The moment one position is filled, the representations and probability distributions of all remaining masked positions change. So, unlike an autoregressive model, “the next position is fixed and only its token needs to be predicted” does not hold. Speculative decoding for diffusion language models must determine both which token to use and which position to use (§1, §2).

Illustrative example (not experimental numbers)

Let us reduce the block width to 8. Three tokens, “The”, “cat”, and “sat”, have already been filled, and the remaining five slots are masks. Suppose the highest-probability candidates (stale argmax) for the masked positions returned by one forward are as shown below.

Position stale argmax candidate Probability
3 “on” 0.90
4 “the” 0.70
5 “mat” 0.60
6 “quietly” 0.50
7 “.” 0.95

In this forward, the target commits only the single most certain position. Position 7’s “.” has the highest probability at 0.95, so it fills position 7 with “.” and examines the remaining four slots again in the next forward. The state retained here consists of the already committed tokens (“The cat sat …”), and what changes from forward to forward is the single filled position and the entire probability distribution over the remaining masked positions.

The key point is that two things diverge in this example. The token that will ultimately go into each position largely matches the stale argmax in this table (“on”, “the”, and “mat” are mostly right). But “which position to commit first” cannot be known from probability magnitude alone. The moment position 7 is filled, the distributions of the remaining slots all shift, so this table becomes the stale (old) distribution from the next moment onward.

Observation: the tokens are already known, but the order is not

Before designing the method, the authors quantified what the drafter should predict for the gain to materialize. To do this, they use a live oracle that peeks at the target’s actual future. They compare three kinds: a position oracle that reveals the true next position, a token oracle that reveals the true token, and a joint oracle that gives both (§3.1).

Original Figure 2 (live oracle, SDAR-8B b32). The left panel shows the throughput ratio versus draft-free by oracle type and budget, and the right panel shows the probability that committed tokens in the next $K$ steps fall within the stale top-$t$ candidates. On the left, read that the position oracle lies above the token oracle on every task; on the right, read that even a few candidates cover almost all future tokens.

The results are clear. Knowing the position is always more beneficial than knowing the token. Going from D8 to D20, the position oracle’s NFE reduction grows from 5.4×→7.2× on GSM8K and from 5.7×→8.2× on MBPP, whereas the token oracle reaches only 3.4–6.5× at D20. A perfect drafter (joint oracle) reaches a throughput of 6.2–7.0× (§3.1, Figure 2).

The reason is already hidden in the stale distribution. The probability that the stale argmax matches the actually committed token is 92% at the first block commit and remains above 90% thereafter. But “the probability that the position the model was most confident about in the last round will be committed next” falls to 3% by block 9. The tokens are almost already known; what is truly unknown is the order. A model trained on this order predicts the next commit position with 75% accuracy, whereas reading the order from stale confidence reaches only 22% (§3.1, Appendix).

Method: a drafter that predicts only order, and coupled-noise verification

SPOT (Speculating Positions Order Trajectory) is split into two parts: what to draft (the order model) and how to verify it (coupled noise).

Drafter: commit-order model

The drafter is a 3-layer Transformer encoder ($d_{model}{=}128$, 8 heads, 0.62M parameters). It reads the stale top-32 probabilities (raw and log) for each masked position, summary statistics, and path features, and predicts the distribution over the next position to be committed $q_\phi(s|y)$. It uses no target hidden states, token embeddings, or text at all (§4.2).

It does not predict tokens. Candidate tokens for each position come from the stale distribution. At $T{=}0$, it uses the stale argmax as the primary candidate, and if the stale top-1 probability is below 0.6, it adds one more second-ranked candidate (token hedge). This exception reduces cases where, even with the right order, the wrong token is rejected during verification (§4.2).

The key is the prefix-conditional approach. When the drafter predicts the next position in some virtual state, it then predicts the next position again in the new virtual state after filling that position, and repeats this recursively to grow a tree of candidate states. The criterion for expanding the tree is prefix mass, defined as child mass = parent mass × (probability that this position will be committed) × (probability that this token will be filled), and since all factors are in $[0,1]$, a child cannot have greater mass than its parent. Thanks to this monotonicity, a search that selects the top-$D$ highest-mass candidates level by level (DDTree) produces the same result as sequential best-first search (§4.2, Appendix).

 flowchart LR
 A["Current block state<br/>some slots committed, some masked"] --> B["Read stale distribution<br/>probabilities for each masked position"]
 B --> C["Order model: predict next commit position"]
 C --> D["Expand candidate tree<br/>child = position + token committed"]
 D -->|"Recurse until budget D"| C
 D --> E["One batched target forward<br/>verify root + all drafts"]
 E --> F["Commit only the longest matching path"]
 F --> A

Original Figure 1 (SPOT overview). (a) The target commits the single most certain position per forward, but the tokens are largely known in advance and only the order is unknown. (b) SPOT reads the stale distribution, predicts the next position with the 0.62M order model, grows a state tree by prefix mass (edge thickness), verifies all of it with a single batched forward, and commits three positions.

Verification uses state equality. Each draft state is appended as a block copy after the cached prefix, and forwarding $(1{+}D)L$ positions at once yields the target’s next commit for the root and every draft state in one pass. A draft is accepted only when its next commit matches the commit the target actually produces at that parent. Since the target’s next commit is unique, what is accepted is always a single path. Therefore, the output never changes no matter how wrong the drafts are — the drafter determines only speed and does not affect correctness (§4.1, §4.2).

Verification: coupled noise that preserves correctness even under sampling

At $T{=}0$, commits are deterministic, so state-equality verification holds as is (Proposition 1). The problem is sampling at $T{>}0$. Drawing samples independently from the same distribution can produce different tokens, so even a correct draft is rejected because its state differs.

SPOT’s solution is for the drafter and the target to share the same Gumbel random numbers. Drawing a token at temperature $T$ is mathematically equivalent to drawing a Gumbel random number $G_{a,v}$ for each position-token pair and choosing $\argmax_v[(1/T)\log p + G_{a,v}]$ (the Gumbel-argmax identity). If both sides share the same table of random numbers on an absolute-position basis, then once the random numbers are fixed, the target’s draw becomes deterministic. Sampling verification then reduces once again to state equality. It is exact conditional on the random numbers $G$, and integrating over $G$ recovers the original sampling distribution exactly (Proposition 2, §4.3).

This coupled verification matters more as temperature rises. At $T{\le}1$, the drawn token is the argmax 99–99.8% of the time, so the difference between the two methods is within 2%, but at $T{=}2$, independent-sample verification accepts almost nothing (257.5 NFE versus 267.1 draft-free), whereas coupled verification keeps drafting (187.2 NFE). The acceptance probability of coupled verification is lower-bounded by the total variation distance $\delta$ between the stale and fresh distributions: at least $(1-\delta)/(1+\delta)$ (§3.2, §4.3).

SPOT-Sets: on decoding that commits several slots at once

So far, this has been exact decoding that commits one position per forward. But faster decoders commit all positions whose probability exceeds a threshold $\tau$ in a single forward (dynamic-threshold decoding). In that case, the unit of drafting becomes a commit set rather than a single position, and the drafter must also determine the tokens. That is because the stale argmax is 83% correct one step ahead but only 44% correct three steps ahead (§4.4).

SPOT-Sets uses a 5.1M-parameter drafter for this. It additionally reads embeddings of the stale top-16 candidate tokens and the target’s last hidden state, and predicts whether each position will exceed $\tau$ at the next step and which candidate token to choose. A node in the tree is not a single position but an entire target step (§4.4).

A small example (illustrative example): in threshold decoding, one forward commits several positions at once, such as {3,4,6}. SPOT-Sets drafts this entire set, and a draft that fills the whole block continues proposing into the next block.

Original Figure 3 (max-commit). (a) The threshold decoder commits the positions $S_\tau$ that exceed $\tau$. (b) Exact acceptance accepts only when the draft step equals $S_\tau$, subset/cut accept a subset of it, and product accepts any step whose geometric mean confidence is at least $\tau$. (c) Max-commit follows the path with the most commits: 7 commits under exact and 9 under product, and product’s output differs from the threshold decoder’s own output.

Here the trade-off between correctness and speed appears again. Exact acceptance keeps the output identical to the threshold decoder, but the authors’ main results use the looser product rule. Product accepts up to the step where the geometric mean confidence is at least $\tau$, committing more per forward, but it no longer reproduces the threshold decoder’s output. The paper therefore also reports an exact variant. To reduce the cost incurred every few forwards at block boundaries, it adds two block-boundary optimizations: cross-block drafting and draft refresh (§4.4, Appendix).

Results: read forward count and throughput separately

When looking at the results, do not conflate the two metrics. NFE is the number of target forwards (the drafter’s own cost is excluded), and the throughput ratio is based on generated tokens per second relative to a draft-free run on the same GPU, same task, and same temperature. One draft round forwards $(1{+}D)L$ positions regardless of acceptance, so the NFE reduction and the throughput gain are not always the same — a recurring point in this paper (§3.1, Appendix).

The key question is this. With the same draft budget, does SPOT use fewer forwards and also achieve higher throughput than the baselines? Below are NFE (lower is better) and throughput ratio (higher is better) for SDAR-8B b32, $T{=}0$, budget D8 (§5.2, main results table).

Method (SDAR-8B, T=0, D8) GSM8K MBPP HumanEval MATH500
draft-free (baseline) 270.8 (1.00×) 269.2 (1.00×) 271.4 (1.00×) 271.8 (1.00×)
Spiffy graph 92.5 (2.48×) 83.6 (2.40×) 87.6 (2.64×) 100.6 (2.29×)
SPOT 70.1 (2.95×) 56.7 (3.38×) 62.5 (3.35×) 84.6 (2.50×)

SPOT uses 16–36% fewer forwards than Spiffy across all tasks and budgets and has 1.04–1.41× higher throughput. Notably, the baselines’ throughput collapses as the budget grows. Going from D8 to D20, the SSD chain falls from 2.3–2.6× to 1.4–1.7× and the BlockSpec tree falls from 1.5–1.7× to 0.86–1.10×, becoming slower than draft-free on MBPP. This is because wide drafts consume $(1{+}D)L$ positions regardless of acceptance, yet accept only 1.1–2.9 tokens per round. SPOT accepts 2.5–7.5 tokens per round (§5.2).

Here SPOT-$\gamma$, with the mass floor $\gamma$ enabled, almost eliminates budget dependence. It discards drafts whose mass is below $\gamma$, matching the actual verification budget to drafter confidence, and the throughput ratio stays nearly flat, from 2.5–3.5× at D8 to 2.3–3.4× at D20. The same ordering holds under $T{=}1$ sampling (16–35% lower NFE and 1.08–1.37× throughput versus Spiffy), and the T=1 results are distribution-preserving, with correctness within 0.04 of draft-free (§5.2, §5.3).

7.9× on threshold decoding

Stacking SPOT-Sets on faster threshold decoding (which by itself is already 3.3–6.1× versus standard, 5.0× on average) raises SDAR-8B to 5.2–9.9×, 7.9× on average. Relative to the threshold decoder, it cuts forwards by 47–48%. The exact variant that preserves correctness also reaches 7.6× (§5.2).

Original Figure 4 (ladder). Throughput versus standard decoding, averaged over four tasks, as each part of SPOT-Sets is enabled in turn (labels show the gain at each step). The set drafter and tree alone reach 6.7×; the mass floor raises it from 6.7→6.9×; the block-boundary optimizations cross-block drafting and draft refresh add the largest gain, from 6.9→7.5×; and product max-commit finishes at 7.9× (§5.5, Figure 4).

Transferability is also central to the claim. Even when a drafter trained with the same recipe is attached to another model without retraining or recalibration, moving the SDAR-8B checkpoint to LLaDA2.0-mini (an MoE model with a different tokenizer) loses only 3–11% NFE and still beats all baselines on GSM8K and MATH500. On LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B, which it has never seen, it reduces 256 forwards to 55–88 and 51–80, respectively. However, these two apply attention over the entire sequence and lack an exact prefix cache, so they use an approximate cache; these rows therefore show “reach” rather than losslessness (§5.4, Appendix).

Limitations and deployment judgment

The authors explicitly acknowledge several limitations (§6).

  1. The gain shrinks when verification is expensive or the acceptance rate is low. With a wide block, verification becomes the bottleneck, and the problem of packing the tree into exactly one sequence under bidirectional attention remains unsolved.
  2. The gain narrows on tasks with low acceptance rates. On the smallest model, SDAR-1.7B, Spiffy takes one throughput win from SPOT on MATH500 D20. This is because forwards are so cheap that the cost of draft verification becomes a larger share. SPOT-γ discards low-mass drafts to reduce verification volume, taking that win back (Appendix).
  3. At high temperature, an order model trained at $T{=}0$ is overtaken by noise-aware ranking. This is true at $T{\ge}2$, and in fact from $T{\ge}1.5$ the target’s own quality collapses (correctness 0.11, 0.00 at $T{\ge}2$), leaving little correctness to preserve.
  4. SPOT-Sets requires brief calibration per model. Because it reads hidden states and token embeddings, unlike SPOT it must re-fit the input layer for each new target. The 5.1M-parameter drafter becomes a greater burden on models where target forwards are cheap.
  5. The main results’ max-commit (product rule) changes the output. To preserve correctness, one must use the exact variant, which somewhat reduces the speed gain.

From a reviewer’s perspective, the points to note are as follows. The 6.8× NFE reduction shown in the paper is on a “forward count” basis, while actual throughput is 2.5–3.4× (SPOT) or 7.9× on threshold decoding; the two numbers must not be confused. Also, the SDAR-8B drafter is trained only on code data (CodeAlpaca), yet it works well even though GSM8K and MATH500 are out of domain, which supports the generality of order knowledge; conversely, the SPOT-Sets drafter trained on a distribution like the evaluation tasks is faster on SDAR-8B, at 8.2× on average (7.9× versus a general chat drafter), so the distribution of the deployment environment affects the results (§5.2, Appendix). The LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B results use an approximate cache and thus do not guarantee losslessness; this must also be distinguished from the lossless results.

In summary, SPOT fits best when lossless acceleration is needed on block-causal diffusion models that have an exact prefix KV cache and do not have excessively wide blocks. Coupled-noise verification preserves the distribution at any temperature (Proposition 2), and in the typical generation setting of $T{\le}1$ its results are within 2% of independent-sample verification, making it the safest deployment configuration. On fast paths that already accept some loss, such as threshold decoding, SPOT-Sets’ product rule provides additional gain; according to the paper, the correctness difference versus exact is within 0.04 per task, but the output itself changes (example rule: exact leaves correctness unchanged, while cut only makes the decoder stricter), so quality must be verified separately when deploying.

item.title: Channel Selection for Mixture-of-Experts Decoding Needs No Calibration Data
item.description:
Paper

Introduction

In settings where the batch size is close to 1, such as conversational services, the latency of a mixture-of-experts language model comes mostly from reading the routed expert weights from GPU memory. Most of the intermediate dimensions inside an expert contribute little to a token, so choosing which channels to read first can substantially reduce the amount read. This paper shows that two objectives that existing channel selectors try to meet through calibration data are in fact not achieved, and presents a selector built from model weights alone, without calibration.

Background: Channels and Retention Rules

In an MoE layer, the router sends a token to a few experts. An expert is a gated MLP. Each intermediate dimension of this expert is called a channel. Channel $j$ owns the $j$-th row of the gate matrix $G_e$ and the up matrix $V_e$, and the $j$-th column of the down matrix $D_e$.

Given an input $x$, channel $j$ computes the following.

  • Gate activation: $\phi(g_j^\top x)$
  • up output: $(v_j^\top x)$
  • Channel activation: $a_j = \phi(g_j^\top x)(v_j^\top x)$

The full routed output is the sum of the $a_j d_j$ produced by each channel, scaled by the expert’s router weight.

For illustration, consider Qwen3-Thinking (the actual structure in §2). A single token goes to 8 experts, and each expert has 768 channels. So at each layer the selector must choose what to read among $8 \times 768 = 6144$ candidate channels. Once it decides to compute channel $j$, it reads row $j$ of gate/up and column $j$ of down, computes $a_j d_j$ exactly, and adds it to the output. Discarded channels are not read at all (as shown later, the reader fills them in approximately).

The central fork in a channel selector is the retention rule. Even with the same scores, the way of deciding which channels to keep changes the amount read and the accuracy.

Rule Input State Change Output
Threshold $\tau$ Same score for tokens A and B Channels with score $\ge \tau$ pass A keeps 6, B keeps 2 Amount read varies per token
top-k ($k=4$) Same score Top 4 scores pass Both A and B keep 4 Amount read is fixed per token

A threshold is intended to give each token as much as it needs, but the actual amount read moves with the input. top-k fixes the amount in advance, but keeps $k$ channels regardless of what the token actually needs.

Consider Fig. 2 of the original. (a) draws the structure in which channel $j$ owns row $j$ of gate/up and column $j$ of down. (b) shows the difference that, at the same score, a threshold changes the retention count per token while top-k fixes it. (c) shows how cost is computed. Modern NVIDIA GPUs fetch memory in 32-byte sectors, so when the needed bytes are scattered, every touched sector is charged in full.

Small example (c) Value
Bytes the selector actually needs 80 bytes
Sectors those bytes occupy 4 (scattered)
Sectors the hardware touches All 4
Read charged $4 \times 32 = 128$ bytes

The paper calls this cost reads. It is the bytes read per token measured as a percentage of the full model’s routed expert reads. The accounting was also checked against a profiler to confirm it matches actual hardware transfers. For batch-1 Qwen3-Thinking, cold-cache DRAM reads are 18.3%, close to the accounted 17.8% (Appendix C).

Read savings are not compute (FLOPs) savings. They are the gain from reading fewer weights in a memory-bandwidth-bound setting.

Calibration Fails Both Promises

A channel selector uses a calibrated threshold for two reasons: to know the amount read in advance, and to improve accuracy by giving tokens the channels they need at that amount. The authors break each of these in turn with experiments.

A Threshold Does Not Fix the Amount Read

The threshold $\tau$ is fixed, but the number of channels crossing it varies with the input.

Consider an experiment that computes channel scores exactly as their actual contribution to the output and calibrates $\tau$ so that about 12% is retained on UltraChat. On separate conversational data not used for calibration, the average retention count matched the target. Yet even on the same conversational data, the middle 90% of Qwen3-Thinking tokens retain only 9.0–16.2%, a wide spread, and on benchmark answers (GPQA-Diamond, IFEval, MMLU-Pro) the scores become smaller, dropping the median to 10.0%.

The retention count decreases as answers get longer. Around 6,000 answer tokens, Qwen3-Thinking retains only 71% of the calibrated count, Gemma 4 92%, and Qwen3.5 88%.

In actual deployment it is simpler. Across all 72 benchmark runs we performed, selectors using a calibrated threshold read less than the target. Prox was calibrated to 18% but actually reads 12.9% on average and as little as 9.9%. The reader’s threshold version also meets the target on calibration data but reads 0.4–5.8%p less on benchmarks (§4.1).

Let us read Fig. 4 of the original. (a) is the distribution of the channel retention ratio per token. The orange threshold curve meets the target on the chat data used for calibration, but on benchmark answers the median drops to 10%. The thick line is top-k, which keeps the same ratio for every token. (b) plots, as the median over 500-token windows, what percentage of the calibrated value the retention count is at each answer length. (c) plots actual amount read against the budget on the horizontal axis. Every point lies below the diagonal, that is, short of the target.

We also checked why it decreases. The retention count follows the answer written so far rather than how much the token needs. At the threshold Prox calibrated to 13%, if the 256-token window at position 6,000 of a Qwen3-Thinking GPQA-Diamond answer is detached from its preceding context and placed immediately after the question, the same tokens retain 57% more channels. Nor do harder tokens receive more channels. The correlation between retention count and the full model’s next-token loss is only −0.29 to +0.14 (§4.1, Appendix E).

Calibration Gives No Consistent Accuracy Gain over top-k

To compare the two retention rules, the scores must be fixed. The authors ran each selector twice with the same channel scores: once with a calibrated threshold and once with top-k. At budgets of 13% and 18%, with generation tasks on 4 MoE models and a likelihood task on OLMoE, and with 3 kinds of scores (Prox, TEAL, and Prox scaled at the output level), they produced 43 comparisons in total.

Same scores, two retention rules compared (§4.2) Result
Ties (within 2 standard errors) 30
top-k ahead 10
Threshold ahead 3, with a margin of at most 2.8 points

That is, in 40 of 43, top-k matches or wins. Here a tie means no difference was detected, not equivalence. Grouped by model as well, no model prefers the threshold at the calibration budget (Appendix Table 14).

Even in a check favorable to the threshold, which reruns the top-k version at the amount the threshold version actually read, top-k matches or wins in 37 of 41 (Appendix F, Fig. 8).

In Fig. 5 of the original, each point is one comparison. The vertical axis is the threshold version’s accuracy minus the top-k version’s, so below 0 (blue) is a top-k win. Gray is a tie, the 10 blue points are top-k wins (four of them from Gemma 4 at 38–45 points), and only 3 orange points are threshold wins (at most 2.8 points). This figure is based on the calibration budget; the version rerun at actual reads is in Appendix Fig. 8.

Long Reasoning Can Collapse under a Calibrated Threshold

The four largest gaps in Fig. 5 all come from Gemma 4. At the 13% budget, top-k with Prox (and its output-scaled variant) beat the threshold version by 38–45 points.

Gemma 4 with the calibrated threshold repeats sentences and reaches the 32,768-token limit. This is not because it reads less.

Condition (Gemma 4, GPQA-Diamond) Prox threshold (calibrated to 18%) Prox top-k
Actual reads 13.3% 13.5%
Accuracy 11.7 56.3
Reaching the limit out of 792 answers 674 145

The cause was also narrowed down. Changing only Prox’s channel threshold to top-k makes the collapse disappear. Changing only the input threshold does not. Neither flooring the channel minimum retention at 4% nor recalibrating on Gemma 4’s own reasoning prevents the collapse (§4.3, Appendix D.1, F.2).

The authors conjecture that this collapse acts like a cliff. Once a sparse model starts repeating, it is hard to stop on its own, and when the error that sparsification adds per token exceeds some model-specific level, accuracy falls sharply rather than gradually. This explanation is a hypothesis, not a proof (§4.3).

A Reader Built from Weights Alone

When top-k is the retention rule, performance depends on two things: how well channels are ranked before reading, and how discarded channels are handled. The observation that changing the scores moves KL divergence far more than changing the retention rule set the design direction of the reader (§5).

The reader is built once from model weights before deployment. It has no values calibrated to the target model. Three settings—128-coordinate rotation blocks, an 80-coordinate partial scan, and rank-32 recovery—are fixed once on OLMoE development data and reused for all models. For each token and layer, the reader runs three stages. It screens all candidate channels, computes the top $k$ exactly, and recovers the rest.

Consider Fig. 6 of the original. The top contrasts the full model, which reads all channels of the routed experts, with the reader, which reads a ternary sketch, the real weights of the retained $k$ channels, and a recovery map. The middle shows the behavior of the three stages. The bottom breaks down the 17.8% reads on Qwen3-Thinking. The sketch accounts for 4.9%, the exactly computed channels for 12.3%, and the recovery map for 0.6%, while the remaining roughly 82% is not read at all.

Stage 1: Screen with a Ternary Sketch

Weights and hidden states have outliers that make low-bit codes inaccurate. So the gate row $g_j$ and up row $v_j$ are rotated in 128-coordinate blocks by a random Hadamard transform $R$, spreading large values evenly within the block. $R$ is orthogonal, so the rotation does not change the activation ($g_j^\top x = (Rg_j)^\top(Rx)$).

The rotated blocks are stored as follows.

Stored item Value Role
Ternary code $\{-1,0,1\}$ Stand-in for the weights
FP16 scale 1 per block Restores the code to its actual magnitude
$\rho_b$ Mean-squared quantization error of the block Used to rank channels by the error remaining after recovery at high budgets

A block shrinks from 256 bytes in BF16 to about 30 bytes, so the sketch adds about 7% to resident memory. At decode time, $x$ is rotated once and multiplied with the sketch to obtain $\hat g_j \approx g_j^\top x$, $\hat v_j \approx v_j^\top x$ (§5.1).

At low budgets such as 12.8% and 17.8%, reading the entire sketch alone accounts for 44–61% of all reads (for OLMoE). So a partial scan is used. From each block, only the ternary codes of the 80 coordinates with the largest $|Rx|$ are read. This increases the number of exactly computed channels by 20–50% at the same budget (§5.1).

Stage 2: Compute the Top k Exactly with Output-Level Scores

The magnitude that channel $j$ adds to the output is $w_j\,\lVert d_j\rVert\,|a_j|$. Here $w_j$ is the router weight, and $\lVert d_j\rVert$ is the norm of the down column, computed once at load time. Replacing the activation $a_j$ with the sketch estimate gives the score

$$s_j = w_j\,\lVert d_j\rVert\,\bigl|\phi(\hat g_j)\,\hat v_j\bigr|$$

(Equation 1). Because the score is at the output level, channels from different experts can be compared directly. So the top $k$ are chosen across all experts the token passes through. One expert may receive many channels and another none at all (§5.2).

The $k$ channels remaining after screening have their real weights read to compute $a_j$ exactly. To read the down weights contiguously, the down projection is transposed once at load time so that prefill and decode use the same layout.

Stage 3: Recover Discarded Channels with a rank-32 Map

The contribution of a single discarded channel is small, but thousands per layer add up to something not negligible. The screening stage has already computed an activation estimate $p_j = \phi(\hat g_j)\hat v_j$ for every discarded channel, so it is reused without reading gate/up again. The remaining problem is the down column $d_j$ of each discarded channel.

Instead of reading full-width columns, all down columns of the layer are stacked to obtain the top 32 left singular vectors $U \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times 32}$, and the coefficient $b_j = U^\top d_j$ of each channel is stored. The final output is

$$\hat y = \sum_{j \in K} w_j d_j a_j \;+\; U\sum_{j \in S} w_j b_j p_j.$$

The first term is the exact contribution of the retained $K$ channels. The second term adds the estimated contribution of the discarded $S$ channels via the rank-32 map (Equation 2). The map adds about 0.5% to resident memory and 0.5–0.8%p to reads (§5.3).

Accuracy and Speed

Accuracy

Accuracy was evaluated on 9 pairs of three post-trained models (Qwen3-Thinking, Gemma 4, Qwen3.5) and three benchmarks (GPQA-Diamond, IFEval, MMLU-Pro). The full model processes the prompt, and the selector runs for each subsequent decoding token. Accuracy is reported as a percentage of the full model’s accuracy. The table below reconstructs only the rows needed for the roughly 18% budget from Table 1. For calibrated selectors, both the target and the actual reads are listed.

Selector (roughly 18% budget) Target Actual reads Mean Worst
Our reader – 17.8 98.1 95.0
Prox score, top-k – 18.5 96.1 90.4
Prox as published, calibrated 18 12.9 68.5 12.1
WINA as published, top-k – 20 28.4 1.1
TEAL as published, calibrated 20 12.6 9.9 0.0

The reader is the most accurate at both low budgets. At 17.8% it averages 98.1% and 95.0% on the worst pair. At 12.8% it still averages 94.5% and 86.9% on the worst pair, better than the worst pair of any other selector.

The notable place is Prox. It was calibrated to 18% but actually reads 12.9%, similar to the reader’s 12.8%, yet its mean accuracy is only 68.5%. Most of the gap comes from Gemma 4’s repetition loop. On the two Qwen models, Prox matches the reader at similar reads. top-k does not rescue a weak score either. WINA with top-k reaches only 28.4% even at 20% reads (§6.1).

Speed

Speed must be viewed separately as kernel performance and full-system performance. The Triton kernel was compared at 17.8% reads, on a single RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU, against the fastest configuration of unmodified vLLM.

Fig. 7 (a) of the original is decode speedup of the MoE block alone. At batch 1 it is 1.90x for Qwen3-Thinking, 1.71x for Gemma 4, and 1.60x for Qwen3.5. At batch 4 it is 2.39/2.34/2.51x, and the maximum is 2.69x for Qwen3.5 at batch 8.

(b) is full-model performance. Further right means faster per user, and higher means more output per GPU. Because attention is unchanged the gain is small: 1.15–1.36x at batch 1, peaking at 1.75/1.74/1.88x at batch 8–16, and converging to 1.00–1.24x at batch 128 (Table 20). On long contexts of 8k–32k tokens it is 1.08–1.54x.

The reason the gain at batch 1 is smaller than the read savings is fixed cost. On Qwen3-Thinking, even though the MoE block accounts for only 18.3% of full-model memory traffic, the block is only 1.90x faster rather than 5x. Fixed costs such as kernel launch do not shrink with read savings. As the batch grows, these fixed costs are shared, so block speedup increases up to batch 4–8. But as the batch grows further, the union of channels selected by the tokens grows again, increasing the amount that must be read and reducing the gain (§6.2, Appendix J).

Limitations and When to Apply It

The authors acknowledge five limitations (§7).

  1. The kernel converts only part of the read savings into speed. It is tuned for one budget (17.8%) and one GPU type.
  2. Selecting channels for the whole batch at once so that the gain carries to large batches is future work.
  3. The number of coordinates in the partial scan (80 of 128) was set on OLMoE and confirmed only on Gemma 4.
  4. The reader changes only the routed experts during decoding. The sketch and recovery map add about 7% and 0.5% to a BF16 checkpoint, and their share is larger in quantized checkpoints.
  5. The tested models are at most 35B parameters.

There are also two patterns the authors conjecture hold more broadly. These are conjectures, not verified results (§7). One is that short likelihood evaluations hide failures in long generation, and the other is that low KL divergence does not imply high accuracy.

From a reviewer’s perspective, the remaining condition is this. The conclusion is limited to ’the case of using a calibrated threshold on the channels of frozen MoE experts.’ The authors themselves state that thresholds may be valid elsewhere, such as in sparse attention or learned routers (§3). The cliff explanation is also a hypothesis, not a proof.

The operational sweet spot is the decode stage when serving a post-trained MoE model at small batch while the prompt is processed by the full model. Conditions not yet verified are very large batches beyond 128, other GPU types, quantized checkpoints (confirmed only on OLMoE), and the prefill stage.

item.title: Extreme Compression of Per-Layer Embeddings via Cross-Layer Latent Vector Quantization
item.description:
Paper Recent language models keep increasing the amount of information packed into a single vocabulary entry. Per-layer embeddings (PLE), first introduced in Gemma 3n, carried over to Gemma 4: instead of a single input-layer vector per vocabulary item, each decoder layer has a different learned vector. This post examines OPTIC, which shrinks this table by about 100× while retaining most of the original performance, starting from the problem setting and proceeding through a small example, the method, results, and limitations.

OPTIC’s core ideas are two. One is to store a single code per token and have each layer unfold that code with its own decoder; the other is to fit the codes and decoders not by “how faithfully the stored vectors are reconstructed” but by “how much difference appears in the output path the model actually uses.”

Why PLE is a problem

A typical input embedding turns one token into one vector. For the token "cat", it simply retrieves the single vector that the token points to in the vocabulary dictionary. PLE adds a layer axis on top of this. Even for the same token, the vector used at layer 1 differs from the vector used at layer 42, and each layer retrieves its vector from its own stage’s residual connection. The residual connection is the pathway that adds a term to the hidden state as it passes through each layer.

Storage grows immediately. E4B has a vocabulary of 262,144, 42 decoder layers using PLE, and a vector width of 256 dimensions, so storing a separate vector for each token-layer pair results in 11 million token-layer vectors (§1, §2.2). In bfloat16 that is about 5.64GB (§2.2). In the same checkpoint, PLE accounts for 35.2% of parameters (abstract). In the smaller E2B it is 45.8% (§1).

Illustrative example: let’s see what a single token actually stores and does (E4B).

Step State
Input One token ID (e.g. "cat")
Stored state 42 256-dim vectors, one per layer = 42×256 = 10,752 numbers, 21,504 bytes in bfloat16
What happens at a layer That layer’s vector is multiplied elementwise by the gate and projected to the hidden width by the output projection matrix
Output The PLE residual added to the hidden state

Compressing this table by about 100× leaves just over 5 bytes per vector (§1). Existing quantization methods spend those few bytes on “a code per vector.” With 11 million vectors each having its own code, the codes become far too short and reconstruction quality drops sharply.

How OPTIC stores and reconstructs

The problem is clear. 5 bytes is not enough to properly hold a single vector. The PLE table has two directions, the token axis and the layer axis, and OPTIC shares both directions at once (§2.2).

  • Token direction: instead of each token storing its 42 vectors separately, each token stores one code.
  • Layer direction: all tokens in a layer share a single affine decoder (matrix multiply plus addition). The size of this decoder is independent of vocabulary size.

Concretely, token t stores M indices. Each index points to a 4-dimensional codeword in its own codebook, and concatenating the M of them yields a latent vector z_t that summarizes the token. Then layer ℓ unfolds z_t into a 256-dim row with its own affine decoder.

$$ \hat e_{t\ell} = A_\ell z_t + b_\ell $$

In the ~100× setting for E4B, M=161 and 256 codewords (K=256) are used. A single token needs to store only 161 indices, i.e. 161 bytes, reducing 21,504 bytes of 42 vectors to 161 bytes (§2.2). In exchange, the codebook (about 330KB) is shared fully, and the decoder weights (~13.8MB) and biases of the 42 layers are shared by all tokens in the respective layer. Total is 56.4MB, 99.94× versus the original 5.64GB (§2.2, Table 16).

Reading the figure above as a state transition: the input is a single ID for token t. The stored state is the M indices placed in vocabulary row t (e.g., 161 bytes). Each index q_{tm} selects one row (highlighted cell) of its own codebook C_m, and concatenating the 161 selected codewords computes the latent vector z_t (length 644). At this point the layer does not intervene yet. Then layer ℓ applies its own affine weight A_ℓ and bias b_ℓ to compute the 256-dim row ê_{tℓ}, and that row leads to the PLE residual of layer ℓ. Cells of the same color indicate the same layer, and the dashed ellipsis indicates omitted layers and codebooks. Importantly, the original PLE is used only in the “fitting step” and not for actual storage and reconstruction (original Figure 1).

The key point is that the cost of storing indices is now proportional only to vocabulary size V and not to V × L. Conventional row-wise quantization must store an index set per vector, which multiplies by the number of layers, whereas OPTIC removes this layer factor (§2.2, Equation 3).

Why fit on the “output path”

Sharing storage alone is not the end. PLE vectors are not used on their own; at each layer they pass through the gate and output projection and are added to the hidden state. Specifically, the PLE row is multiplied elementwise by a gate derived from the layer’s hidden state, then projected to the hidden width by the output projection matrix W_out (§2.3).

Therefore, what matters more directly to model quality is not how similar the reconstructed vector is “in coordinates” to the original, but how much difference remains after passing through the gate and output projection. OPTIC fits the codes and decoders to minimize the error in this projected output rather than in the stored coordinates (§2.3, Equation 4–5).

$$ \Delta r_{i\ell}(\theta) = W^{\mathrm{out}}_\ell \bigl( \tau\, g_{i\ell} \odot (\hat e_{\theta, t_i \ell} - e_{t_i \ell}) \bigr) $$

Here g_{iℓ} is the gate at calibration position i and layer ℓ, τ is a fixed PLE scale, and ⊙ is elementwise multiplication. Gates from the training records are collected from the pre-compression model and used fixed. Gates for synthetic records are filled with 1 (§3.2). The objective is the mean of this projected output error ‖Δr‖² over positions and layers (§2.3, Equation 5).

The fitting procedure alternates two kinds of updates (§2.4, Algorithm 1). One updates the codebooks and decoders continuously (with AdamW) while fixing the codes; the other reassigns each token’s index to the codeword with the smallest error while fixing the codebooks. Reassignment covers all tokens in the vocabulary. To handle rare tokens that do not appear often in natural-language calibration, it uses a per-layer averaged gate metric G_ℓ as a surrogate objective (§2.4, Equation 6–7). Initialization concatenates per-token vectors, subtracts the vocabulary mean, and builds the latent vectors and decoders via PCA scaled by the output-path weights, then starts with an OPQ-style assignment that splits coordinates into codebook groups and runs K-means within each group.

Results: quality preserved, memory reduced

Quality first. The paper reports the geometric mean of “retention relative to the original” across 7 tasks (PIQA, GSM8K, GPQA Diamond, AIME 2026, MMLU-Redux, IFBench, InfographicVQA). Each task’s retention is capped at 100%, so over-performance on one task cannot mask losses on another. If any single task scores 0, the geometric mean becomes 0 (§3.3, Equation 8).

Question: at ~100× compression, how well do existing quantization methods and OPTIC hold up? Below are the E4B results (Table 1).

Method BF16 retention W4A16 retention
PQ 66.3% 82.4%
AQLM Euclidean beam encoder 46.7% 82.8%
Output-path weighted PCA-PQ 93.3% 88.3%
OPTIC 97.8% 96.9%
Frequency-tiered OPTIC 95.7% 95.1%

On BF16 E4B, OPTIC leads the strongest existing method (PQ) by 31.5 percentage points, and on W4A16 it leads the strongest method (AQLM) by 14.0 percentage points (§4.1). On E2B, OPTIC retains 89.1% on BF16 and 91.5% on W4A16, while the frequency-tiered variant is highest at 90.0% and 93.0% (§4.1, Table 1). The frequency-tiered variant gives more code groups to frequent tokens, uses learned shared codewords per group for the remaining tokens, and preserves exactly the PLE rows of special tokens in bfloat16 (§2.5, Appendix A.3).

Looking at actual task scores shows where the difference comes from. On BF16 E4B, GSM8K is 92.8% for OPTIC versus 92.9% original and 73.5% for PQ. IFBench is 41.7% for OPTIC versus 44.0% original and 16.0% for PQ, and InfographicVQA is 67.5% for OPTIC versus 69.7% original and 38.4% for PQ (§4.1, Table 12). The drop for existing methods is especially large in mathematical reasoning, instruction following, and visual question answering. Bootstrap 95% confidence intervals also separate. On BF16 E4B, OPTIC is 95.5–99.0% and PQ is 60.6–70.5%. On W4A16 E4B, OPTIC is 93.9–97.8% and AQLM is 76.8–87.1% (Table 2). These intervals reflect benchmark sampling uncertainty.

OPTIC holds up even at higher compression rates. The curve below plots retention (y-axis) against compression rate (x-axis, log scale).

Dashed lines are existing methods (PQ, OPQ-P), solid lines are the authors’ method. OPTIC retains 97.8% at ~100×, and still holds 90.5% and 84.1% at 594× and 1002×. W4A16 E4B at the same points is 87.7% and 81.8% (§4.2, Table 16). In contrast, output-path weighted PCA-PQ, which improves only row-wise, is good at 93.3% near 100× but falls to 25.1% near 500× and reaches 0 near 1000× (§4.2). The fewer bytes left per vector, the larger the benefit of sharing codes at the token level.

Kernel speed and system performance are measured separately

Beyond quality, how memory and time behave in actual serving is a separate measurement. The authors compared original PLE and ~100× compressed PLE in vLLM on a single RTX 4090 under identical settings (fixed 1GiB KV cache) (§6).

Memory drops substantially from a system perspective. For BF16 E4B, process GPU memory falls from 18.57GB to 13.05GB, a 29.7% reduction, and for W4A16 it falls from 12.95GB to 7.37GB, a 43.1% reduction (Table 7). This is because the PLE resident on the GPU shrinks from 5.64GB to 56.4MB.

Time must be read from both a kernel and a system perspective. In single-lookup measurements where the table is in host memory, dense lookup is faster for a single token (compressed lookup is 0.6×), but from 32 tokens compressed lookup becomes faster, reaching 12.1× at 8192 (Table 11). In terms of total serving time, compressed PLE is only up to 0.40% slower on BF16 and up to 0.69% slower on W4A16 (Table 9). Compressed lookup must perform extra multiplications to unfold codes with the decoder, so under the same cache budget the conclusion is “memory drops a lot, time stays about the same.”

However, situations where memory is the real bottleneck are different. Under the same GPU budget, there are cases where dense PLE either fails to start because it does not fit in the KV cache or processes requests sequentially, while compressed PLE cuts completion time by up to 2.1× (§B.3, Table 10). In other words, the goal is not saving serving time per se; the gain appears when memory becomes latency.

Why this works

Start with the analysis showing that layer averaging alone is insufficient. Replacing each vector wholesale with its layer’s vocabulary mean drops GSM8K from 92.9% to 43.5%, GPQA from 56.9% to 23.0%, and AIME to 0, even though the mean vector accounts for only 8.1% of the table’s total squared norm (§5.1, Appendix E.3). In other words, the information that differs per token is the core of performance.

So is that per-token variation concentrated in low dimensions? The next figure answers this question.

The top panel shows stored coordinates and the bottom panel shows coordinates after output projection; each curve (layer) shows how many principal components explain the per-token variation (x-axis: number of principal components, y-axis: cumulative explained ratio). In stored coordinates, 212–227 directions are needed to explain 90%. After output projection, this drops to 1–205 per layer (median 158) (§5.1, Figure 3). This gap is the basis for OPTIC’s choice to “fit on the output path.” After the gate and projection, important variation is concentrated substantially toward lower dimensions, a signal that a low latent width can be tolerated to some degree.

There are also experiments that isolate and validate the two designs. One is the effect of code sharing. If each token-layer vector gets an independent latent code and the same fitting procedure is applied, E4B BF16 retention drops from 97.8% to 79.3% at nearly the same storage budget (Table 3). The caveat that this difference mixes the effect of sharing itself with the effect of reallocating bytes between codes and decoders is revisited in the limitations section. Decoder freedom also matters. If only the decoder is refit by least squares with indices, codebooks, and biases fixed while limiting rank to 20 per layer, retention drops from 95.09% to 70.55% (§5.2, Table 4).

The other is the effect of output-path fitting. With codes and initialization fixed and only the objective changed, the context-dependent output-path objective gives 1.98 percentage points higher retention on average than Euclidean error and 0.31 percentage points higher than the diagonal approximation (§5.3, Table 5). Also, continuous updates produce most of the gain (63.60% with initialization only, 94.67% with continuous updates), and index reassignment adds 0.65–1.14 percentage points on top (§5.3, Table 6).

Limitations and applicability

To decide whether to use OPTIC in practice, one must separate the limitations the authors state from other conditions.

Start with the limitations the authors state explicitly. Evaluation is limited to Gemma 4 E2B/E4B, and the main comparison uses a single fixed fitting seed, so confidence intervals reflect only benchmark sampling uncertainty (Limitations). The six baselines are reconstructions of the original papers’ methods adapted to PLE, and cannot be read directly against results from their original settings (Limitations). The code-sharing ablation also mixes in the effect of reallocating bytes between codes and decoders, so it does not measure only the “pure sharing effect” (Limitations). Calibration adds synthetic records (gate = 1) covering the full vocabulary to 786,432 natural-language positions (§3.2), so tokens that rarely appear in natural language are fitted with synthetic records alone. The output-path loss is also an approximation that measures error only at each layer’s projected output with gates fixed (Limitations).

From a reviewer’s perspective, three things are worth noting. First, the method is specialized for embeddings with a “token×layer” structure like PLE, so the benefit does not carry over directly to ordinary single input embeddings, which lack the layer axis for code sharing. Second, retention is a geometric mean over 7 tasks, and any single task scoring 0 makes the whole thing 0, so if a low-sample task collapses the metric swings sharply. One should check individual scores to see whether a particular task collapses under extreme compression (1000×), but the paper does not report per-task scores for extreme compression (Tables 12 and 13 contain only the 100× condition; those numbers are not reported in the original). Third, the serving gains above depend on a memory-bottleneck condition, so there is less to expect in environments without it.

In conclusion, OPTIC is promising for settings where “the embedding table makes up a large part of the model and GPU memory is constrained,” especially when serving PLE-family models with many concurrent requests. It can also be combined with W4A16 weight-only quantization. The perspective of fitting where the model actually consumes the vectors rather than where they are stored shows that embedding capacity and compressed representation can be designed together from the start (Conclusion).
