item.title: Intern Lumina U2: A Multi-Codebook Diffusion Large Language Model for Omni-Visual Understanding and Image Generation
item.description:
Paper

Problem: Why It’s Hard to Unify Understanding and Generation in One Representation

There have been many attempts to merge image understanding and image generation into a single model. Most, however, optimize the two abilities separately in different representation spaces. When text is trained as a token classification problem and images are trained with a diffusion/flow objective over continuous vectors, the two objectives push against each other within one backbone, which tends to make training unstable.

Conversely, if images are represented entirely as discrete tokens like text, the objective is unified into one. But because one position is compressed into a single code, it becomes hard to carry fine-grained detail and high-level semantics at the same time.

Intern Lumina U2 sidesteps this dilemma. It represents images entirely as discrete tokens, but bundles 8 codes per position to increase expressiveness, and trains understanding and generation together with a single mask prediction loss. As a result, with only about 1.4B parameters activated per token out of 16.9B total, it ranks first on 6 of 10 image understanding benchmarks (tied with BAGEL on MME-C), sits at the top level among unified models for text-to-image generation, and approaches the top tier for editing (original §1, §7). It beats LLaDA2.0-Uni, which uses the same language backbone, on 8 of 10 benchmarks.

On the inference side, within the same evaluation protocol, it cuts the time to produce one image from 159.9 seconds to 35.9 seconds—about 4.45×—while raising GenEval from 86.6 to 89.3 (original Table 4).

Original Fig. 1 (PDF p.1) shows the breadth of tasks this model handles. You can see a single checkpoint answering text questions as understanding while generating images according to text and editing instructions. The performance numbers in the body are measured values taken from the benchmark tables that appear later, not the “demonstrations” in this figure.

Background: Why a Single Code per Position Is Not Enough

The visual tokenizer of existing discrete unified models quantizes one position of an image into a single code. For example, VQGAN-style tokenizers preserve fine detail for reconstruction but are not aligned with text, while semantic encoders such as SigLIP match text well but cannot reconstruct pixels (original §3.2). A single code lacks the information capacity to carry both at once.

So this paper uses AToken, but in its discrete (FSQ) configuration. AToken is a tokenizer that starts from a SigLIP2 encoder and is trained jointly for reconstruction and understanding, and it quantizes one position into a code from each of 8 codebooks. Each codebook has a vocabulary of 4096 entries, and a code is the index of that entry (original §3.2).

Illustrative example. Given one 256×256 image, AToken with patch size 16 turns it into a grid of 16×16 = 256 positions (original Appendix B, Table 20). To show the code bundle, shrink to a 2×2 grid and look at only position (0,0); that visual token is 8 integers (c₁, …, c₈), each between 0 and 4095. On the input side, the model looks these 8 integers up in the embedding table of their respective codebooks, obtaining 8 2048-dim vectors, concatenates them into 16384 dimensions, and compresses that into one 2048-dim vector with a linear transform. That is, the 8 codes enter the backbone as “one token.” In the actual 256×256 layout, 256 positions plus 16 separators at the end of each row make a sequence of 272 positions (original Appendix B). The 2×2 reduction is for explaining the code bundle and should not be confused with the experimental numbers below.

Why this structure is needed becomes clearer when looking at the generation side. In understanding, images are “conditions,” but in generation, images are “prediction targets.” The figure below shows the overall flow.

Original Fig. 3 (PDF p.7) shows the structure at a glance. Visual input is tokenized by AToken and text by LLaDA2.0’s tokenizer, and the two are merged into one sequence. The MoE diffusion backbone reconstructs masked text tokens with the text head and masked visual tokens with the multi-codebook AR head. The fact that the AR head draws 8 codes per position “sequentially” is the core axis of this model.

Method: How the 8 Codes Go In and Come Out

There are three ways to handle the 8 codes at one position. Unfolding the 8 separately into 8 tokens makes the sequence 8× longer. Keeping one token and predicting the 8 codes independently of one another discards dependencies between codes. Intern Lumina U2 takes the third. It keeps one position as a single backbone token but models the 8 codes jointly as a joint distribution (original §3.4).

Input: Embed each codebook separately and concatenate

The input interface turns the 8 codes at a position into one 2048-dim vector. Each codebook k has its own embedding table E_k (4096 codes + mask/separator entries). When a position is masked, all 8 codes become the mask entry. The input vector is obtained by concatenating the 8 embeddings and applying a single linear transform.

$$x = W_{\mathrm{in}} [E_1(c_1); E_2(c_2); \dots; E_8(c_8)], \quad W_{\mathrm{in}} \in \mathbb{R}^{2048 \times (8 \cdot 2048)}$$

This design has two benefits. Because the codes are merged before entering the backbone, sequence length does not grow 8×, and because each codebook has its own table, there is no need to insert visual codes into the text vocabulary or distinguish them with index offsets (original §3.4). The figure below compares the three candidates.

Original Fig. 4 (PDF p.9) shows the three designs; the adopted third design (D3) places an independent embedding table per codebook, concatenates across spatial positions, and projects. This choice is supported by measurement, not decoration. Under the same conditions, D3’s next-code top-1 accuracy is 0.0459, ahead of the single shared table D1 (0.0426) and offset shared D2 (0.0415) by more than 10 standard errors (original Table 15). D1 requires 2.35× the memory of D3 because of its wider classifier and also converges more slowly (original §7, Table 15).

Output: An AR head that draws the 8 codes sequentially

The output interface predicts 8 codes from a single final hidden state h (2048-dim) of the backbone. It factorizes the joint distribution of the 8 codes in codebook index order.

$$p(c \mid h) = \prod_{k=1}^{8} p(c_k \mid h, c_{\lt k})$$

This is implemented as the multi-codebook AR head. It is a 6-layer causal Transformer that processes a length-8 “depth sequence” for each visual position. The first element is q = W_q h + b_q (the projection of h) plus position embedding s₁; the k ≥ 2-th element is the embedding e_{k-1} of the previously predicted code ĉ_{k-1} plus position embedding s_k. Each block is conditioned on q + u_k via adaLN, so the backbone output directly modulates each prediction step. Finally, a separate classifier W_k^out (4096×2048) per codebook produces the logits (original §3.4).

The difference between training and inference is key to understanding this head. The figure below shows it.

Original Fig. 5 (PDF p.11) places training and inference side by side. During training, ground-truth codes are fed in, and a single teacher-forced causal pass yields the logits for all 8 codes at once. During inference there is no ground truth, so codes are sampled sequentially over 8 steps, appending the embedding of the sampled code to the prefix for the next step. Positions are processed in parallel, codebooks sequentially.

Why “sequential prediction” rather than “independent prediction”? In an ideal conditional model, if the 8 codes are independent given h, the cross-entropy of the two approaches is the same; if they are not independent, sequential prediction’s cross-entropy is no higher (original §3.4). In experiments this difference is in fact large. In a 512×512 comparison with a similar token budget, the parallel independent head scores GenEval 68.94, the AR head 82.78, and the Q-Former-style head only 69.67 (original Table 16). The parallel head falls particularly on counting, position, and attribute binding—tasks that require “exactly one correct combination” of object and attribute. That is, the AR head’s gain comes not from fancier conditioning but from modeling dependencies between codes (original §7).

Sequence and masks: every task in one format

Once the input/output interfaces are set, understanding, generation, and editing must all fit into one sequence format. Every sample is converted into a conversation of “user message (condition) + assistant answer (prediction target).” Conditions are combinations of text, image, video, and 3D assets; answers are text answers or visual answers. Each token in the sequence carries five pieces of metadata: type, turn number, noise status (clean/noisy), block number, and position ID (original §3.5).

This metadata leads to rules that determine the attention mask. Conditions are visible to their own turn and later turns; answers are not visible to conditions. Text answers follow turn-level block diffusion, and visual answers follow spatial mask diffusion. The figure below draws four scenarios.

Original Fig. 6 (PDF p.12) shows four cases. (a) For an image answer, one noisy visual answer follows the clean condition, and all positions are bidirectional. (b) For a text answer, noisy blocks undergo block diffusion and read clean copies of preceding blocks. (c) is the case where, when an image answer follows a text answer as in “think then generate,” the image reads clean copies of the preceding text blocks. (d) is the case in multi-turn where a later turn reads clean copies of earlier answers. Clean copies serve as unmasked context that later blocks/turns and subsequent diffusion steps can reference (original §3.5). Visual answers have no clean copies because later turns do not reference them as conditions.

By changing only the mask rules this way, text generation (block diffusion), image generation (spatial mask diffusion), editing (source image condition + target image), and multi-turn understanding are all trained simultaneously with a single mask prediction loss. The loss for text tokens and the loss for visual positions (the mean negative log-likelihood of the 8 codes) are averaged over the same denominator, and the MoE load-balancing loss is added with weight $10^{-3}$ (original §3.6). At generation time, text expands left to right block by block and denoises within a block in parallel, while images iteratively refine all screen positions in parallel (original §6.1).

Inference Acceleration: How the Expensive Image Sampling Was Reduced

Image generation is far more expensive than text. A single 1024×1024 image has 64×65 = 4160 positions, each requiring 8 codes drawn sequentially, and this process repeats 96 times in the default setting (original Appendix B, §6.2). The paper reduces this cost by changing the sampler without additional training. There are two directions: one is “reduce the computation of one step with caching,” and the other is “reduce the number of steps needed.”

The Mermaid below shows how the image generation loop updates state—what is kept and what is recomputed.

 flowchart TD
 A["Initialize all visual token grid as masks"] --> B["backbone: compute hidden state h for each masked position"]
 B --> C["AR head: predict 8 codes sequentially per position"]
 C --> D["plateau determination via EMA"]
 D --> E["positions passing plateau are committed immediately"]
 E --> F["among non-plateau positions, keep only cosine budget rt masks, commit the rest"]
 F --> G{"Any masks remaining?"}
 G -->|yes| B
 G -->|none| H["AToken decoder reconstructs codes into pixels"]

At each iteration, what is kept is the codes of committed positions, and what is recomputed is the hidden states of still-masked positions. The cache described below reuses “the hidden states of positions whose codes have not changed,” and the plateau determination reduces the number of steps by selecting “positions that can be committed earlier.”

Cache reuse: don’t recompute the same input

In image refinement, the codes of most positions no longer change as steps proceed. The paper layers three reuse techniques (original §6.2.1). First, it runs the conditional and unconditional branches of classifier-free guidance (CFG) as one batch to share backbone computation. Second, while the AR head predicts the 8 codes per position, it caches the key-value states of the previously generated code prefix. Third, the backbone reuses the hidden states of positions whose codes have not changed.

The third cache needs a criterion for judging when it has gone stale. It measures the normalized difference (drift) between the new hidden state and the cached hidden state at recomputed positions, and when this exceeds a threshold, it refreshes the entire cache at the next step. This is taken from the V-verify score of dLLM-Cache (original §6.2.1).

Plateau determination + Halton order: commit earlier

Caching reduces the cost per step but leaves the number of steps unchanged. Reducing steps requires deciding when to commit a position. Yet visual token confidence, unlike text, has very low absolute values. Over 96 steps, the median per-prompt confidence rises only from 0.046 to 0.127, and the 90th percentile does not exceed 0.32 (original §6.2.2, Fig. 8). So the existing approach of “commit when confidence exceeds an absolute threshold” does not fit here.

Instead, the paper uses confidence as a temporal signal. It takes an exponential moving average (EMA, β=0.7) of each position’s sample confidence, and if after the first 4 iterations the rate of change stays below a threshold for P=5 consecutive steps and the EMA value exceeds a floor, it judges that “a plateau has been reached” and commits immediately. The floor prevents “low but flat” confidence from being mistaken for stability (original §6.2.2). Positions passing the plateau are committed immediately, and among non-plateau positions only the cosine budget rt = min(nt, |Ut|) are kept masked. The positions to keep are chosen from the later part of the Halton order (a low-discrepancy sequence) so they spread evenly across the image. This combination is called Plateau-Halton sampling with V-verify, or PHV for short. The chosen settings are δp=0.18, fp=0.005 (original Table 4).

Whether plateau determination actually finds “stable positions” well was confirmed by offline validation. It pairs positions that passed plateau determination with positions in the same image that have similar confidence/EMA but did not pass, and compares the flip rate (the fraction of top-1 predictions that flip when both are kept masked for additional steps). Across 200 prompts, plateau positions have a lower flip rate, and the gap widens with longer retention (H=2: −0.012, H=8: −0.048). In 157 of 200 prompts, plateau positions were more stable (original §6.2.2, Fig. 9). That is, plateau determination is not a perfect indicator but a statistically significant stability signal.

A table that looks at speed and quality together

The table below shows results when optimizations are stacked one at a time on the same checkpoint and the same 1024×1024 protocol (553 GenEval prompts, 1 image per prompt, CFG scale 4.0, temperature 0.9, seed 42) (original Table 4). Latency is wall-clock time per image excluding kernel preheat and including cache warmup, so it is end-to-end system time, not kernel-level. GenEval in this table uses a one-image-per-prompt protocol, so its numbers should not be compared directly with the official multi-sample GenEval in the results table (Table 7) (original Table 4 caption).

Method Steps Backbone forward (cache hit rate) Latency (s) Speed GenEval
Production path 96.0 192 159.9 1.00× 86.6
+ CFG batching 96.0 192 117.2 1.36× 89.0
+ AR head KV cache 96.0 192 84.2 1.90× 88.6
+ hidden state cache 96.0 192 (65%) 64.1 2.49× 89.2
+ V-verify refresh 96.0 192 (63%) 64.5 2.48× 89.3
+ Halton selection (HVV) 96.0 192 (64%) 66.5 2.40× 88.2
HVV, fixed 60 steps 60.0 120 (63%) 42.6 3.75× 89.7
Plateau only (no cache/Halton) 56.9 114 46.5 3.44× 87.2
Plateau + V-verify 56.2 112 (35%) 34.8 4.59× 87.2
PHV (chosen) 60.4 121 (41%) 35.9 4.45× 89.3

The trick to reading the table is to separate the cache series from the step-reduction series. The top six rows fix steps at 96 and stack caches, reducing latency from 159.9 s to the 64 s range (2.5×). GenEval rises from 86.6 to a maximum of 89.3, and the last Halton selection row is 88.2. The lower rows that reduce steps drop to the 35–47 s range, and among them the “plateau only” and “plateau + V-verify” rows fall to GenEval 87.2.

PHV maintaining GenEval 89.3 at 35.9 s is because Halton order better chooses “which positions to commit within the same step budget,” raising GenEval by more than 2 points over using only plateau and V-verify without Halton (34.8 s, 87.2) (original §6.2.2). Note that the cache hit rate (41%, 63%, etc.) is the backbone forward reuse ratio, not the latency reduction rate itself.

Results: Where It Stands Among Unified Models

Results can be split along two axes: “understanding” and “generation.” Comparison targets are divided into understanding-only models (Qwen2.5-VL, LLaDA-V), unified models (Janus-Pro, BAGEL, InternVL-U, LLaDA2.0-Uni, etc.), and generation-only models (FLUX.1, Qwen-Image) (original §7). Unless otherwise noted, the numbers below are for the Ascend base model.

Image understanding and reasoning

In image understanding and reasoning, this model ranks first on 6 of 10 benchmarks (tied with BAGEL on MME-C). The most notable gaps appear on CharXiv (85.9), HallusionBench (64.6), MathVision (36.5), and DynaMath (63.6) (original Table 5). The comparison with LLaDA2.0-Uni, which shares the same language backbone, is especially informative, since LLaDA2.0-Uni uses a semantics-only visual interface. The paper interprets the pattern of leading on 8 of 10 as a result consistent with the expressiveness of the multi-codebook representation (original §7).

For video understanding, the Ascend base model ranks first on MLVU 62.1 and MVBench 61.8, while the NVIDIA reference model ranks first on Video-MME with 56.7. However, the Ascend base model’s Video-MME 52.6 is lower than LLaDA-V’s 56.1 (original Table 6). On 3D MM-Vet, the Ascend base model scores 50.5, ahead of ShapeLLM (47.4) and PointLLM (41.2), but the NVIDIA reference model scores 43.8, behind ShapeLLM. Video and 3D generation are not yet supported.

Text-to-image generation

On the generation side, it is at the top level among unified models on major benchmarks: GenEval 89 (tied for best among unified models), DPG-Bench 87.79, UniGenBench 86.11 (EN overall average), and TIIF-Bench long-form 87.1 (original Table 7, 8). On UniGenBench, the gaps are especially large in the logical reasoning (84.17) and grammar (91.18) dimensions (original Table 8). On WISE it scores 0.56, second among unified models behind LLaDA2.0-Uni (0.68) (original Table 7).

Editing and scientific diagrams

For editing, ImgEdit 3.82 and GEdit-Bench (EN) 6.06 (original Table 14). On ImgEdit it beats BAGEL (3.20) and OmniGen2 (3.44), but on GEdit-EN it is lower than BAGEL (6.52) and OmniGen2 (6.41). For scientific diagram generation, it ranks first on VeriphyT2IBench’s Local score with 76.58, and second on Global overall with 81.22 behind Princigram-BAGEL (82.54). In the domain breakdown, it leads the physics-specialized Princigram family in some domains, such as Local E&M (83.30) and Global Mechanics (84.80) (original Table 11, 12).

Contribution of the core designs

The contributions of the two core designs are separated by ablation. The input interface D3 leads D1 and D2 in next-code accuracy, matches D2 in memory, and uses only 1.9% more parameters (original Table 15). The output head AR is best on all four generation benchmarks versus parallel and Q-Former (original Table 16). These two results support the choice of “independent embedding per codebook + modeling dependencies between codes.”

Cross-platform validation

One thing to note is that the main numbers for this model come from a checkpoint trained on 1024 Ascend 910B NPUs, and a reference model trained separately on NVIDIA GPUs with the same architecture and recipe but a smaller token budget is used for cross-validation (original §5, Table 3, Appendix D). Since the numbers for both platforms are reported side by side in the tables, this can be read as evidence of cross-platform portability and consistency, not an accidental dependence on a single hardware.

Limitations and Adoption Judgment

The authors themselves state two limitations. First, the multi-codebook AR head must draw 8 codes sequentially, adding decoding overhead, and high-resolution generation lengthens the visual sequence (original §8). At 1024×1024 there are 4160 positions each with 8 codes, and even with PHV’s 4.45× reduction it still takes 35.9 seconds per image (original Table 4), which gives a sense of this cost. Second, the current system covers image generation/editing and does not support video/3D generation (original §8).

There are also constraints readable from the tables that the authors do not state directly. On OneIG-Bench, this model’s overall score is 0.494, similar to the best unified model LLaDA2.0-Uni (0.505), but sample diversity is low at 0.150 (original Table 10). The original does not analyze the cause of this degradation. Meanwhile, the authors describe the stability signal of plateau determination as an average tendency rather than a perfect indicator, and plateau positions were more stable in only 157 of 200 cases, so the relationship did not hold in the remaining 43 (original Fig. 9).

Conclusion

This model is suitable for environments that want image, video, and 3D understanding plus image generation and editing all from a single checkpoint. With about 1.4B activated parameters, it delivers top-level understanding and generation performance among unified models, and training and evaluation on both Ascend and NVIDIA platforms confirmed platform portability and consistency.

On the other hand, for cases that need to generate video or 3D, real-time services requiring very low latency at high resolution, or creative uses where sample diversity is central, it is not yet validated or not suitable.

item.title: Matrix-Game 4.0: Harnessing Video Models for Real-Time Playable Game Worlds
item.description:
Paper

Introduction

A game world built by a video generation model alone stores off-screen state nowhere. Every time a corridor you have already passed through is redrawn, it changes, and rules such as health have to be read back from pixels. Matrix-Game 4.0 has the game engine enforce rules and state in code, while the video model is responsible only for rendering the screen.

Problem: why a video model collapses when it plays the game alone

Existing interactive world models (the Genie series, GameNGen, and others) pack both the “world’s dynamics” and the “screen” into the network. The model that generates the next frame is also the only place that remembers world state. The authors cite four limitations of this structure (§1).

  • The external environment never continuously corrects it. The model rolls forward on its own, detached from the world, and state outside the view is not maintained separately.
  • Small errors accumulate in autoregressive generation. Even with external 3D tools, accumulated error in the estimated camera pose collapses the scene.
  • Past frames pile up uncompressed. Memory grows linearly with rollout length.
  • Rules remain at the level of exploration. There are no executable rules that support persistent action consequences and explicit goals.

More fundamentally, the authors argue that a playable world also requires low interaction latency, meaningful game mechanics beyond exploration, and a shared world state for multiplayer (§1).

A small example: what happens when you look back down a corridor

This is an illustrative example, not a measurement. It compares a situation in which the protagonist walks into a castle corridor and then turns around.

Step Pixel-memory model Matrix-Game 4.0
Input A single backward action The same single action
Remaining state The corridor seen on the way in survives only as tokens compressed into context; there are no separate state values The engine stores the off-screen door object in code and updates its position and open state according to rules (§2.1)
Change, omission, rejection Re-imagines the corridor from memory (change). It does not keep door state separately, so it omits it, and it does not check “is this the same door I came through?” (rejection) The proxy draws the door’s location with simple geometry. When a reference image is available, the coding agent fills in a caption such as “a wind-worn thatched hut, a dark red wooden front gate” (§2.2)
Output A corridor with no guarantee that the door passed on the way in has the same color and position A corridor where the door’s position and state match the previous visit. Spatial memory frames help keep revisited locations consistent (§4.1)

The key question is where off-screen state is stored, and this paper moves that responsibility from the network to the game engine.

Method: dividing rules, state, and rendering among three actors

An execution harness is a framework that keeps game logic outside the video model and lets the model render only the screen. Matrix-Game 4.0 wraps the video model in such a harness. Three components run in one loop (Figure 2). The arrows in the diagram below are not names but the values actually exchanged.

 flowchart LR
 P["Player<br/>W key / 'add a shield'"] -->|"Move / shoot actions"| E["Game engine<br/>Hit detection, health and durability updates"]
 P -->|"Request sentence"| A["Coding agent<br/>Writes rule code and registers it with the engine"]
 A -->|"Game code / scene description"| E
 E -->|"Event: oil barrel explosion"| A
 E -->|"Proxy: object position and rotation"| V["Video model<br/>Generates one latent chunk in 1–2 steps"]
 A -->|"Dynamic caption sentence"| V
 V -->|"Key/value from previous chunk"| V
 V -->|"4 generated frames"| P
  • Game engine (referee) computes what actually happened on every frame. It updates health by adding damage taken, compares bullet and object coordinates to detect hits, and stores quest progress. Instead of the screen, it sends the video model a structural render—a proxy that draws roads, buildings, characters, and interactive objects as simple geometry. Even when an object leaves the screen, its state continues according to engine rules (§2.1).
  • Multimodal coding agent (screenwriter and translator) communicates with the engine in both directions. It reads the state and events sent by the engine and turns them into sentences (downward), and it writes the player’s ideas as executable game code and registers them with the engine (upward). “Make monsters swarm in from all sides” does not stop at adding monsters; it defines in code where and how they spawn, how they move and attack, and what constitutes victory or defeat (§2.2). For requests with unspecified details (such as the space behind a door whose contents are not predetermined), it invents the scene layout, story, and NPC dialogue and hands them to the engine, which then manages that state (§2.2).
  • Video generation model (painter) receives the proxy and turns it into frames with materials, lighting, atmosphere, and fine detail (§2.3).

This division leaves one challenge. The real-time performance burden lands entirely on visual generation. The engine only has to run a lightweight simulation, and what remains is “how fast can the video model be made?” (§2).

Conditions: the proxy and caption the engine passes every frame

To preserve structure and fill in only details, the video model needs “conditions” that change from moment to moment. The authors split conditions into two streams: a proxy and a dynamic caption.

Proxy and paired training data

A proxy is a screen that draws terrain, buildings, and characters as untextured geometric shapes; it tells the model what to draw and where. Training data is collected by pairing this proxy with high-fidelity screens.

From Unreal Engine 5 (UE5), four scenes are captured: a medieval castle, an ancient Egyptian desert, an aerial battle over a desert canyon, and the CitySample city. Each capture is recorded at 1280×720 and keeps three aligned videos that share the same camera trajectory and frame indices—a UE5 RGB render, a low-polygon structural render (BBox), and a depth render of the proxy geometry (Figure 3a, §3.1). In the proxy, the sky is black and the ground is a gray checkerboard. Buildings and walls are flat-colored boxes and prisms, trees are cylinders plus spheres, characters are block figures, and every primitive has only a black outline, removing texture, reflection, and shadow. Shooter and aerial clips are about one minute long. There are 114,334 training clips in total, or 1,712 hours (Table 1). Castle, desert, and city each contribute three capture sessions, while the entire aerial capture batch is held out, so no holdout source contributes training clips. Alongside capture, the system records object instance IDs, visibility, and causal interaction events in per-frame metadata (§3.1).

Dynamic captions: descriptions refreshed every frame

A dynamic caption is not a fixed sentence but a description that changes with the current game state. In an interactive game, turning the camera changes which objects are visible, and moving or triggering an event changes object states. A fixed sentence cannot follow these changes.

For every 81-frame clip, camera pose, actions, visible objects, events, and environment are written to a frame-aligned CSV. The system looks up a semantic description table using the IDs of currently visible objects, then fills a template with position, distance, state, and events to build the prompt (Figure 3b, §3.2). This lookup and assembly runs on rule-based templates without a vision-language model (§3.2).

The city-driving example in Figure 4 shows this in action. As the car moves forward, parked vehicles drop out of the description, a pedestrian changes from “standing” to “walking closer”, and newly visible objects are announced under “Changes”. Caption color encodes meaning: orange text comes from object states and events, while blue text comes from position and distance (Figure 4). The proxy supplies structure (position, layout, motion), and the caption supplies semantics (which objects exist and what state they are in). Because they carry different information, together they impose constraints.

Renderer: turning a bidirectional model into a 1–2 step causal generator

The rendering model is Wan2.2 5B’s Fun Control variant converted into a video-to-video (V2V, a method that rewrites an input video) model (§4.1). Starting from the Wan2.2-Fun-5B Control weights, it uses an 81-frame window (704×1280) and performs bidirectional V2V fine-tuning with a flow-matching objective, conditioned on the proxy, the caption, the first frame, and up to three spatial memory frames (§4.2).

After fine-tuning, the model is converted into a causal generator through the three stages of Causal Forcing++ (§4.3). A “chunk” is a block completed at once, consisting of one latent frame (in practice, four video frames).

  1. Teacher-forced autoregressive diffusion: A causal teacher is trained so that each latent frame sees only preceding ground-truth frames plus the first and context frames. This teacher samples chunks with a multi-step ODE solver that integrates over several fine steps.
  2. Causal consistency distillation: With a fixed teacher and an online student plus an EMA student (an exponential moving average copy of the weights), the teacher moves from one point on a 48-level noise grid to the next lower level in one step (classifier-free guidance 3). The online student predicts the clean chunk from a higher level and is trained to match the EMA student’s prediction at the lower level. After 5,000 steps (EMA decay 0.99), the EMA student generates a chunk in 4 steps.
  3. Distribution matching (DMD): The student learns from its own autoregressive rollouts, eventually reducing generation to 2 steps per chunk (4 steps for the first latent frame).

The completed chunk is conditioned on four inputs: the low-polygon proxy drawn by the engine, the dynamic caption, spatial memory frames that preserve consistency when revisiting a location, and the first frame that connects it to the scene already on screen (Figure 5).

The network is a Diffusion Transformer (DiT), the transformer backbone of a diffusion model that denoises noise into a screen. Thirty blocks apply causal self-attention, text cross-attention, and a feedforward network (hidden width 14336) in sequence, and the timestep modulates the blocks through AdaLN (a technique that adjusts normalization statistics by timestep). At 480×864, one latent frame becomes 15×27=405 tokens. Self-attention reads a KV cache—a temporary memory that stores the keys and values of past outputs—containing three spatial memory frames, a reference frame, and the most recent 20 chunks. Once a chunk is complete, the model passes its latent through once more at t=0 without control inputs and writes clean keys and values into the cache (§4.1, Figure 5).

The output head predicts a “velocity”, and the latent is updated with a flow update.

$$ z \leftarrow z - \sigma\, v $$

Here $z$ is the latent, $v$ is the predicted velocity, and $\sigma$ is the noise level. One such update gives 1-step generation, and two give 2-step generation (§4.1). The evaluation setting uses 2 steps per chunk (§6.1).

Opening 60 FPS on a single GPU with kernel optimization

Because a chunk is just one latent frame (four video frames), fewer steps mean less work per invocation. In exchange, the GPU spends more time waiting for the CPU to launch kernels. The bottleneck shifts from “amount of computation” to “launch overhead” (§5, Figure 6a).

Performance is best read as two metrics. Throughput is the steady-state generation rate at which the model produces frames, while latency is the time from a key press to the first frame that reflects it. Latency is measured while the game runs at 60 FPS. The authors remove overhead in the order shown in Table 2.

Setting (cumulative) FPS↑ Latency (ms)↓
Causal Wan2.2 DiT, 4 steps, full Wan VAE 4.5 1110
+ lightweight VAE (TAEHV) 6.5 867
+ RoPE kernel, text KV cache 15.4 551
+ FP8 weights + CUDA Graph 24.2 466
+ 1-step distillation 51.2 376
+ asynchronous I/O pipeline 57.7 367
+ fused Triton kernels 65.8 121
+ ring KV cache 73.7 117
+ split KV FlashAttention 83.4 112

Table conditions: 480×864, chunk size one latent frame (four video frames), KV window 21 latent frames, one NVIDIA RTX 5090.

Overall, FPS rises from 4.5 to 83.4 (about 19×), and latency falls from 1110 to 112 ms (about 9.9×) (Table 2, §5). Each optimization does the following.

  • CUDA Graph: Records the operation order of the DiT backbone once and replays it with a single launch at execution time. Kernel launch overhead disappears. Linear-layer weights are stored in 8-bit (FP8) (§5).
  • Fused kernels: RoPE (an attention technique that encodes position as a rotation), normalization, and FP8 quantization are fused in Triton (a language for building GPU kernels). The query, key, and value projections of a layer share a single quantization of the input, and the caption’s keys and values are recomputed only when the caption changes (§5).
  • Ring KV cache: Instead of shifting the entire KV window whenever the window slides, it overwrites the oldest slot with the new latent frame, eliminating movement cost (Figure 6c).
  • Split KV attention: It splits the self-attention KV window into seven ranges, computes them in parallel, and combines them with log-sum-exp. It caches INT8 K and FP8 V for each range and requantizes only the changed ranges (Figure 6d).
  • Decoding and I/O: It replaces the full Wan VAE decoder that restores latents to a screen with the lightweight TAEHV and runs model input/output through an asynchronous pipeline. Decoding is moved ahead of the clean KV update so that frames can be emitted earlier (Figure 6b, §5).

It is worth distinguishing the low-precision representations. FP8 is the storage format for linear-layer weights, whereas INT8 K and FP8 V are quantization of the attention KV cache, recomputed when the window changes (§5, Figure 6d). Both reduce memory and bandwidth, but they play different roles.

With all these optimizations combined, on a single RTX 5090 the peak GPU memory is about 18.2 GiB for both one- and two-step generation, and one step processes one chunk (four frames) in 48 ms. The text encoder, DiT, and VAE all fit on the same card (§5). Even on 16 GiB cards, under one-step generation with a fixed prompt, it reaches about 67 FPS on an RTX 5080 (about 12.8 GiB) and about 58 FPS on an RTX 5070 Ti (about 10.9 GiB) (§5).

Results: what 112 ms means and comparison with other systems

The integrated system runs a 60 FPS game at 480p on a single RTX 5090 and takes 112 ms from key input to screen update (§1, Table 3). Table 3 compares end-to-end latency with recent interactive generation systems.

System Latency Resolution Hardware
Code World Model (streaming) ~10.2 s 1344×768 1×H200
Magpie ~1.55 s 1280×768 1×H100
AgentGarten ~878 ms 832×480 1×H100
StreamRender-H3 ~517 ms 1344×768 8×GB200
Matrix-Game 4.0 112 ms 864×480 1×RTX 5090

Matrix-Game 4.0’s latency is about one-fifth that of the next-fastest StreamRender-H3, and it is the only system in the comparison that runs on a single consumer GPU (§6.2, Table 3).

However, the latencies in this table use different resolutions, hardware, and timing definitions. For chunk-based systems, latency is recorded as twice the chunk generation time. Streaming Code World Model renders a 17-frame chunk in 5.1 s, AgentGarten renders a 16-frame chunk in 439 ms, and StreamRender-H3’s 258 ms is the sum of three stage times reported on the project page (reference encoding 16.67 ms, 2-step rendering 217.96 ms, causal video decoding 23.8 ms). Magpie’s figure is the sum of engine preparation 0.83 s, transfer/encoding about 0.1 s, and rendering 0.62 s (Table 3 notes). It is therefore more accurate to read the direction—“what used to require several data-center GPUs has moved to a single consumer card”—than to compare absolute numbers 1:1. Release status was checked as of 2026-10-19, and the scope of released code and weights varies by system (Table 3).

Quality is shown not through quantitative metrics but through 40-second holdout rollouts. The distilled causal models for the castle, desert, and city games run at 2 steps per chunk; starting from the ground-truth first frame, they generate 961 frames autoregressively (40 seconds at 24 FPS). The resulting frames follow the proxy’s layout, camera, and object motion all the way through, while the model fills in materials, vegetation, lighting, smoke, and muzzle flashes that the proxy omitted (Figure 7, §6.1, §6.3).

Game customization through the coding agent is also demonstrated (Figure 8). A lone shooter becomes a team battle, with health and ammo control, a durability-limited shield, an automatic shotgun, a game-over condition at zero health, and simple sound effects. The driving game gains a checkpoint time limit, collision penalties, drifting, and even a pursuit mode that intercepts a target vehicle, closes to a set distance, and holds it. All of these rules are stored and evaluated by the engine; the video model only reads the engine output and translates it to the screen (§6.4).

Limitations and applicability

Future directions stated in the paper (§8). The near-term goals are to reduce inference cost and hardware requirements and to release a Steam technical preview. Further directions include improving visual fidelity, a refinement stage for high-resolution output, multiplayer rendering in which multiple players see consistent viewpoints, precise control of generated frames, and expansion to more genres and scenes.

Constraints from a reviewer’s perspective.

  • A separate model is trained for each game. As stated in “We train one model per game” (§4.2), the castle, desert, and city are different fine-tuned models. Generalization to an arbitrary new game has not been demonstrated.
  • The quality of 1–2 step distillation has not been quantitatively validated. §6 presents only qualitative results (Figure 7 rollouts, Figure 8 customization), and fidelity metrics for the distilled student versus the multi-step teacher (FID, PSNR, etc.) are not reported in the paper. The claim that it “preserves structure to the end” is based on visual inspection, not numerical evidence.
  • Dynamic captions are rule-based and depend on the engine’s object descriptions. Because no vision-language model is used (§3.2), latency is low, but description quality is tied to a prebuilt object description table. There is no guarantee that it describes unknown scenes or situations requiring more expressive language well.
  • Training data is limited to four synthetic UE5 captures (Table 1). Whether the model generalizes to photorealistic scenes or styles different from these four has not been verified.
  • The 112 ms latency corresponds to about 6.7 frames at 60 FPS. 60 FPS is the game execution performance maintained by the integrated system (with the renderer’s distillation setting at 2 steps per chunk), while 112 ms is a separate latency from key input to screen update. This latency may be a problem for fighting or rhythm games where timing feel matters, and the paper does not address these genres.

This architecture fits best with genres that have clear rules and visuals that can be represented by structural sketches. Shooters, driving, and flight are good targets because object state is easy for the engine to maintain and the proxy can convey layout and motion sufficiently. Conversely, games with implicit rules or off-screen state that is hard to maintain in code, and styles for which synthetic capture data is hard to obtain, remain unverified.

Tables from the paper

Tables converted mechanically from the arXiv e-print LaTeX source. The numbers are the paper’s own and did not pass through a model.

Table 1. UE5 paired training data. Each clip is a pair of pixel-aligned low-poly and high-fidelity videos at $1280\times720$. Held-out clips come from capture sessions (for air combat, whole multi-machine capture batches) that contribute no training clip.

Scene Game Train clips Hours FPS Held-out
Medieval castle Third-person shooter 17,848 290 24 3 sessions, 683 clips
Ancient Egypt desert Third-person shooter 40,296 643 24 3 sessions, 617 clips
Desert canyon air combat Flight combat 28,720 467 24 whole capture batches
CitySample megacity Driving 27,470 312 17 3 sessions
Total 114,334 1,712

Table 2. Inference speed and latency, applied cumulatively. Each row adds one optimization to all rows above it. FPS is the steady-state generation rate of the model; latency is the time from a key press to the first generated frame that reflects it, with the game running at 60 FPS. Speedup is the FPS ratio to the previous row. Setting: $480\times864$, chunk size of one latent frame (four frames), KV window of 21 latent frames, one NVIDIA RTX 5090.

Configuration FPS $\uparrow$ Latency (ms) $\downarrow$ Speedup
Causal Wan2.2 DiT, 4 steps, full Wan VAE 4.5 1110 –
+ tiny VAE (TAEHV) 6.5 867 1.4$\times$
+ RoPE kernel, cached text KV 15.4 551 2.4$\times$
+ 8-bit weights + CUDA Graph 24.2 466 1.6$\times$
+ 1-step distillation 51.2 376 2.1$\times$

Overall 19$\times$ faster 9.9$\times$ lower

Table 3. Latency, hardware, and openness of recent real-time interactive generation systems. Latency is the end-to-end latency, and resolution is the output resolution at which each system reports its timings. For the systems that generate in chunks, the latency is two chunk generation times. Code World Model (streaming) renders a 17-frame chunk in 5.1 s on one H200. For StreamRender-H3, the chunk time of 258 ms is the sum of the three warm-renderer stage times reported on its project page: 16.67 ms for reference encoding, 217.96 ms for the two-step render, and 23.8 ms for causal video decoding, the last measured at 720p on one GB200. AgentGarten renders a 16-frame chunk in 439 ms on one H100. For Magpie, the latency is the end-to-end time reported by its authors: 0.83 s for the engine to prepare a 20-frame chunk, about 0.1 s for transmission and encoding, and 0.62 s for rendering. Matrix-Game 4.0 latency is measured from a key press to the first frame that reflects it, with the game running at 60 FPS. Open release is checked against the GitHub and Hugging Face pages of each project on October 19, 2026.

item.title: Rethinking Sequence Compression with Test-time Regression
item.description:
Paper

Introduction

In models that handle long contexts, the compression operation that reduces multiple tokens to a single vector becomes a performance bottleneck. This paper reframes compression not as a choice of weighted averaging, but as the problem of finding the coefficients of a regression problem defined by the tokens. TTR-Compressor constructs a label-free ridge regression problem from the input tokens and uses its closed-form solution as the compressed representation.

Why existing compressors discard information

Sequence compression is an operation that transforms T d-dimensional token vectors into a single d-dimensional summary vector. In block-sparse attention, this vector becomes the retrieval key that selects the blocks a query reads, while in visual token merging, this vector itself becomes the visual token seen by the language model. In both cases, the compressor stores the tokens as a single vector, and subsequent layers read only that vector. Information discarded here cannot be recovered later.

Existing approaches fall into three categories. (1) Mean pooling assigns the same weight to every token. (2) Concatenating tokens and passing them through a learned linear projection uses fixed weights per position. (3) Attention-weighted pooling scores each token individually but evaluates each token independently of the others. What all three share is that their weights do not reflect relationships among tokens. They use only first-order statistics—how important each token is individually—and ignore second-order statistics, the correlations between tokens. Consequently, duplicate tokens reinforce one another, and rare features are diluted.

A small example illustrates this difference. The example below is for explanation and is not an actual measured result.

Illustrative example. Suppose four tokens are given, three of which carry essentially the same content A, and only one carries distinct information B. Set all target values to v=(1,1,1,1). Additive pooling (mean) assigns a weight of 1/4 to each token, yielding an influence of 3/4 for the A group and 1/4 for B, a ratio of 3:1. TTR groups token similarities into a Gram matrix and fits them jointly, so the three correlated A tokens are treated as duplicates; the group influence is still 3/4, but B becomes 1/2. The ratio becomes 3:2, weakening the dominance of the duplicate group and increasing the relative weight of the distinct token B. In general, according to Appendix B (Proposition 4, Corollary 1), the relative influence ratio between m fully overlapping tokens and a single distinct token is not m but m(λ+1)/(λ+m) < m, so duplicated evidence has diminishing returns. This number comes from the example in Figure 2(b) of the paper (normalized D=I, λ=1) and its general formula; it is not a measured value.

Category Additive pooling (mean, etc.) TTR (joint regression)
Input 4 tokens: A, A, A (duplicate), B (distinct) Same
Computed weights α 1/4 each for A, 1/4 for B 1/4 each for A, 1/2 for B
Group influence Kᵀα A 0.75, B 0.25 A 0.75, B 0.50
Output ratio 3 : 1 3 : 2
What remains Duplicate A dominates the summary B’s relative weight increases
What is rejected None: A continues to be added The residual left by A’s third token approaches zero, reducing its weight

What changes when tokens become a regression problem

Given tokens X=[x₁,…,x_T], TTR-Compressor defines a ridge regression problem on the tokens themselves and uses the fitted coefficients h* as the compressed representation (§3.1, Eq. 1). Ridge regression fits target values while penalizing the magnitude of coefficients. The key is to solve, for each input, “which coefficients best explain these tokens” and use those coefficients as the summary.

Specifically, it determines two things. One is each token’s key k_t = x_t / ‖x_t‖, retaining only the vector direction so that inner products between keys measure only directional similarity. The other is a scalar target v_t = aᵀx_t, which extracts a single number from each token using one shared learnable vector a (§3.2). This target requires no labels and is derived from the input.

The reason key normalization matters is clear. Since targets are generated linearly as v_t = aᵀx_t, without key normalization (k_t = x_t), the fixed vector a itself becomes the correct answer, and h* converges to a fixed vector independent of the input. In addition, outlier tokens with large norms dominate the Gram matrix, so the model sees magnitude instead of similarity. Normalization removes both problems at once. Indeed, removing key normalization drops the RULER average from 0.509 to 0.253 (§5.4, Table 5).

Solving the regression problem yields the following compressed representation.

$$h^* = (K^\top K + D)^{-1} K^\top v$$

Here K is the key matrix, v is the target vector, and D is the normalization matrix. The result is determined jointly by the statistics of keys and targets, Kᵀv, and by KᵀK, which captures the similarity structure among tokens. KᵀK is the Gram matrix in feature space, and because it groups tokens pointing in the same direction, it produces the property from the earlier example: “duplicates have reduced influence.”

Conventional ridge regression requires tuning the regularization strength λ as a hyperparameter, but tuning it during large-scale pretraining is expensive and cumbersome when model size changes. Instead of a scalar λ, TTR uses a learnable diagonal matrix D = diag(softplus(ρ)) (§3.2, Eq. 3). It learns a different regularization strength for each channel, penalizing less important feature directions more strongly and preserving directions important to the task. The learned diagonal outperforms the best fixed λ (λ=0.001, 0.502) with 0.509 (Table 6), and a learned scalar is also competitive at 0.497, showing that the task loss can find the regularization strength on its own.

Solving small blocks in dual form

Working directly in d dimensions requires solving a d×d linear system, but the number of tokens to compress, T, is typically much smaller than the channel dimension d (e.g., T∈{4, 9, 64} versus d≥1024). In this case, we can switch to the dual form and solve only a T×T system (§3.3, Eq. 7). The dual form is an equivalent transformation that turns a d×d system into a T×T system.

$$TTR(X) = D^{-1/2} \tilde{K}^\top \big(I_T + \tilde{K}\tilde{K}^\top\big)^{-1} v$$

The computation proceeds as follows. Rescale the keys by D to form K̃, factor the T×T Gram matrix I_T + K̃K̃ᵀ via Cholesky decomposition, solve for α, and then apply K̃ᵀα to obtain the compressed representation. Cholesky decomposition factors a symmetric positive-definite matrix into a product involving a lower-triangular matrix, solving the linear system with two substitutions. The complexity is O(T²d + T³), much lighter than the O(Td² + d³) of solving the d×d system directly when T≪d. The actual computation never forms an explicit inverse and uses only triangular solves (§5.3, Table 4; Appendix C).

This structure makes training bi-level (§3.4, Figure 2(a); §4.1). The outer loop learns parameters a and ρ that determine “which regression problem is useful” using the task loss, while the inner loop solves “how to fit” that regression problem in closed form for each input. The only learnable parameters are the target projection a (d values) and the regularization ρ (d values) per compressor, and because the inner solution is a differentiable closed form, gradients flow through it directly. At inference time, the learned parameters are fixed, and only h* is recomputed for each input. This differs from existing test-time training approaches that run gradient descent for every input or approximate it with a single delta-rule step (§3): because computation is independent per block, a single T×T dual solve yields the exact solution.

 flowchart LR
 X["Input tokens: x1,x2,x3≈A, x4=B"] --> K["Normalized keys k_i=x_i/||x_i||"]
 X --> V["Targets v_i=a^T x_i, e.g., (1,1,1,1)"]
 K --> G["Gram matrix G=K K^T: 1 among A, 0 with B"]
 V --> S["α=(G+I)^-1 v = (1/4,1/4,1/4,1/2)"]
 G --> S
 S --> H["h*=K^T α: A influence 0.75, B influence 0.50"]

The matrix coordinate (i,j) is the directional similarity between tokens i and j, where a value of 1 means the same direction and 0 means orthogonal. The fourth value of α grows to 1/2 because B captures the residual not explained by the A group.

Results: block-sparse attention

The first application is block-sparse attention based on HiLS-Attention (§5.1). The context is divided into 64-token blocks, and for each block’s compressed representation, up to 32 relevant blocks are selected and attended to together with a 512-token local window. The compressor stores each block as a retrieval key vector, and the query uses those keys to select blocks to read. Retrieval accuracy therefore directly reflects compression quality. We trained a 345M model on FineWeb with an 8K context for about 30B tokens and evaluated it on RULER’s needle-retrieval tasks (S-NIAH, MK-NIAH).

Before the evaluation, consider one question. With the same attention architecture, how much more hidden information can be found in contexts extending to 32K if only the compressor changes? The table below extracts only the average across compressors and representative long-context numbers (Table 1).

Compressor Avg (4K–32K) S-NIAH-1 @16K S-NIAH-1 @32K
Mean pooling 0.2971 0.470 0.270
Concat + projection 0.3919 0.792 0.582
Attention-weighted pooling 0.3920 0.876 0.740
TTR 0.5092 0.992 0.650
TTR (w/ Conv) 0.5144 0.994 0.988

The interpretation has two parts. First, the choice of compressor itself strongly affects retrieval quality. The gap between mean pooling and attention-weighted pooling reaches about 9.5 points on average. Second, TTR substantially outperforms all competing compressors on average. At 16K extrapolation beyond the 8K training length, the advantage extends to individual tasks, but under 32K extrapolation, standard TTR loses S-NIAH-1 (0.650) to attention-weighted pooling (0.740), and on the 32K four-task average, TTR’s 0.238 versus attention-weighted pooling’s 0.224 narrows the lead. The convolution variant largely mitigates this, recording 0.988 on 32K S-NIAH-1. The paper attributes this to convolution making the target v_t more informative and thereby improving compression quality; the convolution variant leads the strongest baseline by 12.24 points (§5.1).

One caveat is that the gains are confirmed on “finding” tasks, and whether they extend to general language quality is a separate question. In the commonsense reasoning benchmark in Table 2, evaluation contexts are short, so sparse attention is not activated; all compressors are similar in the 48-point range. This is discussed in the limitations section below.

Results: visual token merging and efficiency

The second application is visual token merging in multimodal models (§5.2). High-resolution images produce many visual tokens, making it expensive to feed them directly into the language backbone. The standard design concatenates adjacent 2×2 features and reduces them to one token through a two-layer MLP. Here, TTR fits one regression per spatial group (2×2 or 3×3) to compress 4 or 9 features into a single vector, and a two-layer MLP projects it to the language model dimension. We trained with Qwen3-VL’s ViT encoder and Qwen3-4B-Instruct using a two-stage procedure that trains the merger and backbone sequentially.

The comparison question before the table is this. With the same encoder and language model, how much less information is lost on tasks where fine-grained details such as documents and charts matter when the merger changes?

Merge ratio Merger Avg
2×2 MLP 54.93
2×2 TTR 55.92
2×2 TTR (w/ Conv) 56.03
3×3 MLP 52.27
3×3 TTR 54.30
3×3 TTR (w/ Conv) 54.85

TTR outperforms the MLP at both ratios, and the gain grows with the stronger 3×3 compression (for 3×3, the convolution variant is +2.58 on average versus the MLP). The difference is most pronounced on text-heavy benchmarks where fine details are easily lost during merging: at 3×3, the convolution variant records OCRBench +4.10 (55.90→60.00), InfoVQA +4.54 (35.16→39.70), and ChartQA +3.56 (63.60→67.16) versus the MLP (Table 3). The key point is that TTR (w/ Conv) with 3×3 merging averages 54.85, almost the same as the 2×2 MLP’s 54.93. In other words, it reduces the token count by 55.6% (N/4 → N/9, less than half in terms of token count) while maintaining performance at the level of the standard 2×2 MLP. The paper explains this with a second correlation-structure interpretation: when a merger mixes features with fixed weights, redundant features such as background patches dominate the token and erase details, whereas TTR fits correlated features jointly and reduces the influence of redundancy.

Efficiency must be examined at two levels. The operator itself costs O(T²d) for TTR, heavier than mean pooling O(Td, 0 parameters) but lighter than concat+projection (O(Td²), Td² parameters) or independent attention compressors (O(Td²), ~4d² parameters), and its 2d learnable parameters are relatively few (Table 4). The convolution variant adds kernel parameters, bringing the count to 7d for language and 11d for vision (Appendix C). At the system level, wall-clock time in Figure 3 shows that in block-sparse attention training (8×H100), TTR takes 22.50 hours, slower than mean pooling’s 19.33 hours but similar to other learned compressors (23.12 and 21.57 hours), while in visual merging (2×8×H100) it is slightly slower than the MLP at 2×2 but actually faster at 3×3. Inference latency is similar across compressors and substantially lower than full attention after 16K (Appendix F, Figure 4). In other words, most of TTR’s cost falls on training time, and at inference it is effectively the same as other compressors.

Limitations and when to apply

We separate limitations directly exposed by the authors’ data from those the reviewer must infer.

Constraints directly confirmed in the authors’ experiments. First, training cost is not free. Training is slower than the lightest mean pooling, and at 2×2 visual merging it is even slightly slower than the MLP (Figure 3). Second, under 32K extrapolation, more than four times the training length, standard TTR drops sharply on some subtasks (S-NIAH-1 32K = 0.650). The convolution variant largely mitigates this (0.988), but it adds parameters and convolution operations. Third, the design is sensitive to choices, to the point that removing key normalization collapses performance (0.509→0.253; Table 5).

Unverified points from the reviewer’s perspective. First, it has not been confirmed that improved retrieval accuracy translates into better general language quality. In the commonsense reasoning benchmark in Table 2, contexts are short, so sparse attention is not activated and the compressor does not affect performance; all compressors are similar in the 48-point range (though Concat & Projection has far more parameters and may have benefited in pretraining itself). In other words, the gains are currently limited to tasks of a “finding/retrieval” nature. Second, the validation scale is small. The advantage was shown at 345M, and scaling to a 1B model with 100B tokens maintains the lead at an average of 0.7996 versus 0.735, with the gap widening as context grows (Appendix E.1, Table 7). However, as HiLS-Attention notes, large models can compensate for retrieval errors with greater information bandwidth, leaving room for compressor differences to shrink. Third, the applications are limited to block-sparse attention and visual merging, so generalization to other compression points is unverified, and TTR is efficient only when T≪d; as blocks grow, the O(T²d + T³) cost increases rapidly.

Given these characteristics, TTR-Compressor is well suited to points where small blocks (tens of tokens or fewer) are reduced to vectors with large channel dimensions. Examples include retrieval-key summaries for block-sparse attention and visual token merging that preserves fine details such as those in documents and charts. Conversely, the gains are not yet proven for retrieval in large models where attention-weighted pooling is already sufficient, compression with large block sizes, or situations where inference latency itself must be reduced.

item.title: Large Flow Language Models
item.description:
Paper

The sequential bottleneck of sampling one token at a time

Large language models can compute an entire sentence in parallel during training, but when generating text they must know the preceding token before they can choose the next one. No matter how fast the GPU is, this order cannot be skipped in one pass, so generation latency grows. This post covers Lafa (Large flow language model), which attacks this bottleneck with block-level flow.

Lafa revives an already-trained autoregressive model. A single computation produces candidate tokens for an entire block, and autoregressive prediction verifies and commits them from the front. As a result, it achieves up to 2.54× the throughput of the existing autoregressive baseline at the same quality level. The exact conditions and numbers are revisited below.

Why flow, and why split into blocks

The existing parallel generation method, discrete diffusion, erases tokens with [MASK] and then restores them. Sampling multiple positions independently in one step severs the relationships between positions, which can degrade quality.

Flow differs: it does not erase tokens. It mixes Gaussian noise into token embedding vectors, then integrates the continuous path from noise back to clean embeddings to produce tokens. Because it moves in continuous space, the acceleration and control techniques developed for image and video generation carry over directly. However, existing flow language models were demonstrated only on small-scale, simple tasks; one scaling attempt reported training inefficiency; and how to scale to billions of parameters is not yet established (§1, §2).

Lafa splits flow into blocks. Instead of generating the whole sentence at once, it conditions on the previously committed text (the prefix) and generates token blocks of size $B$ one at a time, chaining blocks causally. The sentence probability is factorized as a product over blocks.

$$p(y\mid c)=\prod_{r} p\bigl(y^{rB+1:(r+1)B}\mid c,\,y^{\le rB}\bigr)$$

Splitting into blocks yields two benefits. First, the prefix key-value (KV) cache—the attention intermediates from previous token computations—can be reused for each block. Second, parallel generation can be confined to within a block (§2.1). Handling tokens on embeddings reduces the dimensionality of a single token from the vocabulary size $|V|$ to the embedding dimension $d$, which also makes training and scaling easier.

Asynchronous flow within a block

If every position in a block escaped noise at the same rate, the left-to-right directionality of text being read would disappear. Lafa gives each position $i$ its own progress clock $\tau^i(t)$. The clocks of earlier positions run faster, so earlier tokens are revealed first. The path from noise $x_0$ to the clean embedding $x_1$ is as follows.

$$I_t^i=(1-\tau^i(t))\,x_0^i+\tau^i(t)\,x_1^i$$

$\tau$ is not fixed. It is learned from data so that training passes slowly through regions with high loss. This concentrates training samples and inference steps around difficult noise levels. The learned schedule generally advances earlier positions first (in Fig. learned_time, the horizontal axis is reference time $t\in[0,1]$, the vertical axis is the per-position $\tau^i(t)$, and the curves correspond to block positions 1, 4, 7, …, 16); this left→right bias is not manually imposed but emerges from training (§2.1).

Illustrative example. Suppose the three embeddings of the prefix “the weather today is” are already committed, and with block size $B=3$ we must produce “sunny/cloudy/.”

Step Input Retained state Changing state Output / discarded values
Start 3 prefix embeddings, 3 noise vectors prefix KV cache — —
Step $k$ reference time $t_k$, current state $\hat x_{t_k}$ prefix KV cache earlier positions’ $\tau$ grow first and $\hat x$ approaches the embeddings intermediate noise $\hat x_{t_k}$
End after $K$ Euler steps prefix KV cache tokens are committed from the final $\hat x$ “sunny/cloudy/.”

The KV of the committed tokens is appended and we move to the next block. This example is for intuition only and is unrelated to the measurements below.

Designing flow to be learned from an autoregressive model

The key is not to train a flow model from scratch but to retrofit an already-trained autoregressive model into a block denoiser. The denoiser is a function that, given a noisy block, predicts the clean-token probability at each position. The problem is that this retrofit must not damage autoregressive prediction or the prefix cache. The paper solves this with three designs (§2.2).

First, tokenwise time conditioning. The prefix receives time 1 (no noise), and each position in the block receives its own time $\tau^i(t)$. This value is injected via adaptive layer normalization (adaLN)—a mechanism that re-normalizes a layer’s output based on its input. Initializing adaLN as the identity function means time conditioning initially leaves the existing computation untouched and is learned gradually.

Second, block bidirectional attention. Tokens within a block can see each other, so less-refined later tokens can help earlier ones. The prefix is still viewed only causally, as before. As a result, the prefix’s keys and values do not depend on block state and can be reused across denoising steps.

Third, fixed embedding norm. If embeddings are updated freely, their L2 norm grows relative to the noise scale, creating a shortcut that makes denoising easier. The pretrained norm is fixed and only the direction is learned.

The training loss sums three terms: autoregressive cross-entropy on the prefix, denoising cross-entropy on block tokens, and squared error between predicted and actual embeddings (Equation 6). Keeping the autoregressive loss also improves flow accuracy. Thanks to this joint training, autoregressive ability is preserved—or even improved—while learning flow. This is consistent with the existing observation that multi-token prediction improves next-token prediction (§2.2, §3.2).

The figure above (original Figure training) shows the state transitions of parallel training. The upper clean sequence produces autoregressive predictions with causal attention, while the lower copy is split into blocks of size 3, where each block sees only the preceding clean tokens and produces denoising predictions bidirectionally within the block. A single forward pass yields both the autoregressive loss and the denoising losses of all blocks, without recomputing overlapping prefixes.

Design effects confirmed by ablation

At 0.5B, block 4, and 32 Euler steps, each design was reverted one at a time and average accuracy was compared (Table design-ablations).

Changed item Comparison condition Average accuracy
Attention Fully causal 32.7%
Block bidirectional 38.0%
Time schedule Synchronous (all positions share the same $t$) 36.2%
Asynchronous tokenwise 38.0%
Embedding Fully frozen 34.4%
Unrestricted updates 36.9%
Fixed norm 38.0%
Loss Denoising cross-entropy only 33.6%
Squared error only 29.7%
Both terms 35.8%
Both terms + autoregressive 38.0%

The original design wins on all four axes: attention, time, embedding, and loss. In particular, adding the autoregressive loss actually raises flow accuracy, so AR preservation and flow generation do not hurt each other.

Reducing the number of steps with flow map distillation

Flow decoding is expensive because it must call the denoiser many times per block. To reduce this, Lafa uses flow map distillation. A student model learns a function $\hat X_{s,t}$ that moves the state directly from time $s$ to $t$, replacing several Euler steps with a single jump. Predictions on the diagonal ($s=t$) are matched to the teacher, while off-diagonal predictions ($s\lt t$) are matched to the composition of two short jumps in a semigroup fashion. The student maintains the prefix cache and can generate in as few as 1 step ($\hat X_{0,1}$) (§2.2).

Draft and verify at once: self-speculative decoding

Reaching AR-level quality with flow decoding requires many steps. Lafa discards the expensive multi-step process and by default draws a block draft with 1-step flow, then verifies it with the autoregressive predictor (§2.3).

The draft comes from a single denoiser evaluation starting from noise. Each position of the draft is compared against the autoregressive prediction from the front, and only the longest matching prefix is committed; the rest is discarded. If even the first token differs, it is replaced with the autoregressive token. The final output is exactly the same as the model’s greedy autoregressive output. Flow is used only to increase speed, and the quality bar equals greedy autoregression.

A naive implementation needs a separate verification forward and a next-draft forward, which costs extra. The paper eliminates this with fused decoding: verification of the previous draft and drafting of the next block are mixed into a single forward pass.

The figure above (original Figure fused_decoding) shows how one stage proceeds at block size 3. The horizontal direction is sequence position, and the vertical blocks are the input fragments fed into each forward.

Stage Input Retained Changed / rejected Output
End of previous stage prefix KV, draft $\hat y$ prefix KV — —
Fused forward clean draft $\hat y$ + $B$ candidate noise blocks prefix KV each candidate assumes “$j$ preceding items accepted” verification logits, $B$ candidate drafts
Verification verification logits vs autoregressive prediction accepted prefix KV drafts and candidates after the mismatch are discarded accepted length $a$, next draft
Next stage extended prefix updated KV cache — repeat

The clean draft is appended like a prefix to produce verification logits via causal attention, and at the same time candidate noise blocks corresponding to “the case where $j$ preceding draft items are accepted” are appended and processed together. From the verification result, the candidate block with the actually accepted length is chosen as the next draft, eliminating a separate re-drafting forward.

Because this method performs both drafting and verification with a single trained model, it is called self-speculative. No separate small draft model or additional parameters are needed. Alternatively, confidence decoding—accepting only prefixes whose token probability exceeds a threshold instead of using autoregressive verification—is possible, but lowering the threshold trades accuracy for speed, so the paper keeps self-speculative as the default (§3.3, Appendix confidence_results).

Results: maintaining quality while increasing speed

The models use Qwen2.5 0.5B·7B Instruct and Qwen3 8B Base as initialization and are trained for only 5–15 epochs (9–27B tokens) on Dolci-Instruct-SFT data. This is at least 18× fewer than the up to 500B tokens reported by comparable-scale diffusion models (Dream, LLaDA, Efficient-DLM) (§3, Table training-hyperparameters). The benchmarks are six covering instruction following, reasoning, and coding: IFEval, BBH, MMLU-Pro, GPQA, GSM8K, and HumanEval.

Learning flow does not hurt autoregression

Comparing average single-token decoding accuracy across the six benchmarks (Table ntp_main), Lafa beats the AR SFT built with the same initialization, data, and training budget at every scale. At 8B it approaches Efficient-DLM’s 63.5% while using at least 18× fewer training tokens. The process of learning flow actually improved autoregressive prediction (Table 1, §3.2).

Scale AR SFT Lafa Difference
0.5B 28.7% 31.6% +2.9%p
7B 58.4% 60.9% +2.5%p
8B 56.8% 63.1% +6.3%p

Parallelism: how far does accuracy hold as TPF rises

TPF (tokens per forward) is the number of tokens committed per forward pass. For AR it is 1 by definition. Since self-speculative output equals greedy autoregression, TPF comparisons are parallelism comparisons at the same AR quality.

In the figure above (original Figure selfspec_frontier), the horizontal axis is TPF and the vertical axis is average accuracy over the six benchmarks. At 7B, block 4 reaches TPF 2.6 and 60.9% accuracy, beating DeepSeek-MTP on both accuracy and TPF, while block 16 reaches 58.0% at TPF 4.9, close to AR SFT’s 58.4% while nearly doubling parallelism. Across all scales, AR-level accuracy is maintained in the roughly 2.5–5 TPF range (Table selfspec_lafa_sixbench).

Wall-clock time: throughput measured in TPS

TPF shows only parallelism, not actual time. Because the cost of a forward pass differs by method, tokens per second (TPS) was measured on a single H100 GPU at batch 1.

In the figure above (original Figure throughput), the horizontal axis is TPS and the vertical axis is average accuracy over IFEval, GSM8K, and HumanEval. Lafa 7B with block 16 reaches 100.2 TPS, 2.54× the throughput of AR SFT’s 39.5 TPS at similar average accuracy (74.5% vs 73.9%). With block 4 it is about 2× faster at 79.9 TPS while achieving higher average accuracy (76.5%). DeepSeek-MTP (53.6 TPS) and MARS (48–49 TPS) reach at most 1.4× even when their accuracy equals or exceeds AR’s. Diffusion-based methods (Fast-dLLM v2, Dream, Efficient-DLM) can achieve higher TPS depending on configuration, but their average accuracy is below AR SFT, and the faster the configuration, the larger the accuracy loss (Table throughput_full, §3.3).

What “maintaining quality” means

Because self-speculative output equals greedy autoregression, the 2.54× is a speedup obtained while preserving the same AR quality. Flow decoding itself requires multiple steps. At 7B and block 4, the 32-step average is 75.2%, already above AR SFT (73.9%), and at 64 steps it reaches 75.9% (Table flow_full, §3.1). Turning multi-step flow into a 1-step draft plus verification is the source of the practical speedup. Flow map distillation improves accuracy in the 1–2 step regime, and at 7B the 2-step student approaches the 4-step teacher.

Limitations and when to apply it

The limitations the paper itself notes are mainly related to flow map distillation. The distilled 1- and 2-step models improve accuracy while reducing the number of steps, but a quality gap remains relative to flow decoding with more steps. Fully incorporating self-conditioning and prefix guidance into distillation is left as future work (§3.1, §4). Confidence decoding loses accuracy when the threshold is lowered, so it could not be used as the default (Appendix confidence_results).

There are also points a reviewer should note. First, the 2.54× was measured at 7B, block 16, a single H100, and batch 1; there is no guarantee the same factor holds for larger models, larger batches, or long contexts. Second, evaluation is limited to instruction, math, and coding benchmarks, so generalization to other domains is not established in the paper. Third, 8B starts from Base instead of Instruct (the paper reports that additional training of the Instruct counterpart degraded performance). This is why IFEval numbers at the 8B scale are generally low (AR SFT is also 38.1%).

Given these conditions, Lafa is suited to serving environments that want higher throughput while preserving the autoregressive model’s greedy output exactly. If you already have a trained model and can train on a small number of additional tokens, you can obtain the benefits of speculative decoding without a separate draft model. Conversely, if you want to change the output distribution itself, or if you have enough latency headroom to run multi-step flow decoding in real time, the method’s strengths are less prominent.
