item.title: Cache Engineering for Agents
item.description:
Paper

The Cost and Accuracy Dilemma of Long Agent Trajectories

LLM agents accumulate long trajectories by repeating reasoning and tool calls for hundreds of rounds. To make inference fast, the already-computed key-value (KV) cache must stay on the GPU and be read again for each next token; as the trajectory grows, storage and read costs increase. The paper measures KV cache reads at 82.4% of total API cost (§1, Figure 13), and points out that accuracy degrades once the number of KVs or the positional span handled by attention exceeds what the model can handle (§1).

The dilemma of context engineering

The existing approach is context engineering, which shrinks the prompt itself by trimming or summarizing text. The problem is that editing earlier text invalidates all KV state appended after it. The invalidated span must be recomputed through re-prefill (running the already-computed prefix through the forward pass again), and the earlier the edit, the longer the tail that must be recomputed. As a result, real harnesses delay reduction until the context hits a threshold, then summarize or delete most of it at once and keep only the most recent rounds (§1, §2). Re-prefill becomes shorter, but useful information from intermediate rounds may be lost.

The paper quantified this dilemma directly. It ran the first 100 BCP (BrowseComp-Plus) tasks with GPT-OSS-120B (four attempts per task, up to 100 rounds) and obtained the following results (§3.2, Figure 3).

Method What it retains Result vs. cost
Full context KV for all tokens Baseline
Trim Only the last 12 tool responses Cost is 1.85× the baseline
Summarize (48k threshold) Replace everything below the threshold with a summary paragraph Cost down about 7%, accuracy down 5%p

A small example: the same 100 rounds, different cache handling

This is an illustrative example (not a measured result). Suppose an agent starts from the user message “Search ICLR” and repeats reasoning → tool call → tool response for 100 rounds. At every decode step, the KV of the new token is appended through append, increasing the active cache.

Step Context engineering Cache engineering
Input 100-round text trajectory (prompt + reasoning + tool responses) Same
Retained state Rounds 1–80 compressed into a single summary paragraph, rounds 81–100 retained Text left untouched; reasoning KV and the KV of the last 12 tool responses retained in the active cache
Changes / omissions Use the summary paragraph as the prefix and recompute the KV for rounds 81–100 (re-prefill) Exclude only the KV of old tool responses from attention (drop)
Output Shorter context after the summary, with possible loss of intermediate information The active cache read at each decode step is shorter, but the remaining KV is used as-is without recomputation

Direct cache deletion is possible because the influence of the discarded history may already be reflected in the computation of the remaining KV (§3.2, Figure 1). The overlapping colored blocks in Figure 1 convey the same idea. The remaining KV was computed while seeing the deleted history and therefore indirectly encodes that information, so the later parts do not need to be recomputed.

What to retain, and how to align positions

What to delete was decided through attention analysis. Old tokens receive less attention than recent tokens, and at similar relative positions, tool responses receive less attention than assistant messages (§3.2, Figure 2). In a layer-wise analysis of 10 BCP trajectories, old tool responses also received less attention than old reasoning in most cases (Appendix A.4.3, Figure 15). The default policy is therefore tool-response rolling drop. Reasoning KV and the KV of the last 12 tool responses are retained, and only the KV of old tool responses is deleted.

Position encoding must be managed separately. Rotary position embedding (RoPE) encodes the relative distance of tokens through cosine and sine rotations. By default, the position index keeps increasing along the logical trajectory. drop does not change the position index, so no matter how much the cache is reduced, the index of the next token keeps rising and eventually hits the model limit. The paper decouples the position index from the logical index and the cache size, remaps the remaining keys to 0…r−1 in logical order, and uses repos to reset the position of the next append to r. Under RoPE, moving a cached key K from position p to q multiplies only the rotation matrix and leaves the value unchanged (§3.3):

$$ K \leftarrow R(q)\,R(p)^{-1}\,K $$

Because this transformation does not recompute hidden states, positions can be changed without re-prefill.

Three cache operations

Cache engineering is defined by three operations (§3.3). It does not touch the logical token sequence; it changes only the cache visible to attention.

  • append is the same as ordinary inference. It appends a new token to the active cache: $C \leftarrow [C; C_{t+1}]$.
  • drop(P) excludes the items in set P from subsequent attention: $C \leftarrow C \setminus \{C_i : i \in P\}$. The values, positional encodings, and logical tokens of the remaining items are unchanged, and later states do not need to be recomputed.
  • repos remaps the positional encodings of the remaining keys in logical order and resets the index that the next append will use.

A sequence of operations written one after another is called a cache operation sequence (§3.4). For the same model, this sequence starts from an empty cache and determines the current cache state.

History dependence: the same tokens can yield different states depending on order

In a conventional KV cache, the same token prefix produced the same cache, and serving systems relied on that reuse. In cache engineering, even if the same tokens remain, a different operation order produces a different KV state (§3.4). Consider the three trajectories in Figure 5.

Trajectory Operation order Retained items Items attended to when computing C KV of the retained C
① append(A) → append(B) → append(C) → drop(A) B, C A, B C was computed having seen A and B
② append(A) → append(B) → drop(A) → append(C) B, C B only (A was already dropped) C was computed without seeing A
③ append(B) → append(C) B, C B only (no A) Computed on a B state that also differs from ②

All three trajectories retain B and C, yet the KV of C differs in all three. The state of B is conditioned on A in ① and ②, but not in ③. Correct reuse and restoration require recording both the token history and the cache operation history (Figure 5).

Serving system AKV: state on the server, stateless interface

To hide history dependence, AKV follows a stateless interface with stateful serving (§4). The agent sends messages as before (each entry in messages is an implicit append) and optionally adds drop and reposition to the cache field. It does not need to track which KV remains on the server. drop specifies after which message the cache of which message should be deleted, and reposition specifies after which message positions should be remapped (operate-after syntax, Figure 6). At the same boundary, drop is applied before repos. The server handles reuse, eviction, and restoration of the physical cache.

For example, in the request below, the server drops the cache of message 0 (user) when message 1 (assistant) ends, then drops the cache of message 1 when message 2 (tool) ends and repos the remaining keys at the same point.

JSON 
{ "model": "gpt-oss-120b",
 "messages": [
 {"role": "user", "content": "Search ICLR"},
 {"role": "assistant", "content": "Searching"},
 {"role": "tool", "content": "ICLR is..."}
 ],
 "cache": {
 "drop": {"1": [0], "2": [1]},
 "reposition": [2]
 }
}
{ "model": "gpt-oss-120b",
 "messages": [
 {"role": "user", "content": "Search ICLR"},
 {"role": "assistant", "content": "Searching"},
 {"role": "tool", "content": "ICLR is..."}
 ],
 "cache": {
 "drop": {"1": [0], "2": [1]},
 "reposition": [2]
 }
}

Serving flow that exposes state changes

Once a request arrives, the server performs the following steps.

 flowchart TD
 A["Agent request<br/>messages + cache operations (drop/repos)"] --> B["Parse the token history and operation history of the request"]
 B --> C["Match the path in the extended radix tree<br/>Distinguish cache versions by drop node Δ and repos node"]
 C --> D{"Does the required KV remain in server memory<br/>with token and operation history exactly matching?"}
 D -- "Yes" --> E["Copy and reuse the remaining KV as-is<br/>No re-prefill"]
 D -- "No (already evicted)" --> F["Restore state in a single prefill<br/>with segment-batch attention"]
 C --> G["Drop-aware eviction<br/>Free only KV not used by any request from physical memory"]
 E --> H["Decode: read only the active cache and generate the next token"]
 F --> H

The serving engine must preserve three properties of existing systems. (1) Reuse only when the state exactly matches, (2) evict unused cache without breaking isolation between requests, and (3) restore evicted state with a single prefill (§4.2). It provides three mechanisms for this.

Extended radix tree with drop nodes. A conventional radix tree shares cache when token prefixes are the same. AKV inserts a drop node Δ at the point where drop is invoked and records which items’ caches were deleted. In the table above, ① and ② share the A–B prefix but differ in when A was dropped, so the C states diverge, while ③ follows a separate branch. Prefix sharing is preserved while later states are distinguished (Figure 5c). repos rotates keys to create versions with different positions and splits them into a new branch. If the position index is the same, the cache is reused as-is; if it differs, it is converted through key rotation (§4.2, A.1.2, Figure 8).

Drop-aware eviction. A cache dropped by one request may still be needed by another. AKV frees physical storage only when an in-flight computation or restoration no longer uses that cache, and it reclaims unused cache even before the request completes. In eviction priority, dropped cache comes before the cache of completed requests, because the latter is likely to be reused in the next round. Storage is emptied but the tree nodes remain as empty slots so that descendant caches can be accessed. Eviction is also independent per position version (§4.2, A.1.2).

Single-prefill restoration with segment-batch attention. Restoring an evicted state requires reproducing the attention visibility created by drop and repos. At each layer, AKV slices the queries at the points where drop and repos occurred and splits them into multiple segments. Each segment performs standard causal attention over its own tokens and the active cache of preceding segments. Deleted cache is invisible to later segments, but remains visible to the earlier segment that originally used it. Only attention is segmented; FFN processes the entire sequence in one batch, avoiding the memory traffic of rereading FFN weights for each segment (§4.2, A.1.1, Figure 10). Restoration happens in a single prefill without multiple forward passes, and when repos is involved, temporary KV versions are created per segment through key rotation and value copying (A.1.1).

Results: score, cost, and serving throughput

The experiments used three models (MiniMax-M2.7, GPT-OSS-120B, and MiroThinker-1.7-Mini) and four long-horizon agent benchmarks (BCP, GAIA-Text, SWE-Verified, and xbench-DS) (§5.1). The baselines were Standard, which uses a high threshold (96k per model, with MiroThinker summarizing at 192k), and Text Engineering, which lowers the threshold to 48k. AKV uses tool-response rolling drop (retaining the last 12 tool responses), with the repos threshold set equal to each model’s Standard summarization threshold.

Average score (pass rate, %) and average cost (cents) — reconstruction of the Average column in Table 1

Model Metric Standard Text Eng. AKV
GPT-OSS-120B Score / cost 51.0 / 11.2 48.3 / 10.2 53.1 / 7.3
MiniMax-M2.7 Score / cost 52.4 / 5.0 52.8 / 5.7 53.7 / 4.4
MiroThinker-1.7-Mini Score / cost 44.1 / 20.4 37.1 / 18.1 45.8 / 14.8

Across all three models, AKV delivers the highest average score and the lowest cost. Average scores are 1.7 points higher than Standard (1.3–2.1 points per model) and 0.9–8.7 points higher than Text Engineering, while cost is 27.7% lower than Standard and 21.9% lower than Text Engineering (§5.2, Table 1).

The score differences come from the range beyond the summarization threshold. On the first 100 BCP tasks, all three methods scored similarly at 88% for contexts at or below 48k, but Text Engineering fell to 54% in the 48–96k range (AKV 70%), and Standard fell to 24% at or above 96k (AKV 37%) (Figure 7). The abrupt context reduction at the threshold is consistent with information loss, whereas rolling drop gradually deletes old tool-response KV (§5.2; Figure 14, Appendix A.4.2).

Cost savings come from two places (BCP, GPT-OSS-120B). Dropping reduces the cache history that later requests read, cutting cache read cost by about 17% versus Standard, and eliminating the re-prefill caused when summarization rewrites text, cutting cache-miss input cost by about 48% versus Text Engineering (Figure 13, Appendix A.4.2).

Serving latency and throughput

The serving experiments ran GPT-OSS-120B on eight A800-80GB GPUs (four prefill and four decode, TP4 each, BF16) and replayed the 80 SWE-Verified tasks with the longest contexts (Table 5, A.1.3; A.1.4).

At the kernel level, at the same batch size, AKV reduces full-attention time by 59.8% and overall decode step time by 16.0% (Figure 12, Appendix A.4.1). Dropping reduces the KV read and attention computation at every decode step.

At the system level, the comparison uses each method’s peak-throughput setting. Standard reaches peak throughput at C=12 and AKV at C=14 (Table 2).

Metric (peak-throughput setting) Standard (C=12) AKV (C=14) Speedup
Average request latency (s) 12.39 9.09 1.36×
P95 request latency (s) 43.16 28.49 1.51×
Input throughput (tok/s) 33,832 51,837 1.53×
Output throughput (tok/s) 313 369 1.18×

The gains grow under high load with concurrency (C) of 14 or higher. As KV pressure increases, Standard performs more re-prefill and can decode fewer requests concurrently, whereas AKV avoids that pressure with a shorter active context (§5.3). The measurement protocol warrants caution (A.1.4). At high concurrency, Standard degrades severely under KV pressure, so it was measured over a fixed one-hour window (some requests were incomplete when the window ended), while AKV’s C=14 and C=16 runs were truncated to the window ending when the first 30 tasks completed.

Refining the cache policy automatically or handing it to the agent

RSI (recursive self-improvement) lets the model improve the cache policy instead of having humans fix it. With MiniMax-M2.7, the policy was refined on 20 BCP tasks and evaluated on 100 held-out tasks; it maintained Standard’s accuracy while reducing cost per task by 15.6–17.8% (§5.4, Figure 4). According to the abstract and §1, the RSI policy reduced cost by a further 7.1% compared with a human-expert design.

Cache-as-Tool exposes cache management to the agent as a tool. The agent decides when to reduce the cache and what to retain. On a 100-task BCP subset, both models recorded their highest pass rates (GPT-OSS-120B 61.0%, MiniMax-M2.7 64.0%). Cost fell from 13.4 to 12.1 cents for GPT-OSS-120B, while MiniMax-M2.7 ran more rounds and rose from 5.4 to 5.9 cents (Table 4).

Limitations and when to apply it

The paper states three limitations of its own (§6). The authors should explore cache engineering strategies more broadly, train agents directly under this approach, and extend serving support to linear attention models.

From a reviewer’s perspective, adoption should be considered carefully under the following conditions.

  • RoPE and KV cache assumptions. drop and repos assume standard attention plus a KV cache. RoPE rotation is a finite-precision operation and may not be bitwise identical to recomputation; the authors state that the correctness argument does not require bitwise equality (A.1.2). Linear attention variants are not yet supported.
  • Dependence on policy quality. Performance depends heavily on the policy for what to delete. In the ablation (Table 3, first 100 tasks per task type), using tool drop without repos reached 55.0% on BCP, failing to surpass Standard (56.0%), while adding repos reached 62.0% (by enabling exploration beyond the position limit, §5.4). In contrast, strategies that delete reasoning cache, whether alone or combined, score lower than tool drop alone on both benchmarks (BCP 56.5, SWE 34.5–36.5 vs. 41.0). On the smaller GPT-OSS-20B, the best average pass rate was 45.2%, only 1.2%p above Standard (44.0%), which the authors attribute to the smaller model’s inability to use retained information effectively (Table 7, A.4.4). Drop itself does not raise the score; a good drop policy does.
  • Evaluation scope. The serving experiments were conducted on a single node (8×A800) and a single model family (GPT-OSS) using replay. Replay does not re-execute tools and uses recorded responses as-is; each method replays trajectories collected under its own policy, so turn counts and output budgets may differ across methods (A.1.4). Behavior under multi-node deployment or workloads mixing live tool re-execution has not been validated. The benchmarks are also limited to four long-horizon agents.
  • Increased complexity. Exact reuse requires tracking both token history and operation history, making tree matching and state management more complex than conventional prefix caching. The stateless interface hides this, but it is difficult to apply directly to existing serving stacks that have not been extended to track operation history.

In summary, AKV’s cache engineering is best suited to agent serving where long tool-call trajectories run for hundreds of rounds and KV cache read and re-prefill costs become a problem. Benefits may be limited in short-session workloads, in settings that use linear attention, or in environments where cache policies are difficult to design carefully.

Tables from the paper

item.title: Speculative Sampling in Interactive Video Generation
item.description:
Paper

Staying Instantly Responsive While Keeping Large Chunks: Speculative Sampling for Interactive Video Generation

When a viewer changes a camera move or an action command, the video being played must change with it right away. But no matter how fast a video generation model is, a new condition only reaches the screen at chunk granularity, and the user waits until that boundary. This paper removes the wait floor imposed by boundaries through speculative sampling that generates at large size while committing the output in small pieces.

1. Why Fast Generation Alone Is Not Enough

1.1 What This System Actually Does

Interactive video serving runs two processes at once. The player consumes an already-computed buffer to put frames on screen, while the generator pre-computes the next segment to fill the buffer. In between, new conditions (camera instructions, action commands, etc.) arrive online.

The model this paper deals with computes in units of latent frames. A latent frame is a representation produced by compressing pixel frames with a video autoencoder (VAE), and a diffusion transformer (DiT) samples these latent frames across multiple denoising steps. The number of latent frames a single DiT call creates together is called the chunk size K; latents within a chunk are modeled jointly through temporal bidirectional attention, and chunks are stitched together autoregressively.

If one latent frame stands in for $r$ pixel frames and the video’s temporal frame rate is $f$, then one latent frame covers $\delta = r/f$ seconds, and one chunk covers $T = K\delta = Kr/f$ seconds. This $T$ is precisely “how long a single batch’s refresh cycle is.”

1.2 Splitting the Reaction Latency into Three Segments

Suppose a condition arrives at $t_{arrival}$, generation starts at $t_{start}$, the first output becomes ready at $t_{ready}$, and it appears on screen at $t_{playback}$. Then

$$ L = R + C + Q $$

where each term points to a different bottleneck. $R$ is the wait before generation begins, $C$ is the computation producing the first output, including DiT sampling and any required VAE decoding, and $Q$ is the wait until the ready output enters the playback window. (§3.1, Eq. (1))

The reason for this decomposition is that the remedy differs per stage. $C$ is what acceleration techniques such as reduced sampling steps or parallelization target, $R$ is what scheduling and resource allocation target, and $Q$ is what the playback commit period targets. “The model is fast” is a statement about $C$ only, not about the total $L$ that a viewer feels.

(Figure 2 in the paper) It draws the segment where, under a periodic reference schedule, one highlighted refresh waits $R$, then generates for $C$, then waits another $Q$ before being displayed. Each chunk is prepared against the next playback window, and the first window $V_0$ is pre-buffered. Since generation, even once finished, must wait until the playback boundary, response latency is not determined by generation time alone.

1.3 The Boundary Wait Remains Regardless of Generation Speed

Suppose that, as in existing schemes, the output reflecting a new condition can be put on screen only at fixed chunk playback boundaries. When generation time $C$ is fixed and arrival phases are uniform, the sum of the two waiting segments caused by alignment satisfies $E[R+Q] \ge T/2$, and therefore $E[L] \ge C + T/2$. (§3.4, Eq. (4); Appendix A.1 Proposition 1)

This lower bound needs to be read precisely. The bound concerns the average combined wait, not a per-request or per-component bound. $E[R+Q] \ge T/2$ is a lower bound on the sum, not on $E[R]$ and $E[Q]$ individually. Whether the waiting piles up before generation ($R$) or after generation ($Q$), the sum is the same. Also, the lower bound does not disappear even when generation time is zero.

1.4 A Small Example: Checking with Numbers

Let’s put the numbers in one by one. At 24 frames per second ($f=24$), if one latent frame represents 4 pixel frames ($r=4$), one latent frame covers $\delta = r/f = 4/24 \approx 0.17$ seconds. Taking the chunk as $K=4$ gives $T = K\delta \approx 0.67$ seconds, and alignment waits average $T/2 \approx 0.33$ seconds each. In other words, even if the DiT finishes in 0 seconds, the viewer waits 0.33 seconds on average.

(This is an illustrative assumption, not a measured figure from the paper. It is an arithmetic example blindly substituting into $T = Kr/f$, independent of the actual model’s $r$ and $f$.)

1.5 So Is Shrinking the Chunk the Answer?

The direct lever on the lower bound is shrinking $T = Kr/f$. With $r$ fixed, use a smaller $K$ or a higher temporal frame rate. But the paper’s preliminary experiments point the other way: larger chunk settings generally show better quality and also exploit GPU parallelism well, so sampling time increased only slightly while producing more latent frames. (§1, §4.2)

Here the paper’s central question emerges. Must the bidirectional modeling window be shrunk in order to gain reactivity. The answer is “no,” and instead of shrinking chunks, the convention of committing at chunk boundaries itself has to change.

2. Method: Speculative Sampling

2.1 Separating the Generation Unit from the Commit Unit

The key is to pull apart two sizes. How much the model predicts together in one shot ($K$, the generation unit), and how finely the system commits output at a time ($q$, the delivery unit). The delivery unit $q$ is the number of latent frames sent together, and this paper uses $q=1$. That is, it emits one latent frame at a time.

Thanks to this separation, “quality from the large window, reactivity from the small window” can be had at the same time.

2.2 Reusing Once-Computed Future, Swapping Only When Needed

The sequence of operations is as follows.

  1. Call the DiT once to jointly sample $K$ latent frames. Pad the 1 latent frame to be emitted next with $K-1$ noise latents, producing the $K$ latents together in a single bidirectional window. (§3.2, Eq. (2))
  2. Do not discard the predictions gained from the padding; store them in a prediction cache. A cache entry records the source/playout position correspondence and the condition version together, so it is managed independently of the state of subsequent calls.
  3. If the condition is unchanged, take the cache out as-is and play it in order. No additional sampling happens.
  4. If the condition changes, keep only the already-committed front part (the locked prefix), discard the not-yet-committed tail, and resample all $K$ latents wholesale under the new condition. The new sample is not made short to fit the remaining length of the old chunk.
  5. Committing the output is the act of making the content irreplaceable, and it can happen ahead of actual playback. A large chunk provides a reusable future, and the controller holds that future in a replaceable state until it is needed.

(Figure 1 in the paper) The three cases are compared side by side: small chunks ($K=1$), chunk-level commitment ($K=4$), and speculative sampling ($K=4$). Gray is the old condition and green is the new condition, and the bold green segment is the refreshed output. The dashed line marks the playback position at the moment the condition arrived; the “Protected” region is the irreversibly committed front part, and “Replaceable future” points to the replaceable rear part. The horizontal position represents the position in the video’s content, not computation time. That is, sampling happens jointly with a large chunk, and only the replaceable future beyond the protected prefix is swapped out.

2.3 Following a Small Example

Let $K=4$, $q=1$, and suppose one DiT call jointly creates latent frames 1·2·3·4.

Time and input Locked front part (committed, irreplaceable) Prediction cache (replaceable) Discarded Output going to screen
One DiT call completed (none) 2, 3, 4 (none) 1 is decoded to pixels and played
1 finished playing, new condition arrives while playing 2 1, 2 resampling in progress (3, 4 invalidated) 3, 4 2 (already committed, so played as-is)
Resampling with $K=4$ under the new condition completed 1, 2 3′, 4′, 5′, 6′ (none) play 3′, then 4′ → 5′ → 6′ in order

How to read it: 1 and 2 are committed and never erased; 3 and 4 are discarded the instant the new condition arrives and replaced with new values (3′, 4′); the new sample is always made as the full $K$ latents, never shortened to fit the old chunk’s remaining length. 5′ and 6′ are a future that no one has consumed yet, so if the condition changes again they too may be discarded.

(This is an illustrative example; the actual controller’s boundary/state decisions and details may differ.)

2.4 Orchestrating with the Two States, Produce and Consume

To run the above flow in a real system, what happens when must be pinned down. The paper turns this orchestration into an extended finite state machine (FSM). There are only two control states, and playback continues in both. (§3.2, Appendix C)

State What this state means What actually happens in this state
Produce One generation job is running Calls the DiT to create $K$ latent frames, decodes completed latent frames with the VAE into pixels, and emits the ready batches at the assigned playback boundaries
Consume No job is running Takes the predictions remaining in the cache in order, plays them, converts them to pixels, and transmits them

There are five kinds of events: condition arrival, output/state readiness, job completion, playback tick, and refill/retry wakeup. On each event the controller updates its registers, then checks whether an actionable branch boundary exists and decides whether to start a new job.

Event What the controller does Effect on state
Condition arrival Records only the pending condition version. It does not interrupt the running job. Produce self-loop. If multiple pending updates exist, merge them into the latest version; discarded versions remain marked ‘superseded’
Job completion Validates the result and clears the slot Stays in Produce if conditions for starting the next job exist, otherwise transitions to Consume
Playback tick Plays the next ready batch and advances the playback cursor Does not change state. The tick itself does not require DiT sampling
Update pending while idle Among the positions after the locked prefix where the condition input is ready, the VAE continuity is valid, and the remaining playout deadline can be met, picks the earliest one and replaces only what follows it Consume → Produce. Infeasible requests remain pending rather than discarding useful predictions
Refill condition met Appends a new chunk when the remaining playable length falls short of the expected compute lead Consume → Produce

(While idle, update replanning and normal refill each start a job for separate reasons. The mere existence of a pending version does not by itself start a job.)

(Figure 3 in the paper) (a) shows the structure in which joint generation fills the prediction cache, and playback progress signals when it must be refilled. (b) is the FSM of the two states Produce (generating) and Consume (reusing predictions) when $q=1$. Condition updates do not stop the running generation but trigger only feasible replans, and playback continues in both states.

2.5 Attaching a Bidirectional Model to Streaming

A bidirectional generator typically provides an image·video-conditioned continuation interface. With a temporally compressing 3D VAE, this interface’s expectation of a ’temporally uncompressed first-frame latent’ collides with the fact that cached interior frames belong to a compressed group.

The paper decodes the held boundary to pixels, then re-encodes its last frame through the VAE’s first-frame path and hands it to the next DiT call. That matches the format the pretrained continuation interface expects. As an alternative, it mentions fine-tuning the model to accept compressed latent continuations directly. (§3.3)

2.6 What Disappears and What Remains

If, when a condition arrives, a prepared prefix is immediately available and there is no additional buffer constraint, the first display is aligned to a latent-frame boundary.

$$ t_{playback} = \delta \left\lceil \frac{t_{start} + C}{\delta} \right\rceil, \qquad Q = t_{playback} - (t_{start}+C), \qquad 0 \le Q < \delta $$

In other words, alignment is bound not to the chunk ($T$) but to the delivery unit ($q=1$, one latent frame). (§3.4, Eq. (5))

Under ideal conditions, $E[L]$ comes down to $C + \delta/2$ (Appendix A.2). However, uniform arrivals do not guarantee uniform completion phases. If $R \ne 0$, $(t_{arrival}+R+C) \bmod \delta$ can cluster around particular values, so the actual $E[Q]$ is set by pipeline timing. This means only the alignment wait shrinks; the computation itself is unchanged.

What remains is generation and its residual wait. When one job fully occupies $C$ seconds per period $T$ ($C \le T$), that job must supply the prefix required by a new branch, and arrivals are uniform,

$$ E[R] = \frac{C^2}{2T}, \qquad E[L] = C + \frac{C^2}{2T} + E[Q] $$

holds. (§3.4, Eq. (6), Appendix A.3)

Plugging the paper’s illustrative numbers $T=5$ s and $C=1.6$ s, the residual wait averages 0.256 s. Excluding $Q$, an idle-state arrival takes 1.6 s, an in-job arrival averages 2.4 s, and the unconditional average is 1.856 s. (A computed example, not a video-system measurement.)

The pivot this equation declares is clear. The responsiveness target moves from ‘shrinking the chunk ($T$)’ to ‘shrinking the generation time $C$ of the first output.’ The gains of DiT sampling acceleration and parallel acceleration are also measured through $C$ and the total resource cost.

2.7 The Cost, Recomputed

The claim is concrete on the cost side as well. If the condition does not change, predictions are reused, so in steady state the number of DiT sampling calls equals that of a matching chunk-unit baseline. Fine-grained delivery does not increase sampling. However, when little playable window remains, normal refill is still needed.

Only when the condition changes does extra work appear, equal to the discarded predictions. If each call produces $K$ useful latent groups at the same cost, and the fraction that ultimately fails to be played and gets discarded is $w$, then the relative DiT sampling workload is

$$ A \simeq \frac{1}{1-w} $$

(§3.4, Eq. (7), Appendix B)

If updates are infrequent, this overhead is small. Appendix B.2’s independent-update model predicts that when the update probability is $p$, $A = \frac{Kp}{1-(1-p)^K}$, and for a Poisson arrival rate $\lambda$, if $\lambda T \ll 1$ then $A - 1 \simeq \frac{\lambda(T-\delta)}{2}$, that is, it drops. That said, $w$ depends not only on update frequency but also on chunk size and the chosen branch positions, and VAE decoding, adapter preparation, overlap truncation, interrupted jobs, and cache reconstruction require separate cost accounting.

3. Results

The experiments split into two layers. One is the effect of chunk size on quality and single forward time; the other is the end-to-end wait from condition arrival to screen display in actual serving. Since the two measure different things, they are examined separately. (§4)

One caveat. The forward-time profile in §4.1 is a shape-level measurement that includes communication and output collection but excludes text encoding, VAE decoding, and the sampler loop, and it differs from generation time $C$. (§4.1)

3.1 Chunk Size Is a Quality–Efficiency Trade-off

Wan1.3B was trained separately on Toy6K for each of $K \in \{1,3,7,21\}$ (1/2/4-step sampling) and evaluated with VBench on 81-frame, 16 fps video at 832×480 and 1280×720, over 946 prompts and 5 seeds. (§4.1)

At the same step count and resolution, $K>1$ generally earns higher VBench total scores than $K=1$.

Steps / resolution $K=1$ $K=3$ $K=7$ $K=21$
4-step 480p 79.00 81.66 81.70 82.13
4-step 720p 78.84 81.59 81.86 81.65

(VBench total scores from the paper’s Table 1. The gain is not monotonically increasing, so the optimal $K$ differs per configuration. Quality was measured from models trained separately per chunk size.)

(Figure 5 in the paper) (a) plots Wan 4-step VBench total scores at resolutions 832×480 and 1280×720, and (b) H200 single-forward latency at 480p for USP1·2·4·8. Quality uses separately trained settings; timing uses a shared checkpoint and synthetic inputs.

At the same time, kernel forward time grows less than expected. Going from $K=1$ to $K=3$ triples the current chunk’s latent-frame count, but forward time grows only 2.05× at 480p and 2.74× at 720p.

Resolution $K$ USP1 USP2 USP4 USP8
480p 1 77.5 63.7 65.9 72.1
480p 3 159.2 91.5 67.0 72.9
480p 7 358.3 194.7 105.2 78.6
480p 21 1406.2 750.0 384.1 211.0
720p 1 218.7 143.4 95.8 72.7
720p 3 599.6 318.4 166.5 119.4
720p 7 1521.4 809.2 443.8 276.4
720p 21 6432.8 3335.5 1737.1 899.7

(The paper’s Table 2(a), H200 single forward in ms. Median of the slowest rank over 30 synchronized forwards, excluding 10 warmup runs.)

Growing parallelism enlarges the effect. 480p $K=7$ reaches 78.6ms at USP8, near USP1’s $K=1$ (77.5ms), and 720p $K=21$ falls from USP1’s 6432.8ms to USP8’s 899.7ms. That said, more GPUs are not always better (480p $K=1$ is faster at USP2, 63.7ms, than at USP8, 72.1ms). The right parallelism keeps large chunks efficient.

LTX-2.3 shows the same direction. $K \in \{1,3,9,15,45\}$ were each trained at 3 steps and evaluated on Internal32 (832×448, 24 fps, 361-frame output). The cached-forward of $K=45$ comes down from USP1’s 2016.2ms to USP8’s 507.9ms. However, LTX reports six VBench visual scores (subject consistency, background consistency, aesthetic quality, video quality, smoothness, dynamism) multiplied by 100 without a combined total, so a single-number “best $K$” cannot be read off for LTX. (The paper’s Table 2(b))

3.2 Large Chunks Are Also Fast in Real Serving

The comparison conditions must be fixed first. (§4.1)

  • Wan1.3B: short/long chunks as K3/USP4 (4×B300) and K21/USP8 (8×B300), VAE on a separate GPU pipeline, 832×480.
  • Sol-H3: 22·124-frame proposals, USP4/USP8 (4/8×B300), 832×480, 24 fps.
  • LTX-2.3: short chunk as K3/USP1 (eager or CUDA Graph), long chunk as K15/USP2 (eager), 832×448, 24 fps, text·media on separate GPUs.

Within the same short/long setting, Baseline (commitment at chunk-boundary granularity) and speculative sampling share model placement, continuation interface, decoding, playback, and scheduling lead time. Each configuration is given thirty 60-second traces at a low frequency (1–2 updates per trace) and a high frequency (3–11 updates). L50/L95 are the 50th·95th percentiles (in seconds) of the ‘condition arrival→display’ response after clock alignment based on minimum RTT, and stall is the fraction (%) of the 60-second window occupied by playback underrun. LTX’s long-chunk implementation does not support CUDA Graph capture, so chunk-size comparison is on an eager basis.

Comparing the long-chunk setting by commitment scheme gives the following.

Model (long chunk) Scheme Low-freq L50 / L95 High-freq L50 / L95
Sol-H3 Baseline 4.49 / 6.44 4.45 / 6.59
Sol-H3 Speculative sampling 1.42 / 2.47 1.41 / 1.95
Wan1.3B Baseline 3.23 / 4.64 3.11 / 4.66
Wan1.3B Speculative sampling 1.32 / 1.91 1.35 / 1.63
LTX-2.3 (eager) Baseline 4.82 / 6.99 5.09 / 6.98
LTX-2.3 (eager) Speculative sampling 2.39 / 4.13 2.39 / 4.24

(Long-chunk rows from the paper’s Table 3. All at 480p-class.)

Across all three models, speculative sampling in long chunks brought L50 down to less than half of baseline’s.

Headroom also appears alongside. The per-GPU kernel activity rate (time-weighted average) drops sharply in the long setting — Wan 17–20% (short chunks 50–52%), Sol-H3 18–23% (short chunks 49–50%) — while LTX eager sits at 21–25%, similar to its short chunks (22–23%). This idle reads as room to serve more concurrent streams. The activity-rate increase at high-frequency updates is somewhat larger, but the long setting stays within 20–25%. The measurement scope differs per model: Wan counts only the DiT GPUs, while LTX includes the text·media GPUs.

The most striking result is Sol-H3. Using speculative sampling on long chunks, L50 lands at 1.42/1.41 s at low/high frequency, below the small-chunk baseline’s 1.87/1.87 s, while playback stall is also 0.000%. A direct demonstration that keeping a large bidirectional window is not the path of giving up reactivity.

Cases where playback stalls stand out in LTX. LTX’s short-chunk eager run measured playback underrun at 19.669% at low frequency and 20.339% at high frequency. Switching to the CUDA Graph variant brings the baseline down to 0.005%/0.021%, but speculative sampling in the same variant remains at 1.781%/4.407%. In long chunks, Baseline stays low at 0.069%/0.065% and speculative sampling at 0.204%/0.524%. In short eager, baseline and speculative sampling were both similar at around the late-19% range, so in this run mode the commitment scheme made little difference to stall.

3.3 Predictions Match Measurement

Overlaying the mean response reduction onto theory, the boundary-wait model can be seen to actually work. Sol-H3’s measured reduction is 0.493/2.814 s in the short/long settings, close to the theoretical predictions of 0.438/2.562 s. The tendency for the reduction to grow with chunk size also matches the prediction. Wan went 0.155 → 1.744 s and LTX eager 0.014 → 2.116 s, following the prediction that ’the larger the chunk, the more boundary wait there is to remove.’ (§4.3)

There is one more summary figure. With speculative sampling applied, the long setting’s L50 stops at a level 0.26–0.39 s above the same model’s short setting (all three models, both request loads). In other words, even with large chunks, the reactivity loss is effectively suppressed to the 0.3 s level.

4. Limitations and When to Use It

The limitations the authors themselves admit are two.

First, predictions only pay when they are reused before the new condition invalidates them. If updates are frequent or continuous, much of a chunk is discarded and DiT compute is wasted. $w$ depends not only on update frequency but also on chunk size and the chosen branch positions.

Second, because of bidirectional attention within a chunk, the retained KV can carry information about later content that is later discarded. Even after KV entries are deleted, that influence can remain in the regenerated continuation. (§5)

Adding from a reviewer’s perspective, there are several constraints.

  • The update frequencies the experiments cover are only two ranges, 1–2 and 3–11 per 60-second trace. A situation where the viewer manipulates the screen continuously has not been validated.
  • L50/L95 measure ‘from condition arrival to display.’ The moment the condition’s effect becomes perceptible — the semantic response — is left to separate measurement (Appendix D).
  • Separately instrumented values of $R$ and $Q$ in actual deployment, and the measured value of the rate $w$ at which prediction reuse actually happens, are not reported in the original (not reported). $A \simeq 1/(1-w)$ is an accounting identity over sampling calls, not a measured value of $w$.
  • The results are confirmed at specific chunk·resolution·GPU configurations of three models, so it is hard to assert they hold as-is under other frame rates, VAEs, and backbones. The added cost of the VAE first-frame-path re-encoding is also a separate cost-accounting item.

When it is worth using in an operating environment can be read from this analysis. It fits scenarios with intermittent updates — for example, commands changing occasionally within a scene (the experiment traces also change actions within a scene) — best. It is also promising when you want to serve a large bidirectional model for streaming without continued training. Conversely, when the condition keeps changing, or when GPU headroom is lacking so that $C$ approaches $T$, the benefit shrinks. In the limiting case $C=T$, the generation worker is always busy, so $E[R]=T/2$ and $Q=0$, and the mean $L$ remains $3T/2$, equal to the fixed-chunk-boundary baseline (Appendix A.3). Fine-grained delivery alone does not improve it.

In the end, this method shifts the design’s center of gravity. It lifts the fixed constraint that chunk size must be shrunk, and instead restores chunk size as a decision variable that jointly controls quality and reactivity. The center of gravity of optimization moves to $C$, the remaining bottleneck: shrinking the generation time of the first output.

Tables from the paper

Tables converted mechanically from the arXiv e-print LaTeX source. The numbers are the paper’s own and did not pass through a model.

Table 1. Wan1.3B quality measurements. Total is the reported VBench aggregate, with its quality and semantic components; the table also includes dynamic degree, VisionReward, and instruction following.

item.title: MemT-1.0: Towards Memory-Native Evolution
item.description:
Paper

MemT-1.0: A Memory Foundation Model That Puts Conversational Memory Inside Model Computation

For a chatbot or coding agent to process an ongoing conversation with full context, it must feed all text so far into the input at every turn. Attention must hold the key/value of that entire text in a cache, and the cache grows in proportion to the token count as the conversation lengthens. Instead of replaying past conversation as text, MemT-1.0 compresses it into a fixed-size state (a matrix) inside the model, and at question time accesses the past history through that state to answer.

Why ‘Fixed-Size Memory’ Is Needed

With full context, longer inputs make both prefill (the stage that processes the entire input first to build a cache) and cache storage grow together, and every generation step must recompute attention over the whole cache. Reducing the input through summarization or retrieval (RAG, selecting relevant documents and putting them in context) lowers storage but can lose information or omit the necessary evidence.

MemT-1.0’s idea is to discard ‘carrying the entire record’. It records past information into a fixed-size matrix state by overwriting. When a new turn arrives, the state is updated but its size stays the same, and when a question arrives, the past history is accessed through this state. Thus, in the fixed configuration, state size becomes independent of token count.

The following is an illustrative example to aid understanding. It differs from actual token segmentation or vector values and is not a measurement result from the paper.

Order Text fed into the model Change in memory state (fixed-size matrix)
Initial (none) All elements are 0
Turn 1 store “My cat’s name is Mochi” The ’name=Mochi’ component is recorded
Turn 2 store “Mochi moved to Busan” The ’location=Busan’ component is added, and the older ’name’ component gradually fades through decay
Question “Where does my cat live now?” Restore ‘Busan’ from the state and generate an answer

The key is the last row. Whether the conversation is 4K tokens or 128K tokens, in the fixed configuration the state is a matrix of the same shape, so storage size is constant. With full context, the key/value cache keeps growing as the conversation lengthens.

The native memory block is split into two parts. Information actually accumulated during the conversation is stored in a dynamic state called local memory, and learned parameters called hyper memory decide how this state is read, written, and erased. The former is initialized to zero for each trajectory (a continuous interaction within a single user session) and keeps changing during the interaction, while the latter is updated only during training and stays fixed during inference. The released models are Nano with 36B parameters (3B active, 10 million dynamic memory) and Flash with 288B parameters (17B active, 336 million dynamic memory). The backbones are Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and a prepared DeepSeek-V4-Flash, respectively.

The Route to Past Information Changes

This explanatory diagram redraws the operations in §2.1–2.2. Both routes receive the same history and question; compare the form in which past information remains available at question time.

Full context: past-token KV accumulates

 flowchart TB
H["Entire conversation history"] --> P["Prefill the full history"]
P --> K["KV cache grows with history"]
Q1["Current question"] --> A["Attend to past KV and current text"]
K --> A
A --> O1["Answer"]

MemT: read history from state and current text through attention

 flowchart TB
I["New segment and previous state M"] --> W["Decay, erase and write"]
W --> M["New state M of the same size"]
M --> R["Read state M with the question query"]
R --> S["Add to current-text attention output"]
S --> O["Answer"]

The growing object in full context is the KV cache of past tokens. MemT updates a state M of the same size and reads it when a question arrives. MemT still maintains attention and KV for the current text. The fixed-size state is also a lossy compression: constant storage does not mean perfect recall of every past detail.

Method: How the State Is Stored and Read

Store: Erase, Write, Forget

In the store stage, each token computes a normalized key $k$, a value to record $v$, and three gates. The erase gate $\beta$ decides ‘how much existing information to erase’, the write gate $\omega$ decides ‘how strongly to record the new value’, and the forget gate $\lambda$ decides ‘how much to blur everything over time’. $\lambda$ is initialized by sampling the initial half-life per key channel (after how many tokens it halves) log-uniformly in the range 2,048–32,768 tokens for Nano and 128–32,768 tokens for Flash, so each channel starts with a different time scale. This value is learned (Appendix B.2).

Within a single channel, the state update is as follows.

$$ M \leftarrow \big(I - u^{\top} u\big)\, D\, M + u^{\top} (\omega \odot v), \qquad u = \sqrt{\beta} \odot k,\quad D = \operatorname{Diag}(\exp(\lambda)) $$

The erase matrix $I-u^{\top}u$ reduces the component along $u$ and keeps its orthogonal component. $D$ decays the entire state through per-channel forgetting. The write term on the right records the new value along the $u$ direction. This update repeats in order for each token, and the state updated through the last token becomes the starting state of the next turn (§2.2.2).

Why ‘Stabilization’ Is Needed

The original erase term of Gated DeltaNet-2 (GDN-2), on which the paper builds, has the form $I - k^{\top}(\beta \odot k)$ and is not symmetric. If $\beta \odot k$ is not parallel to $k$ ($\gamma \neq 0$), energy is amplified in the direction perpendicular to $k$ ($\lVert eA^{\top}\rVert_2^2 = 1+\gamma^2 \ge 1$). The appendix analysis shows that a recursion passing through such a map at every token can become unstable. A sufficient condition guaranteeing uniform contraction even in the worst case is that the forget decay satisfies $d < \sqrt{3}/2 \approx 0.866$, which corresponds to a half-life of about 4.82 tokens (≈5 tokens) (Appendix C).

MemT-1.0 symmetrizes the projection so that erasing and writing use the same direction $u = \sqrt{\beta} \odot k$. Changing the erase to $I - u^{\top}u$ yields a non-expansive map that contracts along $u$ and does not expand the orthogonal direction. The paper explains that this symmetrization avoids GDN-2’s unstable update. The formula above already includes this stabilization. Experimentally, removing this stabilization (the original GDN-2 update) lowers the average over 11 benchmarks by only 0.5 points, but the paper presents it as a theoretical safeguard against state divergence (Table 4, §6.4).

Read: Pull It Out of the State with a Query

In the read stage, a normalized query $q$ is produced from the question tokens, and $q M / \sqrt{d_k}$ is computed. This can be viewed as ‘a weighted sum of the values recorded under keys similar to the query’. It is multiplied by an output gate $G$ to decide how much of this read result to pass through, and a softcap (limiting the magnitude of the SiLU output with $\tau\tanh$, $\tau=2$) prevents blow-ups. This result is added to the original attention output (§2.2.2).

The important difference is that, unlike full-context attention, which revisits all past key/value at every token, MemT’s read of past history ends with a multiplication by a fixed-size state. Attention over the current text and the KV cache are maintained separately. Because the state dimension does not grow, the read computation over past history is also constant.

Capacity Scaling: Mixture-of-Storage

Simply enlarging the state matrix to increase memory capacity grows parameters and computation together. MemT-1.0 uses Mixture-of-Storage (MoS) to expand one memory block into $E$ independent memory experts (§2.3).

Unlike conventional sparse MoE, which selects only the top few experts per token, MoS computes all experts always. A store router and a utilization router each produce per-expert probabilities $\alpha$; the utilization probabilities mix the read results, and the store probabilities adjust the strength of writing and erasing. The two routers share the same expert address matrix $C$ and learn only their projections separately. Increasing the number of experts increases state, parameters, and block computation together, but there is no top-k selection. However, both released models have one expert per layer ($E=1$); the capacity comparison of 2 vs. 4 experts is in §5.4, and the cost measurement for the 4-expert configuration is in Appendix F.

In the scaling experiment, 4 experts scored higher on average than 2 experts at all three checkpoints. After 400 CPT steps, the gains were +0.41 at 200 memory post-training steps, +2.01 at 3,400 steps, and +2.69 at 5,500 steps (§5.4).

Training: Prepare the Backbone First, Then Learn from a Teacher

A memory model inherits both the knowledge the backbone already has and the reliability with which it turns that knowledge into action. The paper argues that in this setting backbone post-training mainly improves reliability, and new knowledge must be supplied by native memory. Tasks the backbone could not solve in any of eight attempts remained at 1.6–4.0% accuracy on four benchmarks even after the preparation process. By contrast, on hard knowledge questions in a separate probe set, accuracy rose from 27% to 91% when the relevant facts were placed in context. The paper interprets this as meaning that much of the remaining gap comes from a lack of information (§3.1).

So DeepSeek-V4-Flash, the backbone of Flash, undergoes separate backbone post-training before memory is attached. The prepared backbone improved by 6.3 points on average across six benchmarks monitored over three tracks compared with the public version, and on SWE-bench Multilingual and IFBench v2 it even exceeded the reported scores of GLM-5.3 Flash (320B total, 18B active) and DeepSeek-V4 Pro (1.6T total, 49B active) at 284B total and 13B active (Figure 2, §3.1).

Training the memory itself is off-policy distillation (§3.3). A frozen backbone that sees the full context acts as the teacher and produces the next-token distribution, and the MemT-1.0 student imitates the same distribution given the current input, the observed response prefix, and the memory state compressing past history. The key point is that the teacher sees the entire past history as text, while the student sees past history only as the memory state. The loss differs by stage. CPT uses cross-entropy on the correct tokens, and memory post-training uses forward KL divergence against the teacher’s top-64 token distribution (temperature 1.0, Table 7). The teacher distribution is renormalized over the top 64.

Training has two stages (§3.4–3.5). Continued pre-training (CPT, 20B tokens) builds language modeling ability to predict the next token within the current segment while accessing prior information only through memory, and memory post-training (14B tokens) adapts the model to reproduce the teacher’s full-context distribution from memory. The contribution of the two stages is separated in the experiments. Removing memory post-training lowers the average by 10.7 points, and removing CPT lowers it by 2.1 points (Table 4, §6.4).

Results: Where It Gets Faster and What It Loses

Memory Performance

On 11 memory benchmarks, MemT-1.0 takes first and second place among parameter-memory methods (Table 2, §6.2).

Category Representative method Average score
Text memory (history provided at question time) MemOS (DeepSeek backbone) 68.6
Text memory Full Context (DeepSeek) 65.0
Parameter memory (history not provided) MemT-1.0-Flash 50.6
Parameter memory MemT-1.0-Nano 47.0
Parameter memory (previous best) Temp-LoRA 38.1

Flash and Nano lead the previous best parameter method, Temp-LoRA, by 12.5 and 8.9 points, respectively. What matters is that these scores were obtained without inserting any past text at question time. However, it still trails the text-memory methods MemOS (68.6) and Full Context (65.0), and the gap is especially large on LongMemEval-S and BEAM-1M, which require preserving detailed evidence (§6.2). The paper explains that processing long trajectories alone does not guarantee stable access to their content; prior information must survive multiple updates and remain distinguishable from other records. Selective retention and query-dependent reading remain open problems.

General ability is compared with the backbone under a noise setting. Before evaluation, irrelevant information is written once into MemT’s memory, and the same information is placed in the backbone’s input context. Then general tasks are solved. Flash shows an average difference of 0.0 and Nano −0.9, largely preserving backbone performance (Table 3, §6.3). Still, there is per-task variation, such as Nano dropping 5.8 points on LiveCodeBench v6, so robustness to distractor memories must be examined at the task level.

Efficiency: Separate Kernel Level from System Level

First is a microbenchmark measuring only one memory block on a single GPU. It uses a 32K-token pack, synthetic hidden states, a 4-expert configuration, and 2,048-token steps. Materializing all expert projections at once raises peak memory to 47.83 GiB, whereas processing steps in windows of 4,096 tokens (2 steps) brings it to 9.49 GiB (80.1% reduction) and increases forward+backward time by only 1.6%, from a median of 463.0 ms to 470.6 ms (Table 1, §4.2). This is a block-level trade-off.

End-to-end system performance is measured with BEAM history, 128-token responses, and a single request on 2 GPUs. Nano is slower than full context for short histories, becomes comparable around 32K, and gains an advantage as histories grow longer. The speedups are about 1.20× at 64K, 1.86× at 128K, and 3.99× at 256K (§6.5, Figure 8).

History length Full Context latency MemT-1.0-Nano latency Speedup
128K 30.07 s 16.19 s 1.86×
256K 94.47 s 23.69 s 3.99×

The paper attributes the long-context latency advantage mainly to low history preparation cost. Full context prefills the entire history and keeps computing attention over past key/value during generation. Nano writes history into memory in 2,048-token units, reads past history only as state during generation, and maintains current-text attention separately. Excluding history preparation, time to first token (TTFT) for the query is nearly constant for Nano at 104–112 ms, while full context rises to 257 ms at 128K and 445 ms at 256K. The TTFT advantages are about 2.44× and 4.19×, respectively. This is because the fixed-size state read computation is independent of the number of past tokens (§6.5, Figure 8).

Storage follows the same split (§6.6, Figure 9).

Method Persistent storage per trajectory (excluding shared weights)
Full Context (256K limit) 5.061 GiB, grows proportionally with history
Temp-LoRA 172.5 MiB (fixed)
MemT-1.0-Nano 40 MiB (fixed)

At a 128K history, Nano’s state is about 66× smaller than full context and does not grow as the conversation lengthens. Conversely, for short conversations DenseRAG, which stores only a few chunks of text and retrieval vectors, is cheaper. DenseRAG has low storage cost when history is short, but its stored text and retrieval vectors accumulate as the conversation grows. Eventually, once history is long enough, DenseRAG’s accumulated record exceeds Nano’s fixed-size state, and from then on Nano has the advantage (§6.6). The storage curve for full context stops at the context window limit (256K), so the value at that point does not represent preserving the entire longest history. Total storage grows with the number of trajectories and the configured memory capacity.

Limitations and Open Problems

A fixed-size state comes at a cost. While the state stays $O(1)$, its capacity to preserve detail is more limited than a scheme that stores in proportion to conversation length $N$ (§8). Because new information keeps entering the existing representation, a trade-off arises between retaining earlier details and adding recent information. This loss of memory fidelity on tasks requiring precise recall remains an open problem.

The paper also sees the fixed-size state as opening a possibility beyond compression: ’the iterative consolidation of accumulated experience’. Since new information enters a representation already refined by previous interactions at every update, unlike a structure where past records keep growing, it could serve as a basis for latent reflection (§8). However, this is a directional interpretation, and the original paper does not report experimental results supporting it.

The relationship between the two kinds of memory is also unresolved. Local memory holds information accumulated during interaction, and hyper memory holds the learned ability to store and use it. Whether experience accumulated in local memory can consolidate into hyper memory parameters through additional training, and how hyper memory’s knowledge is instantiated through local memory, remain open questions (§8).

The validation scope of MoS for increasing memory capacity is also narrow. Both released models have one expert per layer ($E=1$). The 2-vs-4-expert comparison was made only at three checkpoints: after 400 CPT steps, at 200, 3,400, and 5,500 memory post-training steps (§5.4). In addition, the single-GPU microbenchmark measures block cost including per-expert projections, routers, state updates, reads, and backward passes with synthetic inputs, but does not reflect communication and memory costs at full backbone scale (§4.2, Appendix F).

Closing

MemT-1.0 moves past history into a fixed-size state inside model computation, decoupling state size and past-history read cost from conversation length in the fixed configuration, and increasing its latency and storage advantage over full context on long histories. At a 128K history it achieves end-to-end inference about 1.86× faster than full context and per-trajectory logical state storage about 66× smaller, and it ranks first and second among parameter-memory methods on the 11-benchmark average. However, a gap with text-memory methods remains, and the paper leaves improving long-term memory, scaling memory capacity, and reducing memory update cost as future work.

Reference Links

  • Code: https://github.com/MemTensor/MemT-1.0
  • Models: https://huggingface.co/collections/MemTensor/memt-1

item.title: DLite: History-free Speculative Decoding for Agentic AI
item.description:
As a coding agent reads files and calls tools, its conversation and execution history grows. Adding a small model to draft answers faster can create another burden if that model must separately process and retain the same long history.

DLite lets the target model handle the history, while the small drafter uses the target’s internal representations to propose upcoming tokens. It removes the drafter’s separate historical KV cache. It does not remove the target’s cache or discard historical information.

Paper · Code

Why can adding a small model help?

A language model usually generates one token at a time. A token is a unit of text processing, such as a word or part of a word. Instead of running the large model once for every token, a small model can propose several candidates for the large model to check together. This is the basic idea of speculative decoding (§2.1).

The two roles are distinct. The drafter proposes candidates quickly; the target model verifies them and determines the actual output. The approach benefits from accepting many candidates while keeping drafting costs small. A slow or frequently rejected drafter reduces that benefit.

Agents accumulate tool results and prior conversation. Conventional drafters process this history themselves and store internal data in a KV cache for later generation. A KV cache retains information about processed tokens so the model need not recompute everything from scratch. When the target and drafter maintain separate caches, newly confirmed tokens also require updates on the draft side (§3.1).

The left of Figure 1 illustrates agent execution with repeated long inputs and short outputs. The right shows fewer tokens being produced per verification round on such workloads. The question is not merely whether a small model is available, but whether it can keep proposing useful candidates while handling a growing history.

Overall pipeline: what stays and what disappears?

After processing the history, the target supplies hidden states to DLite. These are intermediate neural-network values, not a human-readable summary. The drafter uses them together with the latest confirmed token to propose new candidates (§4.1).

The following is an illustrative example of candidate verification. It uses visible English words for clarity, rather than an actual tokenizer’s segmentation or measured results from the paper.

In the first panel, the full history and target cache remain. The drafter receives target representations and information about the current position. Thus, “history-free” means that the drafter keeps no separate historical KV cache, not that it forgets the history.

In the second panel, the drafter proposes jumps over a dog. The third assumes a verification outcome that accepts jumps and over, then rejects a. In that case, dog is not confirmed either, and generation continues with the from the verification procedure. This does not describe a simple comparison against a reference string; it illustrates which candidates survive an acceptance or rejection decision.

One round performs the following operations.

Stage Operation Result used next
Target computation Process the input so far Target cache and hidden states
Candidate preparation Compute representations for several positions together Position-wise representations
Candidate generation Select each candidate using earlier draft selections Candidate token block
Target verification Check candidates and confirm the accepted prefix Confirmed output and next-round information

The drafter does not store the long history again, but target computation and verification remain. These must be distinguished from the work DLite removes (§4.1, Figure 3).

Prepare positions together, then use earlier selections

Computing several upcoming positions together is efficient. But choosing their words independently can make the sequence less coherent. When selecting the word after jumps, for example, the model needs to account for having actually selected jumps.

DLite separates these operations. Its parallel backbone computes representations for several positions together. A small sequential head then uses earlier draft selections when choosing subsequent candidates. The larger computation runs in parallel; only the small computation that accounts for earlier candidates runs sequentially (§4.1.1–4.1.2).

The sequential head handles information inside the current candidate block. It does not reread the entire conversation or file contents. It also incorporates sequential information in the hidden representations before projecting them into vocabulary scores, rather than projecting first and refining afterward. This avoids repeating an expensive intermediate vocabulary projection.

Figure 3 connects the explanation to the model’s components. Follow the path from target representations to the drafter, and the placement of the sequential head after parallel computation. The illustrative figure shows how candidates change; this source figure shows how implementation components connect.

The architecture also needs training preparation. The authors first use an intermediate teacher with a similar structure that can access historical cache, then train DLite to align directly with the target. Removing draft-side cache during inference comes with an additional training procedure (§4.2).

Results: acceptance length and speed are different

The experiments use Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B as targets on NVIDIA H800 serving hardware, with a speculative block size of 7. Two metrics need separating. Acceptance length measures output per verification round; speedup measures improvement over ordinary token-by-token generation (§5.1).

The following results are from SWE-Bench. DSpark is another drafting approach used for comparison (Table 3).

Target Method Average acceptance length Speed versus ordinary generation
Qwen3-4B DSpark 1.89 1.64×
Qwen3-4B DLite 3.15 2.68×
Qwen3-8B DSpark 1.94 1.60×
Qwen3-8B DLite 3.19 2.74×

For 4B, the change from 1.89 to 3.15 is about a 66.7% increase in acceptance length. The 2.68× speedup, however, is relative to ordinary generation, not DSpark. A direct speed comparison divides 2.68 by 1.64, giving approximately 1.63×. Accepting more candidates and speeding up a service are related, but they are different measurements.

On shorter general-purpose tasks, differences are smaller. For example, 4B GSM8K acceptance length is 6.27 for DSpark and 6.38 for DLite (Table 1). Rather than expecting large gains everywhere, examine how useful this design is when histories grow long.

Speedup also changes with concurrency. For 4B Alpaca, DLite’s throughput relative to ordinary generation is 2.58× with 1 concurrent request and 1.32× with 64. Evaluation should match the service’s actual concurrency and input lengths (Table 4).

Limitations to check before adoption

The serving engine must expose target hidden states and pass them to the drafter. Assessing compatibility therefore requires examining that implementation path, beyond the model’s name. The target KV cache remains necessary, so the memory cost of the whole long input does not disappear.

Training costs remain too. The intermediate teacher and two-stage training are part of the authors’ procedure. The results do not imply that attaching an arbitrary pretrained small model will reproduce these gains (§4.2).

From a reviewer’s perspective, applicability remains a question. The targets evaluated are 4B and 8B Qwen3 models on H800 serving hardware. Larger targets, different architectures, or placing the drafter and target on separate devices require further validation. Acceptance length and speed measurements also do not directly measure task success rates.

DLite is worth examining for agent services that repeatedly reuse long histories. The central question is who processes the history and who reuses the result, rather than whether all cache usage reaches zero. The design retains target-side history processing while reducing redundant historical storage and updates in the drafter.
