item.title: Contextual Correction of Parallel Drafts for Speculative Decoding
item.description:
Paper

TL;DR — Parallel diffusion drafters like DFlash produce a whole block of tokens at once, but within the block they predict each token without knowing the identity of the preceding tokens. DCOCO is a lightweight corrector that re-selects contextually appropriate tokens by scoring the adjacent transitions among already-drafted candidates in a single batched operation, with no extra drafter forward pass. Across 4 backbones and 10 benchmarks it is up to 6.6× faster than vanilla and up to 18% faster than the strongest speculative baseline, and it retains a 6–23% margin even at concurrency of 4–32 streams.

Core Idea

Speculative decoding accelerates LLM inference with the idea that “a lightweight drafter proposes tokens and a heavy target model verifies them in one pass.” The problem is the tension between drafting speed and acceptance rate.

The authors focus on exactly one thing. The currently popular parallel drafters (which predict an entire block at once in a diffusion-based manner, as DFlash does) are fast, but within a block they do not see the actual selection made in the preceding slot. As a result, tokens that look plausible individually combine to simultaneously assign high probability to “New York” and “San Diego,” producing an unnatural continuation like “New Diego” (§2). This lowers the acceptance rate and ultimately erodes the speed gain.

Existing methods such as DSpark and Domino try to solve this problem with a sequential module, but that sequential module sits on the critical path of every decoding cycle. DCOCO (DFlash Contextual Corrector) answers “yes” to the question of whether intra-block dependencies can be restored without reintroducing a sequential module (§1).

The key lies in two observations.

  1. The drafter already has the answer. For Qwen3-8B, in 59% of slots where top-1 is wrong, the verifier’s actual token is present among the top-16 candidates (§2). Correction can therefore be reduced not to “generating new tokens” but to re-selection among candidates that already exist.
  2. Verification stops at the front. Speculative verification accepts only a contiguous prefix and halts at the first rejection. Improving later slots therefore matters only if all earlier slots are accepted, so correction must concentrate on the quality of the early prefix (§2).

Combining these two turns the corrector into the following task: “keep the top $K$ candidates per slot, score all $K^2$ transitions between adjacent slots in parallel, then greedily choose from the front.” The decisive difference from DSpark and Domino is that neural scoring is parallel and only the selection is sequential (a simple walk over the grid).

Background: the Problem They Solved

Structure of Speculative Decoding

The verifier scores the proposed block $\hat y_{1:B}$ in a single forward pass, decides slots from left to right, commits the longest accepted prefix, and then adds one token of its own. Under greedy decoding, slot $j$ is accepted if it matches the verifier’s greedy choice; under stochastic decoding it is accepted by the standard speculative sampling rule $\min\{1, q_j(\hat y_j)/p_j(\hat y_j)\}$ (§3.1).

Writing the acceptance of slot $j$ as $a_j\in\{0,1\}$, the acceptance length is

$$ A(\hat y) = \max\{ m : a_1 = a_2 = \dots = a_m = 1 \}, $$

and each round commits $A(\hat y)+1$ tokens. Throughput is ultimately determined by the expected acceptance length and the wall-clock time per round. And this single structural fact — “verification stops at the first rejection” — governs every design choice in DCOCO, because if slot 1 is rejected, the corrected token in slot 5 is never even examined (§3.1).

Candidate Coverage: the Missed Headroom

The authors recorded DFlash’s candidates during $T{=}0$ speculative decoding and compared them against the actual continuation to measure top-$k$ coverage — “the fraction of draft slots whose top-$k$ candidates contain the token the verifier ultimately commits” (§2).

The results are regular. On Qwen3-8B, at the first slot top-16 is about 95.1% and top-1 (the drafter’s own choice) is 81.4%, a small gap, but at the last slot top-16 is still 60.8% while top-1 falls to 15.4% (Fig. 1, Tab. 7). Averaged over the whole block, top-1 is 40.0% vs top-16 75.5%. That is, at deep slots nearly one in two slots has the correct answer in its candidate pool, yet the drafter increasingly fails to pick it. This “missed correct answer” is exactly the headroom the corrector re-selects from.

The New Approach: DCOCO

DCOCO operates in two stages. (1) Given the realized tokens, it re-assigns a stronger contextual score to the drafter’s per-slot candidates, and (2) it re-selects the block according to those scores (§3).

1) A Learned Corrector over the Block Grid

At each slot $i\in\{1,\dots,B\}$, DFlash leaves a hidden state $h_i\in\mathbb{R}^d$ and the top $K$ candidates. Here $c_{ik}$ is the token id of the $k$-th candidate at slot $i$, and $\ell_i(k)$ is its draft logit. These candidates form a dense first-order grid of $B\times K$ nodes, with every candidate at slot $p$ connected to every candidate at slot $p+1$.

Each transition is assigned a score:

$$ S_p(a,b) = \underbrace{\ell_{p+1}(b)}_{\text{draft unary logit}} + \underbrace{\Delta_\theta(s_p,\, z_{pa},\, z_{p+1,b},\, \ell_p(a),\, \ell_{p+1}(b))}_{\text{learned correction}}, $$

where $\Delta_\theta$ is a shared 2-layer MLP, $z_{ik}$ is a candidate representation, and $s_p$ is a candidate-independent pair state (§3.2). The corrector reads only the hidden states, candidate ids, and logits left by a single DFlash pass.

  • Candidate representation $z_{ik}$: it fuses $b_{ik}$, obtained by projecting and normalizing the embedding of $c_{ik}$ from the frozen token embedding table $E$, with $g_i$, obtained by projecting and normalizing the slot hidden state $h_i$, via concatenation. Because the token embedding and hidden state differ in scale by more than two orders of magnitude, it uses a non-affine layer normalization.
  • Pair state $s_p$: it concatenates the hidden states of adjacent slots, $s_p = W_{\text{pair}}[h_p; h_{p+1}]$. Since $s_p$ depends only on slots, it is computed once and reused across all $K^2$ transitions between them.

There are two key design tricks. First, the MLP’s output layer is initialized to zero, so initially $\Delta_\theta\equiv 0$ and every transition score reduces to the successor’s draft logit $S_p(a,b)=\ell_{p+1}(b)$, thereby reproducing the drafter’s original proposal exactly at initialization (§3.2). Second, all projection and MLP parameters are shared across slots and transitions, and the $(B-1)K^2$ transition scores are computed in a single batched operation before path selection.

2) Prefix-first Greedy Selection

On the scored grid, simply maximizing the total path score lets high scores at later slots compensate for low scores at earlier ones — but later tokens contribute only if the earlier prefix survives. Because of this asymmetry, DCOCO uses a prefix-first greedy rule:

$$ k_1 = \arg\max_k \ell_1(k), \qquad k_{p+1} = \arg\max_b S_p(k_p, b) \quad (p=1,\dots,B-1). $$

The first slot keeps the drafter’s top candidate, and each subsequent slot picks its successor only from scores conditioned on the selected predecessor. The absence of lookahead into future transitions is actually an advantage: this walk costs only $O(BK)$ (added on top of the $O(BK^2)$ scoring), and if $\Delta_\theta\equiv 0$ it agrees exactly with the drafter’s argmax (§3.3).

3) Training: Supervise Only on Verifier-Correct Prefixes

The drafter and corrector are optimized jointly. The label $(a^\star_p, b^\star_p)$ for transition $p$ is the pair of verifier argmax tokens at the two slots under a teacher-forced context, and it is activated with mask $m_p=1$ only when it lies within each slot’s top-$K$. The correction loss multiplies a cross-entropy, normalized over the $K^2$ transitions by a joint softmax, by an exponential decay weight:

$$ \mathcal{L}_{\text{corr}} \propto -\sum_{p=1}^{B-1} e^{-(p-1)/\rho}\, m_p \log \frac{\exp S_p(a^\star_p, b^\star_p)}{\sum_{a,b=1}^{K}\exp S_p(a,b)}, \qquad \rho = 4. $$

This softmax exists only during training; at inference time $S_p$ is used without normalization. The exponential weight is a fixed proxy reflecting the prefix-survival structure — “a later transition contributes only if the earlier slot is accepted” (§3.2, App. A). The supervision simply drops rather than suppresses transitions the drafter finds unreachable, since the verifier-correct prefix is the only state in which the corrector’s output is actually consumed (App. A).

4) Deterministic Proposals Even Under Stochastic Decoding

This is an interesting theoretical result. DCOCO selects tokens deterministically even under stochastic decoding, so each slot’s proposal distribution becomes a point mass $p_j(v)=\mathbf{1}[v=\hat y_j]$. The acceptance probability of standard speculative sampling then simplifies to $\min\{1, q_j/p_j\}=q_j(\hat y_j)$, and on rejection the residual distribution becomes $r_j(v)=q_j(v)\mathbf{1}[v\neq\hat y_j]/(1-q_j(\hat y_j))$. Repeating this at every slot preserves the verifier distribution exactly — that is, stochastic target decoding does not require stochastic draft selection (App. D). No softmax normalization on transition scores and no candidate-distribution sampling are needed.

How It Works: Walking Through a Concrete Example

Let us reproduce the “New Diego” problem in miniature. Say the block size is $B=4$ and the number of candidates per slot is $K=3$. Suppose a single DFlash pass left the following (the same example tokens and scores as Fig. 2 in the paper).

  • Slot 1: These(4.2), The(3.6), A(2.8)
  • Slot 2: key(0.4), keys(2.7), locks(1.1)
  • Slot 3: is(0.2), are(3.1), was(0.8)
  • Slot 4: missing(2.8), here(1.6), broken(0.5)

If the drafter simply picks each slot’s top-1, the result is “These key is missing” — every word is plausible, yet the grammar is off. The identity of the problem is that the adjacent context — that “These” should be followed by “keys” and “keys” by “are” — is not reflected in the drafter at all.

DCOCO lays this block out into a $4\times 3$ grid. It builds each slot’s candidate representation $z_{ik}$ (embedding + slot hidden state) and pair state $s_p$, and scores all $3\times 3=9$ transitions between adjacent slots with the shared MLP $\Delta_\theta$. For instance, the 9 transitions of (Slot1→Slot2) are all computed in parallel as:

$$ S_1(\text{These}, b) = \ell_2(b) + \Delta_\theta(s_1, z_{1,\text{These}}, z_{2,b}, \dots) $$

Since during training $\Delta_\theta$ was trained to assign high scores to adjacent pairs that the verifier actually selects, such as “These + keys” and “keys + are,” it adds a correction to the draft logit $\ell_2(\text{key})=0.4$ so that $S_1(\text{These}, \text{keys})$ overtakes $S_1(\text{These}, \text{key})$.

Then comes the prefix-first walk. Slot 1 is fixed to top-1 These (→ These). Slot 2 picks keys, which maximizes $S_1(\text{These}, \cdot)$ (→ These keys). Slot 3 now picks are, which maximizes $S_2(\text{keys}, \cdot)$ conditioned on the selected keys (→ These keys are). Finally, Slot 4 picks missing via $S_3(\text{are}, \cdot)$. The final proposal is “These keys are missing” — an ungrammatical string produced by the drafter’s top-1 combination has been turned into a grammatically correct sentence with no extra drafter forward pass.

The important point here is that only the selection is sequential, while the 9 scorings are all bundled into a single batched operation. To fix this example, DSpark and Domino must run a recurrent module that sweeps slot by slot, whereas DCOCO finishes with one parallel scoring plus an $O(BK)$ walk.

Performance Validation: Main Results

Setup

The verifiers are four backbones — Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B, Llama-3.1-8B — and the benchmarks are 10 covering math (GSM8K, MATH-500, AIME-25), code (HumanEval, MBPP, LiveCodeBench), and general (MT-Bench, Arena-Hard-v2, Alpaca, SpeedBench). All drafters were trained with block size 16 on about 800K prompts (stem/math/code from Nemotron Post-Training v2 + CodeAlpaca-20k). Serving uses vLLM 0.27.0 on a single NVIDIA B200, BF16, TP=1 (App. C). The primary metric is end-to-end tokens per second (TPS), and the secondary metric is the average acceptance length $\tau$, which separates “quality improvement” from “serving overhead” (§4).

Why Accepted Length and Actual Throughput Must Be Read Together

The most honest choice in this paper is making TPS the primary metric. The corrector can increase acceptance length while eroding wall-clock time with its own scoring cost, and that trade-off shows up only in TPS (§4). The paper therefore reports $\tau$ (mechanism) and TPS (outcome) side by side.

On Qwen3-8B (thinking off), DCOCO achieves an average acceptance length $\tau$ of 4.985, which is +8.1% over Domino (4.613), +17.2% over DSpark (4.254), and +27.4% over uncorrected DFlash (3.913). And this $\tau$ improvement translates directly into a TPS improvement (Fig. 3, Tab. 2).

Overall Results: First Place in All 12 Cells

In all 12 combinations of four backbones × (thinking on/off) × ($T{=}0$/$T{=}1$), DCOCO recorded the best average speedup (§4.1, Tab. 2). In each cell it leads the strongest baseline by 8–19%. For Qwen3-8B, math and code benchmarks go up to 3.7–6.1× over vanilla, while open-ended chat is 1.8–1.9× (greedy decoding). The up to 6.6× in the abstract comes from Qwen3-4B on AIME-25.

Averaging over the 10 suites for Qwen3-8B (thinking off, $T{=}0$):

System Avg TPS vs vanilla
No-spec(vanilla) 265.6 1.0×
DFlash(uncorrected) 783.1 2.95×
DSpark 765.6 2.88×
Domino 839.3 3.16×
DCOCO 959.7 3.62×

That is, it is 14.3% faster than the strongest competing corrector Domino and 22.6% faster than uncorrected DFlash (Tab. 1).

The Decisive Difference Revealed Under Concurrency

LLM serving batches concurrent requests to raise GPU utilization. As concurrency grows, the verifier’s cycle time is amortized across streams, so the share of overhead the corrector adds per cycle keeps growing. This is exactly the graveyard of sequential correctors.

On Qwen3-8B (thinking off), DCOCO records the highest throughput across the entire range of concurrency from 4 to 32 streams, with a margin over the strongest baseline of +16.6%→+23.0% at $T{=}0$ and +16.1%→+12.4% at $T{=}1$ (Tab. 8). By contrast, Domino and DSpark keep an almost unchanged acceptance length, yet accumulate sequential-correction overhead and eventually become slower than uncorrected DFlash.

Fig. 3 makes this phenomenon clear. The vertical axis is the ratio relative to DFlash, the solid line is the acceptance length $\tau$, the dashed line is throughput, and the shaded region is the gap between them (= the corrector’s per-cycle overhead). Domino’s $\tau$ curve stays above parity (1.0), but its throughput curve slides below — overhead has swallowed the acceptance gain. In contrast, DCOCO’s two curves move nearly together with a thin shaded region and remain above parity. This phenomenon reproduces across all four backbones (App. B).

Path Selection and Ablation

Comparing path selection rules (§4.3) on the same learned score grid, Global-Sum (maximizing the total sum) yields lower $\tau$ and TPS than greedy on all 9 suites. Geometric discount ($\lambda=0.75$) is comparable to greedy in acceptance length (average 5.258 vs 5.254), but greedy achieves +2.8% on average higher throughput. In the end, greedy wins with its $O(BK)$ walk and no discount hyperparameter (Tab. 3).

Ablation (App. A) validates the corrector’s two input paths.

  • Removing the pair state: acceptance length $-$7.3%/$-$5.6% ($T{=}0$/$T{=}1$), throughput $-$6.3%/$-$4.6%.
  • Removing the candidate representation: acceptance length $-$4.8%/$-$3.7%, throughput $-$4.6%/$-$3.3%.
  • Freezing the backbone (fixing the drafter for 6 epochs and training only the corrector): throughput $-$15.9%/$-$12.9%.

That is, both input paths are essential, and their contribution is largest on math and code. Co-adaptation is also key: even with a frozen backbone the corrector is a pure drop-in that yields +4.4% TPS over DFlash, but it is 15.9% below joint training. Conversely, extending the baselines to 12 epochs improves them by no more than 2%, confirming that DCOCO’s gain comes from the corrector itself, not from “training budget” (Tab. 4).

Our Take: Strengths, Limitations, and Why This Research Matters

Strengths

  1. A clean answer to “restoring dependencies without sequencing.” Whereas DSpark and Domino take the compromise of “parallel draft + sequential correction,” DCOCO revives dependencies without sacrificing parallelism. The separation of fully parallel neural scoring with only an $O(BK)$ selection walk is this paper’s most elegant contribution (§1, §3).
  2. Redefining the problem as “re-selection.” It is decisive that correction is reduced not to “generating new tokens” but to “re-selecting among the existing top-$K$ candidates.” The measurement of top-16 coverage 75.5% vs top-1 40.0% (Fig. 1) shows that this redefinition is not vacuous but grounded in real headroom.
  3. Honesty about metrics. The design of using TPS as the primary metric and $\tau$ as the mechanism metric probes exactly the trap of correctors that “raise acceptance length but lose in wall-clock time.” The fact that the concurrency experiment demonstrates this trade-off makes the paper’s conclusion a system-level claim, not a single benchmark number.
  4. Low cost. On Qwen3-8B the corrector is only about 2.23M parameters (drafter $d=4096$, 5 layers), and its per-cycle cost is merely 3–4% over uncorrected (App. A, §4.1). The concluding sentence “a correction made cheap enough is pure profit” is backed by the numbers.

Limitations

  1. Single GPU, single framework. All experiments were performed on a single NVIDIA B200 + vLLM 0.27.0 + TP=1 (§4, App. C). Behavior under multi-GPU tensor parallelism or other runtimes (e.g., TRT-LLM) is unverified.
  2. Single-seed training. Each method was trained once with seed 42, and variance across training seeds was not measured (App. A). The standard deviation for $T{=}1$ is only over “3 generation seeds,” not variability across independent training runs.
  3. Room to argue over baseline fairness. Comparisons use “each method’s native configuration,” and DCOCO uses 6+6 epochs (drafter 6 + joint 6) whereas the baselines use 6 epochs. The authors defend fairness by showing that extended training gives the baselines less than 2% gain (Tab. 4), but this can still be a point of contention for readers demanding “exactly the same block size and the same budget.”
  4. Drafter dependence. DCOCO is built on top of a specific parallel drafter, DFlash. Transfer to other parallel/diffusion drafters is natural but not empirically demonstrated, and sensitivity sweeps for hyperparameters such as block size, $K$, and $\rho$ are limited.
  5. Limits on open-ended chat. Math and code speed up to 3.7–6.1×, but open-ended chat like MT-Bench and Alpaca stays at 1.8–1.9× (§4.1). This is a limitation of the drafter’s base acceptance rate itself, a structure DCOCO amplifies rather than overcomes.

Why It Matters

The real contribution of this research is not a specific number but a perspective that flips the problem. It replaces the implicit premise that “reversing the weakness of parallel drafting (intra-block independence) requires sequencing” with “the correct answer is already in the candidate pool, and scoring adjacent transitions in parallel restores it without sequencing.” And by showing that this replacement shines even under concurrent load — indeed all the more so — it draws the practical conclusion that “making correction cheap is the pure profit of speculative decoding.” At a time when speculative decoding is becoming standard in real serving stacks, this approach, which fills the last weakness of parallel drafting, is worth attention.

What’s Next?: The Road Ahead

The authors do not explicitly lay out a grand future roadmap, but next steps follow naturally from the paper’s limitations and structure.

  1. Generalization to other drafters and backends. The most direct task is to verify whether DCOCO’s “parallel scoring + prefix-first walk” still holds an advantage on parallel drafters other than DFlash (e.g., other diffusion/CTC-based ones) and under multi-GPU and other runtimes.
  2. Systematic sweeps of $K$, block size, and $\rho$. The number of top-$K$ candidates and the exponential decay $\rho$ are the knobs that directly control the trade-off between “candidate headroom” and “scoring cost.” Quantifying their cost-acceptance curves would yield tuning guidance for deployment.
  3. Adaptive candidate counts. It is promising to exploit the fact that coverage drops sharply with slot depth (Fig. 1) in reverse, reducing scoring cost by using a small $K$ for shallow slots and a large $K$ for deep slots.
  4. Acceptance-rate-based training weights. The current exponential weight with $\rho=4$ is a “fixed proxy” for prefix survival. Estimating actual acceptance probabilities and making the per-position training weights data-adaptive is the logical follow-up (explicitly mentioned in §3.2).
  5. Designs targeting batch serving. Since the concurrency experiment already shows that correction overhead is the deciding variable, system optimizations that fuse scoring more finely at the CUDA-kernel level or exploit shared computation within a mini-batch will be the source of the next gain.

In short, DCOCO has offered a new baseline for speculative decoding: “the cheapest way to recover the lost context of parallel drafting.” What comes next will be extending this idea to more diverse hardware, drafters, and load conditions to draw the boundary of the proposition that “correction is always pure profit.”

item.title: Towards Looped Models Done Right, Part II: Rethinking at Fixed Points
item.description:
Paper

TL;DR

In looped language models, the state converges to a fixed point $z^\star = F_\theta(z^\star; x)$ as the recursion depth grows, and near the fixed point the “endpoint” can stand in for the entire trajectory. This paper uses that one property to reduce four different costs at once across pretraining, serving, and RL: (1) training backpropagates only through the last $b$ recursions (truncated BPTT), (2) decoding caches only the last KV bank for each token (terminal KV sharing, a $3\times$ cut in cache), (3) prefill is distilled into a lightweight student that predicts the fixed point directly, giving up to a $1.79\times$ speedup, and (4) RL reuses gradients from stored rollout states to make updates $2\times$ faster. It also improves the two devices that actually produce this fixed point — the depth prior and input injection — as a “learned prior” and “orthogonal injection (OrthoInj)” respectively, lowering perplexity across the whole range from 100M to 1.6B parameters (source: §1).

Core Idea

The claim of this work can be summarized in one sentence: “If you just train properly to create a fixed point, you can remove most of the ‘cost proportional to depth’ that loop models pay.”

Concretely, it splits into two branches.

  • Four shortcuts the fixed point provides (source: §3): The fact that the endpoint can stand in for the trajectory translates directly into cost savings at each stage — training, inference, and post-training — as shown through theory (a Lemma) and experiments.
  • Improving the two devices that create the fixed point (source: §4): What actually forms the fixed point are the depth prior (at which depth supervision is received) and input injection (how the input persists at the fixed point); existing options (Huginn’s PLN prior, Parcae’s injection) each have limitations, so this work replaces them with a learned prior and orthogonal injection.

Background: The Problem They Solved

In Loop Models, “Depth” Is Cost

Looped language models apply the same layer block repeatedly (source: §2). Starting with the Universal Transformer, recent work such as Huginn and Ouro uses them for test-time compute scaling and latent reasoning. The essential cost of this structure, however, arises “on every iteration” (source: §1):

  • Training: The full recursion must be stored and backpropagated, so activation memory scales with depth.
  • Decoding: Each recursion uses its own KV, so the KV cache grows with depth.
  • Prefill: Every recursion must be run for each prompt token.
  • RL: Every rollout must re-run the recursion for scoring.

“Should We Learn a Fixed Point?” Is Still Unresolved

The field has split into two camps (source: §1). One gives up on the fixed point and fixes the number of loops to a small value (Loopie, Smelt, Ouro). The other deliberately forms a fixed point and loops deeply (the DEQ, STaR, EQR line). This paper pushes the latter camp’s position that the fixed point is the key to cost reduction.

The core observation is empirical. Terminal KV sharing (reusing only the last KV) barely degrades GSM8K performance in Huginn, but collapses at four loops in Ouro. This difference aligns exactly with whether the state converges: Huginn’s state approaches a fixed point, while Ouro’s does not (source: §1, §2).

What Is a Fixed Point

Let the state after $r$ recursions for input $x=(x_1,\dots,x_N)$ be $z^r=(\mathbf{H}^r, C^r)$. Here $\mathbf{H}^r$ is the hidden state and $C^r$ is the KV bank recorded at the $r$-th update. The shared update map $F_\theta$ defines $z^{r+1}=F_\theta(z^r;x)$, and if $F_\theta(z^\star;x)=z^\star$ holds, then $z^\star$ is the fixed point (source: §2).

Convergence is measured by the per-token relative change $\rho_{r,t}=\lVert h_t^r-h_t^{r-1}\rVert_2/(\lVert h_t^{r-1}\rVert_2+\epsilon)$ ($\epsilon=10^{-8}$). An important finding: convergence is heterogeneous. Even within the same sequence, tokens converge at different depths, the order is not causal, and the Spearman correlation between convergence depth and position is a weak $0.14$ (source: §2). This heterogeneity is exactly why “which depth receives supervision” matters.

Experimental Model Configuration

The experiments are run on a dense Llama-block loop model based on Huginn (source: §5.1, Tab. 1). The layout is 1+2×R+1: one prelude block → a 2-block recursion core repeated $R$ times → one coda block. That is, $R=5$ recursions give a logical depth of $12$ blocks. There are three scales: Small (100M, 21.5B tokens), Medium (400M, 85.9B), and Large (1.6B, 343.6B). They use the Jais64k tokenizer, the TxT360 multilingual mixture, a sequence length of 8,192, and AdamW with a WSD schedule.

New Approach: Learned Depth Prior + Orthogonal Input Injection (OrthoInj)

To actually get the benefits of the fixed point, training must form it. The two devices governing its formation are the depth prior and input injection, and this paper improves both.

1) Learned Depth Prior — Learning “Which Depth to Supervise”

The sampled training depth determines “how converged the state is when supervision arrives,” and therefore how well it tolerates terminal KV sharing (source: §4.1).

  • Fixed-depth training: Concentrating supervision on a single depth gives the best predictions at that depth, but it breaks KV sharing. In the 1.6B model, sharing halves GSM8K from $50.6 \to 21.2$ (source: §1).
  • Huginn’s PLN prior: Spreading depth over a shifted Poisson–lognormal distribution supports sharing, but dilutes supervision at the target depth below the level sharing requires.

The authors therefore learn the depth prior. Instead of PLN, they place a categorical distribution $p_\phi=\operatorname{softmax}(\phi)$ over the depth set $\mathcal R=\{1,\dots,R_{\max}\}$ and update the logits $\phi$ from prediction feedback (source: §4.1, Alg. 1):

$$ \mathcal J_{\mathrm{prior}}(\phi) = -\widehat{\mathbb E}{n}\bigl[\operatorname{sg}(A_n)\log p\phi(r)\bigr]

  • \lambda_H, H(p_\phi)
  • \lambda_m\bigl(\mathbb E_{p_\phi}[R] - \bar R\bigr)^2 $$

The role of the three terms is clear.

  • Prediction quality: For each microbatch, sample a depth $r$, map the next-token CE $\ell$ at that depth to a reward $u=\exp(-\ell)$ (inverse perplexity), center it with an EMA baseline, rescale it PopArt-style, and multiply by the advantage $A_n$. Depths that predict well get higher probability.
  • Entropy regularization $H(p_\phi)=-\sum_r p_\phi(r)\log p_\phi(r)$: With feedback alone, supervision concentrates on a narrow depth and fixed-point formation weakens. Increasing $\lambda_H$ spreads the allocation toward deeper depths (the region where the settled prefix context supports sharing). In other words, $\lambda_H$ is the knob that trades off performance against memory efficiency.
  • Budget control: Keeps the expected depth from drifting away from the target $\bar R$. Since the prior is used only in training, this term pins the forward-pass compute to $\bar R$.

Unlike RL-Halting and Ouro’s “state-dependent exit distribution,” this prior is unconditional, so (1) it can start from a predefined prior (PLN), (2) it saves compute by running the forward pass only to the sampled depth, and (3) it does not decide the stopping point at inference, allowing the entropy term to deliberately increase KV sharing (source: §6, Appx.).

2) Orthogonal Input Injection (OrthoInj) — Making “the Input Remain Intact at the Fixed Point”

Input injection adds the embedding to every recursion so that the fixed point is conditioned on the input. The general additive form is $\zeta_t^r = M h_t^r + q_t$ (source: §4.2). Here $M$ controls the state carryover and $q_t$ is the injection vector. Parcae uses a diagonal carryover $M=\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\exp(-\Delta\odot\alpha))$ (entries of $\Lambda$ in $(0,1)$, $\lVert\Lambda\rVert_2<1$).

The problem is that the carryover $\Lambda h_t^r$ can have a component along the injection vector $q_t$. Depending on the sign of this component, it amplifies or cancels the input. Measured on Parcae-Decay, the cosine between the carryover and $q_t$ reaches $0.81/0.87/0.91$ for S/M/L, so the input enters the core at $2.2\times/2.8\times/3.4\times$ its injected magnitude (source: Appx.). OrthoInj projects out this component:

$$ \zeta_t^r = Q_{q_t}\Lambda h_t^r + q_t, \qquad Q_{q_t} = I - \frac{q_t q_t^{\top}}{\lVert q_t\rVert_2^2 + \epsilon} $$

$Q_{q_t}$ is the projection that removes the component along $q_t$. As a result, at every recursion (including the fixed point), the component of $\zeta_t^r$ along $q_t$ becomes exactly $q_t$, and only the orthogonal component evolves freely. Since $\lVert Q_{q_t}\rVert_2\le1$, the contraction property of the carryover ($\lVert Q_{q_t}\Lambda\rVert_2\le\lVert\Lambda\rVert_2<1$) is also preserved.

How It Works: A Concrete Example

Toy Example: The Fixed Point of a Contraction Map

Let us look at the idea with a very simple one-dimensional map. If the state update is $z^{r+1} = 0.5\, z^r + 3$ and $z^0=0$, then the fixed point is $z^\star = 0.5 z^\star + 3 \Rightarrow z^\star = 6$. Running the iteration gives:

$r$ 0 1 2 3 4 5 …
$z^r$ 0 3 4.5 5.25 5.625 5.8125 $\to 6$

Because the contraction factor $a=0.5<1$, the difference between adjacent states shrinks geometrically: $|z^{r+1}-z^r|=0.5^r \cdot 3$. That is, near the fixed point the state barely changes no matter how much more you iterate. This is the principle shared by every shortcut in this paper: you can use the endpoint $z^\star$ instead of the trajectory.

The same story holds from the gradient perspective. Differentiating the loss with respect to $z^\star$ gives $\mathrm dz^\star/\mathrm d b = 1/(1-a)=2$, which is the sum of the Neumann series $1+a+a^2+\cdots$. In practice, this infinite sum can be cut off at $b$ terms (truncation), and the error $a^b$ shrinks geometrically in $b$ (source: §3.1).

How This Principle Becomes Four Shortcuts

  1. Training — truncated BPTT: Instead of backpropagating through all $R$ recursions, backpropagating through only the last $b$ suffices. Near the fixed point the visited states converge to $z^\star$, so the TBPTT gradient converges to a truncated Neumann estimate of the equilibrium gradient (implicit gradient) (source: §3.1, eq. 1). The surprising part is that truncation itself forms the fixed point. At a fixed depth of $R=5$, full BPTT raises perplexity by more than $25\%$ when extrapolated to $R=64$ and by $21\%$ under terminal KV sharing, whereas TBPTT backpropagating only the last 2 ($b=2$) raises them by no more than $2\%$ and $3\%$, respectively (source: §3.1).

  2. Decoding — terminal KV sharing: Keep only the last KV bank of each prefix token, and let all recursions of subsequent tokens read from it. At $R=5$, keeping only $4$ of $12$ banks cuts the cache by $3\times$, and the perplexity increase is no more than $0.85\%$ (source: §3.2). Theoretically, the Lemma supports this: if the prefix KV converges to $C^\star_{\lt t}$ and the update map is contractive with $\kappa<1$, then “joint iteration” and “frozen-prefix decoding” converge to the same fixed point $h^\star$ and give the same next-token distribution (source: §3.2, Lemma 1).

  3. Prefill — distillation: Since decoding reads only the last bank, prefill need not “reproduce all KV of every recursion” — it only needs to predict the endpoint. A lightweight student $S_\psi$ predicts $\widehat z = S_\psi(e)\approx z_\theta^R(x)$ from the prelude output $e$, and the teacher applies one recursion to $\widehat z$ to produce all KV banks. The loss is a normalized hidden-state regression plus a next-token KL:

$$ \mathcal L_{\mathrm{distill}}(\psi) = \mathbb E_x\left[ \frac{\lVert\widehat z - z_\theta^R(x)\rVert_F^2}{N d \sigma_T^2}

  • \frac{1}{N}\sum_{t=1}^{N}\operatorname{KL}\bigl(p_t ,\Vert, \widehat p_t\bigr) \right] $$

Since the student is initialized from the teacher’s recursion core, before training it roughly outputs “the state after 1 recursion,” and the loss pushes this toward the depth-$R$ endpoint (source: §3.2, §5.5).

  1. RL — reusing rollout states: RL typically runs the forward pass twice (once for sampling, once for scoring). Near the fixed point, it computes the Neumann-$(b-1)$ gradient directly from the stored endpoint $z^R$ without re-running the recursion (source: §3.1, Alg. 2). Run the recursion block through $z^R$ only once to record its autograd graph, then iterate $v \leftarrow g + J_R^{\top} v$ for $b-1$ steps to obtain the gradient. The update cost becomes independent of $R$.

Validating Performance: Key Results

Depth Prior: Superior Across All Scales While Preserving Sharing

Four priors (fixed $R{=}5$, fixed PLN-5, learned $\lambda_H{=}0$, learned $\lambda_H{=}0.01$) were compared at an average depth of 5 (source: §5.2, Tab. 3).

  • Fixed-depth training breaks KV sharing: Under sharing, GSM8K drops by more than half at M and L, and perplexity is the highest.
  • The learned prior lowers validation PPL by $0.7$–$1.8\%$ versus fixed PLN-5 (using only up to $1.6\%$ extra training FLOPs), and the downstream average is higher at every scale.
  • The entropy term is essential at L: Without it, GSM8K drops from $47.92 \to 36.47$ (source: §5.2).
  • It dominates Untied 4 at the same physical depth and approaches Untied 12 at the same logical depth: The downstream-average lead grows from $2.2 \to 5.0 \to 8.9$ points for S→M→L. At L, the gap to Untied 12 narrows to $1.5$ points downstream average and $0.9$ points on GSM8K (source: §5.2).

In other words, at 1.6B the learned prior matches the downstream average of fixed-depth training with the full cache, using a $3\times$ smaller KV cache (source: §1, Tab. 3).

The training curves and depth distributions are shown in the figures below. Fixed depth piles up at one point, fixed PLN spreads widely, and the learned prior shifts mass between them toward “depths with good predictions.”

Increasing the entropy coefficient $\lambda_H$ from $0$ to $0.1$ shrinks $p_\phi(5)$ from $67.4\% \to 14.0\%$, spreading supervision toward deeper depths. As a result, the KV sharing penalty decreases monotonically (from $+0.96\% \to -0.22\%$ under sharing), and while PPL at $R=5$ rises slightly, PPL at deeper depths ($R=32$) falls — a clear trade-off between performance and memory (source: Appx.).

Orthogonal Injection: Beating the Strongest Baseline (Parcae)

OrthoInj is compared against DEQ-QKV, Huginn-Linear, and Parcae-Decay (source: §5.3, Tab. 2):

  • It lowers validation PPL by $0.3$–$1.4\%$ versus the strongest baseline, Parcae-Decay.
  • It has the highest downstream average at every scale, and the training loss at the end of training is also the lowest at every scale.

Each of the two switches (orthogonal projection, removing the prelude RMSNorm) lowers the loss, and their effects add up (source: Appx.).

RL: Reusing Rollout States Speeds Up Updates by $2\times$

The L learned-prior model was fine-tuned with Dr. GRPO at $R=6$ for comparison (source: §5.4, Tab. 4).

  • Reuse + Neumann-4 cuts scoring and backprop time by $1.99\times$ (GSM8K) and $2.02\times$ (MBPP+).
  • All four methods raise GSM8K pass@1 from $40.6\% \to 60$–$63\%$ and MBPP+ from $30.9\% \to 37$–$41\%$.
  • Accuracy is within run-to-run variance of BPTT: The gradient cosine between the reuse and recompute controls is $0.997$–$0.999$, essentially identical, so the pass@1 gap ($1.6$ points on GSM8K) is at the level of run-to-run variation (source: §5.4).
  • On MATH500, which is not trained in RL, transfer of $3.9$–$5.4$ points still occurs.

Distilled Prefill: Trading Latency for Accuracy

The learned-prior model was distilled into a 2-block student (using only $1/4$ of the teacher’s pretraining tokens) (source: §5.5, Tab. 5).

  • Up to $1.79\times$ faster prefill on 8K prompts (S $1.55\times$, M $1.66\times$, L $1.79\times$).
  • The downstream-average loss is $1.0$ (S), $2.3$ (M), and $4.5$ (L) points, growing with scale.
  • At the same latency it beats stopping the teacher early: It is $0.5$–$0.9$ points higher than an $R=2$ teacher.
  • Teacher initialization is the key to quality, and the KL term lifts generation performance (source: Tab. 6).

That prefill depth and decode depth can be separated (thanks to terminal sharing) is also an interesting result. As the figure below shows, the prefill gain saturates at $R_{\mathrm{pre}}=5$, whereas decode depth has a much larger effect (source: Appx.).

Our Perspective: Strengths, Limitations, and Why This Work Matters

Strengths: One Principle Cuts Through Many Problems

The greatest virtue of this paper is that it organizes four different cost problems under a single concept (the fixed point). Truncated BPTT and terminal KV sharing are shortcuts that already existed, but the authors explain “why these work” through the single framework of fixed-point convergence, and from there naturally derive two new shortcuts (distilled prefill, rollout-state reuse) (source: §1, §3). This is a rare structure in which explanatory power leads directly to new invention.

The theory–experiment alignment is also strong. The Lemma proves the limit in which “if the prefix converges, terminal sharing holds without loss,” and experiments show that the sharing penalty decreases from $0.85\%$ to $0.11\%$ as $R$ grows, matching qualitatively (source: §3.2, Appx.).

Finally, the framing that “what forms the fixed point is training design such as truncation, the depth prior, and injection” is practically very powerful. Simply reducing $b$ creates the fixed point, and the learned prior and orthogonal injection are layered on top, so each improvement connects to a clear mechanism.

Limitations: The Limits of Scale and Evidence Are Clear

The points worth criticizing are also clear.

  • Scale: At most $1.6$B parameters, a single seed per configuration, and a single multilingual mixture. Whether these gains hold at 7B and above remains open (source: §7).
  • Scaling of the distillation gap: The downstream loss of distilled prefill grows with scale — $1.0 \to 2.3 \to 4.5$ points for S→M→L. If this trend continues, distillation may become less attractive for large models, and the authors explicitly acknowledge this (source: §5.5, §7). Indeed, distilling an $R=25$ teacher is faster but loses more quality.
  • Breadth of evaluation: Downstream tasks are centered on relatively “easy” tasks (LAMBADA, PIQA, ARC, etc.), and validation on strong reasoning benchmarks (hard coding/math) is limited.
  • Assumptions: The theory (Lemma) relies on contractiveness ($\kappa<1$) and local Lipschitz conditions, but verifying or guaranteeing these in real large transformers is a separate matter.

Why It Matters

The goal of “decoupling inference cost from depth” has direct value in today’s era of LLM serving and agents. In particular, the result of cutting the cache by $3\times$ via terminal KV sharing while barely losing accuracy, and the result of speeding up RL updates by $2\times$, squarely target two practical pain points: the memory bottleneck and the post-training bottleneck. Moreover, the framework is not confined to a specific model (Huginn) but applies to recurrent structures whose states converge in general.

What’s Next?: The Road Ahead

Open questions the authors themselves leave, together with directions that follow naturally from the limitations:

  • Larger scale: How the four shortcuts scale beyond 1.6B to 7B and above is the top validation task (source: §7).
  • Better distillation: MoE student architectures, reallocating the distillation token budget, and better loss objectives can narrow the distillation gap. Furthermore, using the student as a standalone language model or as a drafter for speculative decoding, and connecting recurrent state refinement to flow-based language modeling, are future tasks the authors leave (source: §5.5, §3.2).
  • Robustness and practical deployment: Beyond the single-seed, single-dataset limitation, reproduction across multiple configurations and datasets and validation of real-service deployability are needed (source: §7).

In one sentence, this paper transforms the rather academic concept of “the fixed point of loop models” into a practical engine that simultaneously reduces the costs of training, serving, and post-training. Whether those gains hold robustly at large scale will decide the fate of this approach.

item.title: SparseDecoding: Decoding-Aware Pruning for Accurate and Efficient LLM Inference
item.description:
Paper

TL;DR

Observing that LLM autoregressive decoding is memory-bound, this work collects the calibration for pruning not from “fixed text” but from “tokens the model generates itself,” and attaches a decoding-specific (SpMV) $N{:}M$ kernel to it, achieving up to $1.48\times$ end-to-end decoding speedup.

Key Idea

The blind spots of existing training-free pruning fall into two branches. One is the mismatch of data distribution. OBS-family pruning such as SparseGPT computes the Hessian from activations collected over fixed text like C4 and WikiText. In actual inference, however, the model feeds its own just-generated tokens back as input. The Hessian computed from fixed text and the Hessian computed from generated tokens diverge, and as a result the activation distribution of the pruned model drifts further and further from what it was at pruning time (source: §1, Fig. 1a).

The other is a gap at the system layer. Existing $2{:}4$ Sparse Tensor Core kernels (cuSPARSELt, etc.) are optimized for SpMM (matrix×matrix), delivering $1.31\sim1.46\times$ speedup in the prefill stage, but in SpMV (matrix×vector), which dominates decoding, they actually become slower than dense, at $0.85\sim0.87\times$ (source: §1, Fig. 1b).

SparseDecoding solves both problems at once along the algorithm axis (decoding-aware calibration) and the system axis (N:M SpMV kernel).

Background: The Problem They Solved

In long-output applications such as document writing and code generation, autoregressive decoding accounts for most of the LLM inference cost. Decoding processes hidden states one token at a time, so it is bound by memory bandwidth. Pruning is the most natural remedy: it zeros out low-importance weights, reducing the number of nonzero elements that must be read from memory during decoding (source: §1).

The problem is that, because of training cost and data constraints, training-free (one-shot) pruning is effectively the standard for LLMs. The OBS (Optimal Brain Surgeon) framework, the best-known member of this family, minimizes the per-layer reconstruction error via a second-order Taylor approximation, where the calibration activations determine “which weights to remove and how to correct the remaining weights” through the Hessian $H = 2X_\ell X_\ell^\top$ (source: §3.1). In other words, the calibration data is what governs pruning quality.

Yet existing methods feed fixed sequences via teacher forcing to collect activations. This suits static-input inference, but in autoregressive decoding, pruning errors in the early stages change the subsequent context, and the effect accumulates so that the activation distribution gradually drifts away. The authors measured that this divergence grows quickly enough that every layer reaches 90% of its peak within 12 decoding steps (source: §1, Fig. 1a).

The New Approach: SparseDecoding

Algorithm Axis: Decoding-Aware Calibration

The core idea is simple. Collect the activations used for pruning from the dense model’s own autoregressive generation process — but discard the prefill-stage activations and keep only the decoding-stage activations (source: §3.2).

Concretely, for a prompt set $\mathcal{C}=\{q_m\}_{m=1}^{K}$ from the target task, the dense model generates the continuation of each prompt by itself.

$$ y_t^{(m)} \sim P_\theta\big(\cdot \mid q_m,\, y_{\lt t}^{(m)}\big) $$

After distinguishing the prefill positions $\mathcal{P}_m$ and the decoding positions $\mathcal{D}_m$ of prompt $q_m$, it records the input activation $x_{\ell,t}^{(m)}$ of each linear layer $\ell$ targeted for pruning, and gathers only those with $t\in\mathcal{D}_m$ to form the matrix.

$$ X_\ell^{\mathrm{AR}} = \big[\,x_{\ell,t}^{(m)}\,\big]_{m=1,\ldots,K;\; t\in\mathcal{D}_m} $$

Then the same per-layer reconstruction objective as before is defined over these activations.

$$ \widehat{W}_{\ell} = \operatorname*{argmin}_{\widetilde{W}_{\ell}} \left\lVert \left( W_{\ell} - \widetilde{W}_{\ell} \right) X_{\ell}^{\mathrm{AR}} \right\rVert_{F}^{2} \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \operatorname{sparsity}(\widetilde{W}_{\ell}) = S_{\ell} $$

The pruning solver itself is left untouched; only the calibration matrix changes. The authors confirmed that the same gains appear with either the SparseGPT or Wanda solver (source: §4.4, Tab. 5). No additional training and no new optimizer are required.

System Axis: N:M SpMV Kernel

For pruning to translate into real speed, the sparse pattern must be executed efficiently on hardware. Decoding processes a single vector at batch-one or small batch, so it is closer to GEMV/SpMV. Inspired by nmSPARSE, the authors designed a decoding-specific $N{:}M$ SpMV kernel (source: §3.3). Two design principles stand out.

  1. Bitmask indexing: By representing each row’s sparse pattern as a bitmask, instead of storing a separate 32-bit int32 index for every nonzero element, one bit maps to one column. At 50% sparsity, 2 bits of metadata per nonzero element suffices. That is 16× less than nmSPARSE’s int32 and 4× less than a uint8 offset, which is especially favorable for memory-bound batch-one decoding (source: §3.3).
  2. Fixed-step traversal: For 50% $N{:}M$ with $M\le32$, each aligned 32-bit mask has exactly 16 set bits. Every row then has the same number of traversal steps, evening out the workload across GPU threads and letting the compiler fully unroll the loop. Each step finds the column of the next nonzero via bit-scan and clears that bit.

How It Works: A Concrete Example

Intuition for Bitmask Traversal

Suppose one row of the weight matrix has 8 weights and $4{:}8$ sparsity is applied (4 kept per group of 8). Say the original weights are as follows.

PLAINTEXT 
column index: 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7
weight: 0.8 0.1 0.9 0.2 0.7 0.3 0.6 0.4
column index: 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7
weight: 0.8 0.1 0.9 0.2 0.7 0.3 0.6 0.4

If after pruning 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, and 0.4 are removed and only 0.8, 0.9, 0.7, and 0.6 remain, the bitmask with “keep=1, remove=0” becomes as follows.

PLAINTEXT 
bitmask: 1 0 1 0 1 0 1 0 → 01010101 (0x55; column 0 = least significant bit)
stored values: [0.8, 0.9, 0.7, 0.6] (ascending column order)
bitmask: 1 0 1 0 1 0 1 0 → 01010101 (0x55; column 0 = least significant bit)
stored values: [0.8, 0.9, 0.7, 0.6] (ascending column order)

During decoding, this row is multiplied with the input vector. With the traditional scheme, the column index would have to be read separately for each stored value, but in the bitmask scheme the position of a set bit is itself the column index. The kernel finds the lowest set bit via bit-scan in a fixed-length loop to learn the column, clears that bit, and moves on. The traversal of a row is fixed at the number of stored values (4 in this example, 16 in a 32-bit mask), so every thread carries the same workload.

Intuition for Calibration

Conventional C4 calibration feeds “ground-truth text” to collect activations. SparseDecoding instead gives the prompt (“Write the preface to a long fantasy novel”), lets the dense model actually write the novel, and then builds the Hessian from the decoding activations of that generation process. Pruning is then aligned with “the state the model actually encounters.” The reason for discarding prefill activations is that decoding is a special state of token-level self-conditioning (source: §3.2).

Performance Validation: Main Results

1) Decoding Speedup (Speed)

N:M Llama-3.1-8B (tok/s) Llama-3.3-70B Qwen3-14B Qwen3-32B
Dense 96.26 21.67 39.76 19.15
2:4 136.30 (1.42×) 30.17 (1.39×) 53.18 (1.34×) 27.69 (1.45×)
4:8 136.43 (1.42×) 31.64 (1.46×) 53.86 (1.35×) 27.83 (1.45×)
8:16 136.89 (1.42×) 29.90 (1.38×) 53.42 (1.34×) 27.77 (1.45×)
16:32 136.89 (1.42×) 32.13 (1.48×) 53.73 (1.35×) 27.81 (1.45×)

Since every pattern keeps 50% of the weights, the differences between patterns are differences in kernel efficiency, and all patterns are faster than dense. Context 512, A100 80GB, GPT-Fast (source: §4.3, Tab. 3). This is the exact opposite of the earlier finding that the existing $2{:}4$ Sparse Tensor Core was slower than dense at decoding (Fig. 1b).

2) Generation Quality (WritingBench, 1–10 points)

WritingBench is a long-form writing benchmark spanning 6 domains, 100 subdomains, and 1,000 prompts (source: §4.1). SparseDecoding beats C4 calibration across every model and every sparsity.

Model Dense C4 (50%) Ours (50%) C4 (2:4) Ours (2:4)
Llama-3.1-8B 3.70 2.25 2.54 1.34 1.52
Llama-3.3-70B 4.65 3.82 4.01 3.10 3.29
Qwen3-14B 5.97 4.62 5.35 1.85 4.18
Qwen3-32B 6.48 5.34 6.09 2.99 5.31

The most dramatic point is $2{:}4$ sparsity in the Qwen family. C4 effectively collapses quality, at 1.85 for Qwen3-14B and 2.99 for Qwen3-32B, whereas SparseDecoding lifts them to 4.18 and 5.31, respectively (source: Tab. 1). In the Llama family the gains are relatively small (1.34→1.52, etc.), which ties into the limitations discussed below.

3) Code Generation Generalization (ClassEval)

The same procedure works for code generation as well (only the calibration prompts are swapped for LiveCodeBench problems). It leads by 4–15 points across all 8 model-sparsity combinations. Notably, at $2{:}4$ sparsity, while C4 gives Pass@1 = 0.0% on Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen3-14B, SparseDecoding recovers 4.0% and 6.0% (source: §4.2, Tab. 2). This is evidence that “how the calibration is collected” is as decisive as “which text the calibration is.”

4) Theoretical Justification

In the appendix, the authors define the calibration discrepancy $\epsilon_{\ell,C}^{(k)}$ and prove that it is exactly equal to “the worst-case relative error between the calibration objective and the reconstruction objective at decoding time” (source: Appx. A, Thm. 1). Empirically, the fraction of modules where AR calibration shows a smaller discrepancy than C4 reaches 87%–99%, with a median discrepancy ratio $\hat{\epsilon}_{\mathrm{C4}}/\hat{\epsilon}_{\mathrm{AR}}$ of 1.81–3.26. This is quantitative evidence that decoding-aware calibration is consistently closer to the decoding objective than fixed text is (source: Appx. A, Tab. 6–7).

5) Ablation: The Source of the Gain Is Not “What” but “Whom and How”

  • Self-generation vs cross-generation: Pruning a 14B model with a 32B model’s generated tokens underperforms self-generation (4.13 vs 4.18 at 2:4). Sequences produced by another model reintroduce the distribution gap (source: Tab. 4).
  • Solver-invariance: Even with Wanda, SparseDecoding leads consistently (Qwen3-14B at 2:4: C4 2.41 vs 3.30). The gain comes from the calibration activations, not the solver (source: Tab. 5).
  • Corpus-invariance: SparseDecoding also outperforms fixed corpora such as Pile and RedPajama (source: Tab. 9).

Our View: Strengths, Limitations, and Why This Research Matters

Strengths

The most praiseworthy aspect is that it aims precisely at the problem. It dismantles the long-taken-for-granted assumption that pruning presupposes “static input,” shifting to the perspective that “pruning must be aligned with the decoding state.” On top of that, its system design focuses on SpMV rather than SpMM to secure speed — a model example of not losing sight of the “measured wall-clock” that academic research often omits. The flow is clean: it shows with data that existing $2{:}4$ kernels became slower at decoding (Fig. 1b), then closes that gap with its own kernel.

Also, the low barrier to adoption — swap only the calibration matrix and it can sit on top of either the SparseGPT or Wanda solver — raises its practical value. The fact that it attaches theory (Thm. 1) to quantify “why it works” is also notable.

Limitations

There are several points worth fairly noting.

  1. Small gains on the Llama family. At $2{:}4$, Llama-3.1-8B goes 1.34→1.52 and Llama-3.3-70B 3.10→3.29, in contrast to the multi-point jumps of the Qwen family. This means calibration sensitivity varies greatly by model family and size, and there is a lack of condition analysis for “when it is effective” (source: Tab. 1).
  2. Calibration cost is quietly expensive. Since it must actually generate 1M tokens with the dense model, the upfront stage is heavier than streaming C4. No quantitative comparison of the gain against this cost is provided.
  3. Reliance on the evaluation judge. WritingBench is an LLM-as-judge benchmark using DeepSeek-V4-Flash as the judge, so the absolute scores (low values like 3.70) need to be interpreted with caution. Relative comparisons within the same judge and setting, however, remain valid.
  4. Sparsity is limited. Only $N{:}M$ 50% and unstructured 50% were covered. Whether this framework holds up under more aggressive sparsity (e.g., 75%+) is left open.
  5. Single GPU, A100 only. Even 70B was run on an A100, but it is unverified whether the SpMV kernel’s gain persists in a multi-GPU tensor-parallel environment (source: §4.1).

Why This Research Matters

Now that LLM inference cost has become the bottleneck in real-world use, this work strikes back at the perception that “pruning only makes things faster while ruining quality.” In particular, reframing the pruning quality problem not as a matter of “data selection” but as a matter of “how data is collected” is a general insight that can be reused for all “calibration-based compression” research — pruning, distillation, quantization, and beyond.

What’s Next?: The Road Ahead

The authors do not lay out a long list of explicit future plans, but in light of the limitations above, the natural next steps are visible.

  • Extending sparsity: Explore the quality-speed Pareto frontier beyond 50%, at 2/3 and 3/4 sparsity. The fixed-step property of bitmask traversal remains usable.
  • Condition analysis: Predict and verify “on which models and tasks decoding-aware calibration matters most” using the theoretical frame (the discrepancy of Thm. 1).
  • Multi-GPU scaling: Validate the SpMV kernel’s performance under tensor parallelism and pipeline parallelism, and check whether it can be integrated into production serving stacks (vLLM, etc.).
  • Combining with other compression techniques: Apply the “decoding-aware” principle to a broader pipeline, for example jointly with quantization or in interaction with speculative decoding.

This research, in which a single simple principle — collect calibration from “the state the model actually lives in” — lifts both quality and speed together, reminds us once again that in inference optimization the real goal is “measured wall-clock” rather than “theoretical FLOPs.”

item.title: MC-Sparse: Deconstructing and Closing the Dense-Sparse Attention Gap in Diffusion Transformers
item.description:
Paper

TL;DR

By making the attention of a diffusion transformer (DiT) sparse at the token level without training, while caching and reusing accurate KV selections and dense–sparse output residuals at anchor steps, it achieves up to a $2.32\times$ denoising speedup in video and 3D generation with no quality loss (source: Fig. teaser, §Abstract).

Key Idea

Sparse attention is the primary way to reduce the latency of diffusion transformers operating on long sequences, but the lower the density, the more the generation quality collapses. The key insight of this paper is that “the quality degradation of sparse attention is not a single problem of selection accuracy, but the result of three distinct errors compounding.”

  • Structural binding error: block-level selection drags in the irrelevant neighbors of important tokens, and queries with different attention patterns are forced to share a single selection (source: §Method).
  • Selection error: because important blocks are chosen using the approximation of mean-pooled scores, genuinely important interactions are missed (source: §Method).
  • Discarded tail error: tokens excluded from the selection still carry nonzero attention mass, so even with perfect selection a residual remains relative to the dense output (source: §Method).

MC-Sparse addresses these three errors with token-level KV selection, tile-aligned query grouping, and temporal residual compensation, respectively. And it solves the problem that this precise selection and grouping is expensive by exploiting the stability of attention across denoising steps: computing them only at anchor steps and reusing them at the remaining steps (source: §Intro).

Background: The Problem They Solved

Diffusion transformers have become the de facto standard backbone for video generation (HunyuanVideo, Wan2.1, MiniMax-H3) and 3D asset generation. But as resolution and duration grow, sequence length expands to tens to hundreds of thousands of tokens, and the quadratic cost of attention $O(n^2)$ becomes the main culprit behind inference latency (source: §Related Work).

Sparse attention is the natural solution to reduce this cost. Attention mass is indeed concentrated on a small number of token interactions. The problem is that aggressive sparsity causes generation quality to drop sharply.

Most existing methods use block sparse attention (BSA). Queries and keys are grouped into blocks, and for each query block a few important KV blocks are kept whole. This aligns well with GPU compute tiles and is fast, but it estimates block importance using mean-pooled query and key representations (source: §Intro).

The problem with this design is that two kinds of error are entangled. The authors point this out precisely.

“This design entangles two errors: the approximate score used to choose blocks, and the coarse block layout that itself limits which interactions can be chosen. As a result, it is hard to know how much of the quality gap comes from the selector, how much from the block structure, and how much remains even after improving both.” (source: §Intro)

In other words, without precisely dissecting “why sparse attention is worse than dense,” they bolted together a block structure and an approximate score, so it was impossible to know what to fix. This paper starts by dissecting this “dense–sparse gap” through controlled oracle comparisons.

A New Approach: MC-Sparse

MC-Sparse (Meta-Cached Sparse Attention) is a training-free method that unifies three design principles into a single framework (source: §Method).

  1. Token-level KV selection: select individual KV tokens rather than blocks, eliminating KV binding.
  2. Tile-aligned query grouping: group similar queries into tiles of exactly the same size ($C$), reducing query binding while aligning with GPU tiles.
  3. Temporal reuse of accurate selection + residual compensation: at anchor steps, choose KVs using accurate attention probabilities and record the dense–sparse output residual to reuse at subsequent steps.

The authors’ hypothesis, summarized in one sentence:

“By caching and reusing token-level selection based on accurate attention probabilities at anchor steps, one can simultaneously reduce the structural, selection, and tail errors of block sparse attention without training, obtaining results closer to the dense output and larger speedups.”

The key is metadata caching. At an anchor step, (the query grouping $\mathcal{G}$, the selected KV indices $\mathcal{S}$, the output residual $\mathbf{R}$) are cached, and at reuse steps this metadata is used as-is while only the attention is recomputed with the current $\mathbf{Q}, \mathbf{K}, \mathbf{V}$ (source: §Method, Alg. 1).

How It Works: A Concrete Example

First, let us examine the three errors with a $4\times4$ toy example. Suppose there are 4 queries ($q_1..q_4$) and 4 keys ($k_1..k_4$), the block size is 2, and the density budget is 50% (2 keys kept per query). Assume the attention mass matrix (each row sums to 1) is as follows.

$k_1$ $k_2$ $k_3$ $k_4$
$q_1$ 0.40 0.08 0.50 0.02
$q_2$ 0.08 0.40 0.50 0.02
$q_3$ 0.02 0.50 0.08 0.40
$q_4$ 0.02 0.50 0.08 0.40

Query block A = {$q_1,q_2$}, B = {$q_3,q_4$}; KV block 1 = {$k_1,k_2$}, 2 = {$k_3,k_4$}.

① Structural binding error (block oracle). The block mass of $q_1$ is 0.48 for block 1 and 0.52 for block 2, so block 2 is chosen. However, the true top 2 for $q_1$ are $k_3$(0.50) and $k_1$(0.40), summing to 0.90, and the block choice forcibly drags in the irrelevant $k_4$(0.02). This is KV binding. On top of this, although $q_1$ and $q_2$ in block A have opposite patterns ($q_1$ prefers $k_1$, $q_2$ prefers $k_2$), they are forced to share the same selection. This is query binding (source: Fig. sources_of_gap).

② Selection error (token oracle, shared query block). The per-key summed mass of block A is $k_3=1.00$, $k_1=0.48$, $k_2=0.48$, so the top 2 {$k_3,k_1$} are chosen. $q_1$ is perfect (0.90), but $q_2$ only gets 0.50+0.08=0.58. This differs by 0.32 from $q_2$’s true top 2 {$k_3,k_2$}=0.90. Mean-pooled scores make such omissions even worse, and the authors pinpoint the root cause with the following inequality (source: §Method).

$$ \operatorname{Softmax}\!\left(\bar{\mathbf{q}}_g \mathbf{K}^{\top}/\sqrt{d}\right)_j \;\neq\; \frac{1}{|\mathcal{G}_g|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{G}_g} A_{ij} $$

That is, scoring with the group-mean query and averaging the attention probabilities of individual queries yield different values.

③ Discarded tail error (per-query oracle). Even if each query chooses its own optimal 2 ($q_1$ gets 0.90, $q_2$ gets 0.90), a mass of 0.10 is discarded for each, leaving a residual relative to the dense output. Even perfect selection cannot close this error (source: Fig. sources_of_gap).

MC-Sparse addresses these three errors as follows (source: §Method).

Tile-aligned grouping — Fast PDDP. Similar queries must be grouped into exactly $C$ each to reduce query binding while aligning with kernel tiles. The problem is that standard clustering such as $k$-means cannot guarantee equal-sized groups, so padding to fit tiles increases the executed interactions (Align. 1.45~2.08). The authors use a median-split version of PDDP (principal direction divisive partitioning): sort each group along the principal component direction, then recursively split at the median so that every group has exactly $C$ members. Instead of a naive implementation that is expensive on GPUs, they develop Fast PDDP, which processes all heads in parallel via batched power iteration (source: §Method).

Accurate selection — two-pass selector. To compute attention mass accurately at anchor steps, probabilities are needed, but FlashAttention uses online softmax and does not expose logits. So it is handled in two passes: the first pass obtains the dense output and the log-sum-exp, and the second pass recomputes the QK scores to recover the probabilities, sums the per-group mass, and chooses the top-$K$. The dense matrix is never actually materialized (source: Appx. two-pass).

Residual compensation. At anchor step $\tau$, the following is recorded (source: §Method).

$$ \mathbf{R}_{\tau} = \mathbf{O}^{\mathrm{full}}_{\tau} - \mathbf{O}^{\mathrm{sparse}}_{\tau} $$

At a reuse step $t$, sparse attention is computed with the cached grouping and indices, and then the residual is added.

$$ \widehat{\mathbf{O}}_t = \operatorname{SparseAttn}\!\left(\mathbf{Q}_t,\mathbf{K}_t,\mathbf{V}_t;\ \mathcal{G}_{\tau},\mathcal{S}_{\tau}\right) + \mathbf{R}_{\tau} $$

The key evidence is the observation that the dense–sparse residual varies less across denoising steps than the attention output itself (source: Fig. residual_stability). The more stable the residual, the better the previous step’s residual approximates the next step’s tail error.

The overall pipeline alternates between anchor and reuse steps (source: Alg. 1, Fig. pipeline).

 flowchart TD
 A[Anchor step] --> B[Accurate selection via Dense Attention]
 B --> C[Cache query groups G · KV indices S · residual R]
 C --> D[Reuse step]
 D --> E[Sparse Attention with current Q, K, V + R]
 E --> D

Performance Validation: Main Results

The evaluation has two axes. Fidelity measures with PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS “how close the sparse output is to the dense-attention output.” Efficiency is measured by density, the fraction of retained interactions, and by the speedup over dense denoising (source: §Exp).

Video generation. On MiniMax-H3-Base (768p), MC-Sparse achieves $1.80\times$ at 15% density and $1.61\times$ at 25% density. Notably, at 15% density it records 27.30 dB PSNR, which is about 4 dB higher at a lower density than Sol-Attn (23.66 dB @ 32.4%) and PISA (23.45 dB @ 30.0%) (source: Tab. video, Fig. teaser). On HunyuanVideo-13B it achieves 32.89 dB PSNR and $1.82\times$ at 25% density, and on Wan2.1-14B-T2V/I2V it attains the best PSNR/SSIM and lowest LPIPS among all sparse baselines (source: Tab. video).

3D asset generation. On HY3D-Internal, it achieves a $2.32\times$ speedup at 15% density while reducing the geometric fidelity Chamfer distance from PISA’s 0.976 to 0.177. Vol-IoU-1536 is 82.91 and F1@0.001 is 96.33, the best among those evaluated. In contrast, the compared methods use higher density yet still have broken surfaces and lost detail (source: Tab. 3D, Fig. geo).

Ablation. On Wan2.1-1.3B-T2V (480p), adding, in turn, accurate selection reuse → token-level → query grouping → residual compensation on top of vanilla BSA raises PSNR from 20.96 to 27.05 dB (density 0.2), showing that each component contributes meaningfully. Among them, residual compensation gives the largest gain (+3.54 dB @ s=0.2) (source: Tab. ablation). Interestingly, applying the same residual compensation to vanilla BSA (+1.25 dB) or PISA (+0.49 dB) yields a much smaller gain, meaning that residual compensation only becomes effective when combined with MC-Sparse’s accurate selection and grouping (source: Tab. compensation).

System efficiency. Token-level selection induces irregular memory access, risking a slow kernel, but the token-sparse kernel implemented in CuTeDSL achieves 96–99% of the ideal $1/s$ speed. PISA’s kernel reaches 82–87% and SVG2’s kernel 80–81% (source: Tab. kernel). Fast PDDP reduces the amortized grouping cost by $3.96\times$ at 480p and $6.14\times$ at 720p compared with Flash-KMeans (source: Tab. grouping). The additional cost of anchor steps, when converted to the overall total, is comparable to roughly a 5–6% increase in density (source: §System Efficiency).

Our Perspective: Strengths, Limitations, and Why This Work Matters

Strengths. The most compelling point is that diagnosis → design → implementation form a single line. It separates “why sparse is bad” into three errors through oracle comparisons, attaches components that precisely address each error, and quantifies each component’s contribution through ablations. Being training-free, it does not touch existing model weights, which is highly practical, and its generality is confirmed across the two domains of video and 3D. In particular, achieving “higher PSNR at lower density” is a result that goes beyond a simple speed-quality tradeoff.

Limitations. The parts the authors explicitly acknowledge are limited, but the analysis reveals some points.

  1. Dependence on dense computation at anchor steps. To produce accurate selections and residuals, dense attention must be run at anchor steps. Amortized, this is at the 5–6% level, but even “sparse” does not completely eliminate the dense pass.
  2. Attention stability assumption. The validity of caching rests on the assumption that “attention patterns and residuals are stable across denoising steps.” In segments with abrupt motion onset or scene changes, the reused selection can become stale and degrade quality.
  3. Evaluation scope. It focuses on video and 3D generation, and no extension to other long-sequence workloads such as image generation or autoregressive LLM decoding is shown. Also, HY3D-Internal is an internal model, so those experiments are hard to reproduce externally (source: §Exp, Appx).
  4. Constraints of comparison. Because the PISA kernel did not operate efficiently on the relevant models, the speed was only estimated as an upper bound using the Sol-Attn kernel, and SpargeAttn could not be compared directly for latency because it uses INT8/FP8 (source: Appx. evaluation protocol). The numbers themselves are handled fairly, but it is not a fully controlled comparison.

Why this work matters. Sparse attention is prone to falling into the trap of “losing quality while trying to be fast,” and this paper precisely decomposes where that quality loss comes from, separating whether the room for improvement lies in the structure (blocks), the selection (approximate score), or the residual (tail). This diagnostic framework becomes a useful lens for evaluating any sparse attention method thereafter. On top of that, by also nailing GPU efficiency with tile-aligned grouping (Fast PDDP) and a token-gathering kernel, the key contribution is sidestepping the dilemma between “precise but slow” and “fast but inaccurate.”

What’s Next?: The Road Ahead

The authors do not enumerate specific future work at length in the conclusion. Suggesting reasonable next steps in light of the limitations:

  • Adaptive anchor schedules. Instead of a fixed interval ($\{10,26\}$), measure the rate of attention change in real time to increase reuse in stable segments and add anchors in rapidly changing segments. This can directly capture the segments where the stability assumption breaks.
  • Combination with a trainable indexer. Currently, being training-free is a strength, but attaching a lightweight indexer to approximate the accurate selection could further reduce the dense-computation burden of anchor steps.
  • Domain extension. Application to image generation and autoregressive LLM decoding. In particular, LLM decoding may have attention patterns that change more abruptly between decoding steps, so separate verification is needed for whether the residual stability assumption holds.
  • Reproduction on open models. Replacing the HY3D-Internal experiments with open 3D generation models to secure reproducibility is also a direction that would increase academic impact.
